Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verse 4:

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿How many a town We have destroyed! Our might came upon it by night, or while they were taking their afternoon rest.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is He, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): Warn these worshippers other than Me, and those who set up gods and idols as equals to Me, of My wrath, that I will not let My punishment fall upon them and destroy them, [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "to let My punishment fall upon them", but the context requires what I have established.]] just as I destroyed the nations who followed their way before them. Indeed, I have often destroyed, before them, people of towns who disobeyed Me, denied My messengers, and worshipped other than Me. [[See the explanation of "kam" (how many) above, 5: 352;

= the explanation of "al-qaryah" (town) above, 8: 543;

= and the explanation of "al-ihlak" (destruction) above, 11: 316, note 1, and the references there;

= and the explanation of "al-ba's" (might) above, p. 207, note 2, and the references there.]] = ﴿Our might came upon it by night﴾, meaning: Our punishment and vengeance came upon them at night before they had reached morning [[See the explanation of "al-bayat" (by night) above, 8: 562, 563; 9: 191, 192.]] = "or while they were taking their afternoon rest," meaning: during the day, at the time of the midday rest.

* *

It has been said: "How many" because the intended meaning of the speech is what I have described, the report of the great number of calamities that befell the earlier nations due to their denial of His messengers and their opposition to Him. This is how the Arabs speak when they wish to report a large number, as al-Farazdaq said:

How many an aunt paternal and maternal you have, O Jarir, and a she-camel that milked my tall she-camels...

[[His Diwan: 451; al-Naqa'id: 332. This verse and its explanation have been mentioned earlier in the takhrij of another verse of the poem, 9: 495, 496, note 1.]]

* *

If someone says: God, exalted is His remembrance, only reported that He "destroyed towns." What, then, in His report of destroying "the towns" is evidence that He destroyed their people?

It is said: "The towns" are not called "towns," nor is "the town" called "a town," unless there are dwellings in them for their inhabitants and people living in them. So in destroying them is the destruction of those in them among their people.

* *

Some scholars of Arabic held that the speech takes the form of a report about "the town," while what is meant is its people.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: What we have said about this is more correct, because it agrees with the apparent sense of the recited revelation.

* *

If someone says: How is it said: ﴿How many a town We have destroyed! Our might came upon it by night, or while they were taking their afternoon rest﴾? Is a town destroyed except by the coming of God's might and the descent of His vengeance and wrath upon it? How, then, is it said: "We destroyed it, then Our might came upon it"? And if the coming of God's might upon it was after its destruction, what is the sense of that coming upon a people who had already perished and vanished, and who are unaware of what descends upon them or upon their dwellings?

It is said: There are two interpretations of this, both sound and clear in their method:

The first: that its meaning is: "How many a town We have destroyed," by abandoning them, leaving them to fail to follow what We sent down to them of clear proofs and guidance, and their choosing to follow the command of their leaders who misled them from obedience to their Lord. ﴿Then Our might came upon it﴾ when they did that, ﴿by night, or while they were taking their afternoon rest.﴾ So "God's destruction of them" is His abandoning them from His obedience, and "the coming of God's might upon them" is a recompense for their disobedience to their Lord by His abandoning them.

The second: that "the destruction" is the very "might," so that mention of "the destruction" implies mention of "the coming of might," and mention of "the coming of might" implies mention of "the destruction."

Since that is so, it is the same for the Arabs whether the speech begins with the destruction and then joins the might to it, or begins with the might and then joins the destruction to it. This is like their saying: "You visited me and so you honored me," since "the visit" is "the honor." It is equal to them whether they put "the visit" first and "the honor" after, or put "the honor" first and "the visit" after, saying: "You honored me and so you visited me."  [[See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 371.]]

* *

Some scholars of Arabic claimed that there is an omitted element in the speech, without which the speech would not be sound, and that the meaning is: "How many a town We have destroyed, so that the coming of Our might upon it was before Our destruction." [[This is the view of al-Farra in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 371, where he says: "If you wish, the meaning is: How many a town We have destroyed, and the coming of might was before the destruction, so 'kana' (was) is elided."]] This is a view for which there is no evidence of its soundness from the apparent sense of the revelation, nor from a report that must be accepted. When a statement lacks evidence of its soundness from some of the aspects that must be accepted, its unsoundness is clear.

* *

Another of them also said: The meaning of "fa" (then) in this place is the meaning of "wa" (and). He said: The sense of the speech is: "How many a town We have destroyed, and Our might came upon it by night." This is a view that has no meaning, since "fa" has among the Arabs rulings that "wa" does not have in speech. Directing it to the more common meaning among them, wherever a way to that is found, is more appropriate than directing it to something else.

* *

If someone says: How is it said: ﴿Our might came upon it by night, or while they were taking their afternoon rest﴾, when you know that the usual function of "aw" (or) in speech is to introduce doubt, and it is not permissible that there be doubt in God's report? It is said: The interpretation of that is contrary to what you have suggested. The meaning of the speech is: "How many a town We have destroyed, so that some of them were struck by Our might by night, and some of them while they were taking their afternoon rest." Had "wa" been placed in this position instead of "aw," the speech would have been like an absurdity, and the more common meaning of the speech would have become: that the town which God destroyed was struck by His might by night and at the time of afternoon rest. That would be a report that the might destroyed one who had perished and annihilated one who had vanished, and that is a bad statement. [[Khalf (with a fatha and then a sukun): one says "this is khalf of speech," meaning inferior and worthless; from the proverb: "He stayed silent a thousand times, then spoke a khalf."]] But the sound speech is what the revelation brought, since it did not separate the towns that were struck by might by night from the towns that were struck while they were taking their afternoon rest. Had it been separated, it would only have reported about them with "wa."

It has also been said: "Then Our might came upon it" is a report about "the town," that the might came to it, and the speech is kept in the form in which it began at the start of the verse. Had it been said, "Then Our might came upon them by night," it would have been sound and eloquent, returning the speech to its meaning, since the might was directed at the inhabitants of the town rather than its buildings. Although its buildings and dwellings also received the might in the form of ruin, similar to what its inhabitants received, the speech in His words ﴿or while they were taking their afternoon rest﴾ returned to specifically reporting about its inhabitants rather than its dwellings, for the reason we have described: that the intended target of the might was the inhabitants, even though their destruction included the destruction and ruin of their dwellings. [[See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 371.]]

Had it been said, "or while it was taking its afternoon rest," it would have been sound, since the hearers had understood the intended meaning of the speech.

* *

If someone says: Is not His saying ﴿or while they were taking their afternoon rest﴾ a report about the time of day at which God's might came upon them?

It is said: Yes. If he says: Is it not the case that in the speech of the Arabs, times in such a context are expressed with "wa," which indicates time?

It is said: That is so, but they may omit it in such a position, finding it burdensome to combine two conjunctive particles, since "aw" is among the conjunctive particles for them, [[In the manuscript: "idh kana wa-'indahum min huruf al-'atf" with a blank and "(kadha)" written above it, and "(t)" in the margin. What is in the printed edition is close to correct.]] and likewise "wa." They say: "You met me impoverished, or I was traveling," meaning: "or and I was traveling," omitting the "wa" while intending it in speech, for the reason I have described. [[See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 372.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verse 5:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿So their cry was not, when Our might came upon them, except that they said, "Indeed, we were wrongdoers."﴾

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is He, the One who mentions Himself, says: Their cry, the people of the town We destroyed, when Our might and Our force came upon them by night or while they were napping, was nothing but their admission against themselves that they had been evildoers toward their own souls, sinners against their Lord, and opponents of His command and prohibition. [[See the explanation of the phrase "sinners against their Lord" above, p. 171, note 1, and the references there.]]

* *

By His saying, may His remembrance be exalted, ﴿da'wahum﴾ ("their cry") in this place He means their supplication (du'a').

* *

The word "da'wa" (claim/cry) in the speech of the Arabs has two meanings: the first is supplication (du'a'), and the second is the claiming of a right.

From "da'wa" in the sense of supplication is the saying of God, blessed and exalted: ﴿And that was their cry still﴾ [Surah al-Anbiya': 15]. And from it is the saying of the poet: [[Kuthayyir 'Azza.]]

"And if my leg went numb, I called you, seeking relief / by your calling from its numbness, and it becomes easy."

[[His Diwan 2: 245, in the section of additions; Nihayat al-Arab 2: 125; and Lisan (m-dh-l). "Madhalat rijli" (with fatha and sukun) and "madhalan" (with two fathas): my leg became numb. They used to claim that when a person's leg went numb and he called out the name of someone he loved, its numbness would leave.]]

* *

We have already explained earlier that "al-ba's" and "al-ba'saa'" mean hardship, with evidence proving its soundness, sufficient so that it need not be repeated in this place. [[See the explanation of "al-ba's" above, p. 299, note 3, and the references there.]]

* *

In this verse there is clear evidence for the soundness of what has come down in the report from the Messenger of God ﷺ, his saying: "No people perish until they have been given an excuse from themselves."

* *

Some have interpreted it in this way as well.

14323- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Jarir narrated to us, from Abu Sinan, from Abd al-Malik ibn Maysara al-Zarrad, who said: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: The Messenger of God said: "No people perish until they have been given an excuse from themselves." He (the narrator) said: I said to Abd al-Malik: How does that happen? He said: Then he recited this verse: ﴿So their cry was not, when Our might came upon them﴾, the verse. [[The report 14323: Abd al-Malik ibn Maysara al-Hilali al-Zarrad, trustworthy, related by the group; he is mentioned above under nos. 503, 504, 1326; he died in the second decade of the second century. He did not meet Ibn Mas'ud or any other Companion, so its chain is broken (munqati').

Ibn Kathir mentioned this report in his Tafsir 3: 448, citing al-Tabari, without takhrij. Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur 3: 67, attributing it to no one other than Ibn Abi Hatim.

"A'dhara min nafsihi" means: when it becomes possible to punish him for his sin from himself. The meaning is that they are not destroyed until their sins and defects multiply, so that they are given an excuse from themselves, deserve punishment, and the one who punishes them has justification for inflicting the torment upon them.]]

* *

If someone says: How is it said, ﴿So their cry was not, when Our might came upon them, except that they said, "Indeed, we were wrongdoers"﴾? How could they make that claim when God's might had already come upon them with destruction? Did they say that before destruction? If they said it before destruction, then they said it before the might came, whereas God reports that they said it when it came, not before that. Or did they say it after it came upon them, and that is a state in which they had already perished, so how is it permissible to describe them as saying that when they witnessed God's might, and the reality of what the messengers had threatened them with of God's force?

[[In the manuscript the sentence reads thus: "wa-haqiqatu ma kanat al-rusul ta'iduhum min sattwat Allah wa-laysa kull al-umam", with a waw, and without "qala"; the first editor was right in what he did, though I think there is a lacuna in the speech.]]

It is said: Not all nations were destroyed in a single instant with no interval between its beginning and its end. Rather, some of them were drowned by the flood. Between the first appearance of the cause by which they knew they would perish and its final stage, which encompassed the destruction of all of them, there was a period that is not hidden from anyone of understanding. Others were granted enjoyment of life after the sign of destruction appeared before their eyes for three days, like the people of Salih and their like. Then, when they witnessed the first signs of God's might, with which the messengers of God had threatened them, and became certain of the reality of God's force descending upon them, they called out: ﴿"Woe to us! Indeed, we were wrongdoers"﴾, but their faith did not benefit them, given the coming of God's threat and the descent of His vengeance upon them. Thus our Lord, exalted is His praise, warned those to whom He sent His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ about His might and punishment for their disbelief in Him and their denial of His Messenger, and about what befell those nations before them when they disobeyed His messengers and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verse 6:

The explanation of His words: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: He, may His mention be exalted, says: We will surely question the nations to whom My messengers were sent: "What did you do regarding what the messengers brought you from Me of My command and My prohibition? Did they act upon what I commanded them, and refrain from what I forbade them, and obey My command, or did they disobey Me and oppose that?" ﴿And We will surely question the messengers﴾, meaning: We will surely question the messengers whom I sent to the nations: "Did they convey My messages to them, and deliver to them what I commanded them to deliver, or did they fall short in that, neglecting and not conveying it to them?"

* *

And thus the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have interpreted it.

Mention of those who said that:

14324 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih related to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom He sent messengers, and We will surely question the messengers﴾, he said: Allah will question the people about what they answered the messengers, and will question the messengers about what they conveyed.

14325 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent﴾ up to His words: ﴿absent﴾, he said: The Book will be placed on the Day of Resurrection, and it will speak of what they used to do.

14326 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi regarding: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent and We will surely question the messengers﴾, meaning: We will surely question the nations: "What did they do regarding what the messengers brought?" And We will surely question the messengers: "Did they convey what they were sent with?"

14327 - Al-Harith related to me, saying: 'Abd al-'Aziz related to us, saying: Abu Sa'd al-Madani related to us, saying: Mujahid said regarding: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent﴾, the nations: ﴿and We will surely question those to whom We sent [messengers] about what We entrusted them with: Did they convey?﴾ [[Report 14327: Abu Sa'd al-Madani was mentioned in report no. 14322; I do not know who he is, and I have found no biography of him.]]

Commentary on the interpretation of His saying: ﴿So We will surely relate to them with knowledge, and We were not absent﴾ (7:7)

Abu Ja'far said: May He be exalted in remembrance says: "We will surely inform the messengers and those to whom We sent them with certain knowledge of what they did in the world, concerning what I had commanded them and what I had forbidden them" [[See the explanation of "al-Qasas" above, 9:402 / 12:120]] "and We were not absent," from them and from their deeds which they used to do.

* *

If someone says: How can He question the messengers, when He sent them to the people and He states that He will relate to them with knowledge of their deeds and actions in that matter?

It is said: This questioning from Him, may He be exalted in remembrance, is not a questioning seeking guidance, nor a questioning to learn from them what He does not know. Rather, it is a questioning of rebuke and affirmation, its meaning being a statement, as a man says to another: "Did I not do good to you and you did evil?" and "Did I not join ties with you and you severed them?" Likewise God's questioning of those to whom He was sent, by His saying to them: "Did My messengers not come to you with clear proofs? Did I not send to you warners to warn you of My punishment and My retribution on this day, of those who disbelieved in Me and worshipped other than Me?" As He, majestic is His praise, informed that He will say to them on that day: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan? Indeed he is to you a clear enemy. And that you worship Me; this is a straight path﴾ [Surah Ya-Sin: 60-61], and similar speech whose outward form is that of a question, but whose meaning is a statement and narration, and which is further a rebuke and affirmation.

As for the questioning of the messengers, which is a narration and statement: when the polytheist nations were questioned on the Day of Resurrection, it was said to them: ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you reciting to you the verses of your Lord?﴾ Many of them denied that and said: "There came to us no bringer of good news nor warner." Then it is said to the messengers: "Did you convey what you were sent with?" or it is said to them: "Did you not convey to these people what you were sent with?", as the report has come from the Messenger of God ﷺ, and as He, majestic is His praise, said to the community of our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation that you may be witnesses over mankind, and the Messenger over you a witness﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 143]. So all of that is a questioning from God to the messengers in the manner of calling them as witnesses against the nations to whom they were sent, and to those sent to them in the manner of affirmation and rebuke, and all of that carries the meaning of narration and statement.

As for the questioning which is negated of God, from His creation: it is the questioning which seeks guidance and verification about what the questioner does not know while the one questioned knows it, so that the questioner may learn that knowledge from him. That is impermissible to attribute to God, because He is the Knower of things before they exist, while they exist, and after they exist. This is the questioning which He, majestic is His praise, negated of Himself by His saying: ﴿So on that day none will be questioned about his sin, man or jinn﴾ [Surah al-Rahman: 39], and by His saying: ﴿And the criminals will not be questioned about their sins﴾ [Surah al-Qasas: 78], meaning: no one of them will be questioned about that by one seeking verification, [[In the printed and manuscript texts: "no one of them whom knowledge verifies," which is not correct; the correct reading is what is adopted here.]] so as to learn that knowledge from the one he asks, for He is the Knower of all of that and of everything other than Him.

* *

We have already mentioned what has been related regarding the meaning of this in other places, so we disliked repeating it.

* *

It has been related from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to say, regarding His saying ﴿So We will surely relate to them with knowledge﴾, that their books of deeds will speak to them, recording their deeds against them.

This is a view not far from the truth, but the sound report from the Messenger of God ﷺ is that he said: "None of you will be there but his Lord will speak to him on the Day of Resurrection, with no interpreter between them. He will say to him: 'Do you remember the day when you did such and such and did such and such?' until He reminds him of what he did in the world" [[This report, which al-Tabari authenticated, I did not find in full; I found its opening in the narration of Ibn Khuzaymah, from Abu Khalid 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Aban al-Qurashi, who said: Bashir ibn al-Muhajir narrated to us, from 'Abdullah ibn Buraydah, from his father, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "None of you will be but that God will be alone with him on the Day of Resurrection, with no veil and no interpreter between them" (Hadi al-Arwah 2:108, 109). Al-Haythami cited it in Majma' al-Zawa'id (346) with the wording: "None of you will be but that God, mighty and majestic, will speak to him..." and then said: "Al-Bazzar narrated it, and in its chain is 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Aban, who is abandoned (matruk)." It will come in the commentary on no. 14333.

As for reports with the meaning of this report, they have come with sound chains. Al-Tirmidhi narrated it with this wording in the chapters on the description of the Resurrection, from the hadith of 'Adi ibn Hatim, and said: "This is a hasan sahih hadith."]] — and submission to the report of the Messenger of God ﷺ is more fitting than submission to other than it.

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth; so whoever's scales are heavy, those are the successful﴾ (7:8)

Abu Ja'far said: "al-Wazn" (the weighing) is a verbal noun from the saying of the speaker: "I weighed such-and-such, I weigh it, weighing (wazn) and weight (wiznah)," like: "I promised him, I promise him, a promise (wa'd) and a promise (widah)."

It is in the nominative case, governed by "al-haqq" (the truth), and "al-haqq" is its predicate. [See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an, 1: 373.]

* *

The meaning of the speech is: And the weighing on the Day when We will question those to whom messengers were sent and the messengers themselves is the truth. By "al-haqq" he means justice.

* *

Mujahid used to say that "al-wazn" in this place means judgment.

14328. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "And the weighing on that Day," means judgment.

* *

He also used to say: the meaning of "al-haqq" here is justice.

Mention of the report to that effect:

14329. Ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Mujahid: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾, he said: justice.

* *

Others said: the meaning of His saying: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾ is the weighing of deeds.

Mention of those who said that:

14330. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding His saying: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾, the deeds are weighed.

14331. Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of God: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾, he said: Ubayd ibn Umayr said: A man, tall and large, who eats much and drinks much, will be brought, and he will not weigh the wing of a gnat.

14332. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾, he said: Ubayd ibn Umayr said: A tall, large man will be brought, and he will not weigh the wing of a gnat.

14333. Al-Harith narrated to me, saying: Abd al-Aziz narrated to us, saying: Yusuf ibn Suhayb narrated to us, from Musa, from Bilal ibn Yahya, from Hudhayfah, who said: The one in charge of the scales on the Day of Resurrection is Jibril, peace be upon him. He said: "O Jibril, weigh between them!" So he returns some of them to others. He said: "And there is no gold or silver there." He said: "If the wrongdoer has good deeds, some of his good deeds are taken and returned to the wronged; and if he has no good deeds, some of the sins of his companion are loaded upon him, and the man returns with the weight of mountains." That is His saying: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾.

* *

The interpreters differed regarding the interpretation of His saying: ﴿So whoever's scales are heavy﴾.

Some of them said: its meaning is: whoever's good deeds are many.

Mention of those who said that:

14334. Ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Mujahid: ﴿So whoever's scales are heavy﴾, he said: his good deeds.

* *

Others said: the meaning of that is: whoever's scales are heavy, by which his good and bad deeds are weighed. They said: that is the "scale" (al-mizan) known to people, which has a beam and two pans.

Mention of those who said that:

14335. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: Amr ibn Dinar said to me, regarding His saying: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾: "We see a scale and two pans. I heard Ubayd ibn Umayr say: A tall, large man will be placed on the scale, and then he will not stand even against the wing of a fly."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view in this matter, in my opinion, is the view we have mentioned from Amr ibn Dinar, that this is the known "scale" by which things are weighed, and that God, may His praise be great, weighs the deeds of His creatures, their good and their bad, as He, may His praise be great, said: ﴿So whoever's scales are heavy﴾, the scales of his righteous deed = ﴿those are the successful﴾, meaning: those are the ones who attain success, achieve the fulfilment of their desires, and eternal abiding in the Gardens. [See the explanation of "al-falah" (success) above, p. 130, note 2, and the references there.] This is because of the abundance of reports from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) saying: "Nothing heavier is placed in the scale than good character," [al-Tirmidhi related in his Sunan, in the Book of Righteousness and Kinship, chapter "What has come concerning good character," from Abu al-Darda', who said the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Nothing is heavier in the scale of the believer on the Day of Resurrection than good character, for God dislikes the lewd and foul-mouthed." He then said: "And on this subject, from A'ishah, Abu Hurayrah, Anas, and Usamah ibn Shuraik. This is a good, authentic hadith." al-Suyuti said in al-Durr al-Manthur 3: 71: "It was also related by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, Ibn Hibban, and al-Lalaka'i, from Abu al-Darda'."] and similar reports which confirm that this is a scale by which deeds are weighed, as I have described.

* *

If someone ignorant of the proper direction of the report of God about the scale, and the report of His Messenger (ﷺ) about it, should deny this, and say: "Does God have any need to weigh things, when He knows the measure of everything before He creates it and after, and in every state?" Or he says: "How are deeds weighed, when deeds are not bodies described by heaviness and lightness? Things are only weighed so that their heaviness may be known from their lightness, and their abundance from their scarcity, and that is only possible for things described by heaviness and lightness, abundance and scarcity?"

It is said to him, regarding his saying: "What is the manner of God's weighing of deeds, when He knows their measures before they exist?": Its weighing is like His recording of it in the Mother of the Book and His copying it into the books, without any need on His part for it, and without any fear of forgetting it, for He knows all of that in every state and time, before its existence and after its being; rather, so that it may be a proof against His creatures, as He, may His praise be great, said in His revelation: ﴿Every nation will be called to its record: today you will be recompensed for what you used to do. This is Our record, speaking against you with truth﴾ [Surah al-Jathiyah: 28-29], and so on. Likewise His weighing of His creatures' deeds by the scale is a proof against them and for them, either by their shortcoming in obedience and their neglect, or by their completion and perfection. [This is one of Abu Ja'far's proofs, which demonstrates the subtlety of his insight, the precision of his judgment, the clarity of his exposition, and his ability to hold meanings firmly without wavering. May God reward him for His Book and His religion with the best reward, on the day when every soul is paid in full what it has earned.]

* *

As for the manner in which that is possible, it is as follows:

14336. Musa ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Masruqi narrated to me, saying: Ja'far ibn Awn narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn Ziyad al-Ifriqi narrated to us, from Abd Allah ibn Yazid, from Abd Allah ibn Amr, who said: A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection to the scale, and it will be placed in the pan, and there will be brought out for him ninety-nine registers (sijill), in which are his errors and sins. He said: Then there will be brought out for him a scroll like a fingertip, in which is the testimony that there is no god but God, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger (ﷺ). He said: It will be placed in the pan, and it will outweigh his errors and sins.

* *

Thus is God's weighing of the deeds of His creatures: the servant is placed, and the records of his good deeds in one of the two pans of the scale, and the records of his bad deeds in the other pan, and God, blessed and exalted, causes heaviness and lightness in the pan by which he is more deserving to be weighed, as a proof from God against His creatures, just as He did with many of them: by making their hands and feet speak, as witnesses against them, and similar of His proofs.

And whoever denies this is to be questioned, and it is said to him: God has informed us, may His remembrance be exalted, that He makes the scales of some people heavy on the Day of Resurrection and makes the scales of others light, and the reports from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) have abundantly confirmed this. So what has compelled you to deny that the scale is the one whose description we have given, the one people recognise? Is it an intellectual argument that makes it remote for its soundness to be grasped by reason? And there is nothing in God's weighing His creatures and recording their deeds, in order to make them know the heavier of the two portions by the scale, that departs from wisdom or enters into injustice in a judgment. So what has ruled this out for you, by an intellectual argument or a report? Since there is no way to the truth of saying that what reason does not reject is false, except by one of the two aspects I have mentioned, and there is no way to that. And in the absence of proof for the soundness of his claim from these two aspects, the clear falsity of his statement is evident, and the soundness of what the people of truth have said on this matter is evident.

This is not the place for extensive elaboration on this meaning against one who denies the scale as we have described it, since our purpose in this book is to explain the interpretation of the Qur'an and nothing else. Had it not been so, we would have added similar examples to what we have mentioned, but what we have mentioned is sufficient for one who is granted understanding of it, God willing.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verses 9–10:

The interpretation of His words: ﴿And those whose scales are light — those are the ones who have lost their souls, for they had been wronging Our signs﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His mention be exalted, says: And whoever's scales of good deeds are light, so that they do not weigh heavy through their acknowledgment of God's oneness, their faith in Him and in His Messenger, and their following of His commands and prohibitions — those are the ones who have cheated themselves of their portion of God's abundant reward and His honor (see the explanation of "loss" above, p. 153, footnote 2, and the references there) = ﴿for they had been wronging Our signs﴾, meaning: for they had been denying the proofs and evidences of God, not acknowledging their validity and not being certain of their reality (see the explanation of "wronging" (zulm) above in the lexical indexes, root ẓ-l-m), as in the report:

14337 – Ibn WakI' narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿And whoever's scales are light﴾, he said: "His good deeds."

* *

It has been said that "fa-ulā'ika" and "man" are in the singular form, because their meaning is plural. Had it come in the singular, it would also have been correct and eloquent. [See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:373.]

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿And We had certainly established you in the earth and made for you therein means of living; little do you give thanks﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His mention be exalted, says: And We had certainly settled you, O people, in the earth, and made it for you a place of rest where you settle, and a cradle which you spread out, and a bed which you lay out (see the explanation of "establishing" (makkana) above, vol. 11, p. 263) = ﴿and made for you therein means of living﴾, by which you live throughout your days, [such as] foods and drinks, as a favor from Me to you and a kindness from Me to you = ﴿little do you give thanks﴾, meaning: and little is your thankfulness for these blessings which I have bestowed upon you, while you worship others than Me and take a god other than Me.

* *

"Ma'ayish" is the plural of "ma'ishah."

* *

The readers differed in its recitation.

The majority of the readers of the major cities recited it: ﴿ma'ayisha﴾ without hamza.

Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj recited it as "ma'a'isha" with hamza.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct recitation in this matter, in our view, is ﴿ma'ayisha﴾ without hamza, because it is a "mafa'il" form from the speaker's saying "'ishta, ta'ish" (you lived, you live). Its mim is an added letter, and the ya' is in the rule (of the pattern) mobile, because its singular is "ma'ishah" (maf'alah), whose ya' is mobile; the movement of the ya' from it was transferred to the 'ayn in its singular. When it was made plural, its movement was returned to it, because what precedes it is quiescent and it is itself mobile. The Arabs do likewise with the ya' and waw when what precedes them is quiescent and they are mobile, in analogous plurals that come in the pattern "mafa'il" as we have described. This differs from what comes as a plural in the pattern "fa'a'il," where the ya' is an added letter and not a root letter. For what comes as a plural in this pattern, the Arabs make a hamza, as in their saying "hadhihi madā'in" (these are cities) and "ṣaḥā'if" (pages) and their analogues, because "madā'in" is the plural of "madīnah," and "madīnah" is "fa'īlah" from their saying "madanat al-madīnah," and likewise "ṣaḥā'if" is the plural of "ṣaḥīfah," and "ṣaḥīfah" is "fa'īlah" from your saying "ṣaḥafat al-ṣaḥīfah." So the ya' in its singular is an added, quiescent letter; when it is made plural, a hamza is made, because in the plural it differs from the ya' that was in its singular, since in its singular it was quiescent and in the plural it is mobile. Had you made "madīnah" a "maf'alah" from "dāna yadīnu" and made its plural "mafā'il," the eloquent form would have been to omit the hamza in it and keep the ya' mobile. The Arabs sometimes make a hamza in the plural of "maf'alah" in the roots with ya' and waw, though the eloquent form of their speech is to omit the hamza in it when it comes in the pattern "mafā'il," by analogy of their plural to the plural of "fa'īlah," just as "maf'al" is likened to "fa'īl," so they say "masīl al-mā'" (water-course) from "sāla yasīlu," then make its plural as the plural of "fa'īl," saying "hiya amsilah" in the plural, likening it to the plural of "ba'īr" which is "fa'īl," since they make its plural "ab'irah." Likewise "al-maṣīr," which is "maf'il," is made plural as "muṣrān," likening it to the plural of "ba'īr," which is "fa'īl," since its plural is "bu'rān." [See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:373–374.] On this basis al-A'raj made a hamza in "ma'ayish." That is not the eloquent form in their speech, and the best recitation of God's Book is in the most eloquent and best-known of dialects, not the strangest and most anomalous.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verses 9–10:

The interpretation of His words: ﴿And those whose scales are light — those are the ones who have lost their souls, for they had been wronging Our signs﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His mention be exalted, says: And whoever's scales of good deeds are light, so that they do not weigh heavy through their acknowledgment of God's oneness, their faith in Him and in His Messenger, and their following of His commands and prohibitions — those are the ones who have cheated themselves of their portion of God's abundant reward and His honor (see the explanation of "loss" above, p. 153, footnote 2, and the references there) = ﴿for they had been wronging Our signs﴾, meaning: for they had been denying the proofs and evidences of God, not acknowledging their validity and not being certain of their reality (see the explanation of "wronging" (zulm) above in the lexical indexes, root ẓ-l-m), as in the report:

14337 – Ibn WakI' narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿And whoever's scales are light﴾, he said: "His good deeds."

* *

It has been said that "fa-ulā'ika" and "man" are in the singular form, because their meaning is plural. Had it come in the singular, it would also have been correct and eloquent. [See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:373.]

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿And We had certainly established you in the earth and made for you therein means of living; little do you give thanks﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His mention be exalted, says: And We had certainly settled you, O people, in the earth, and made it for you a place of rest where you settle, and a cradle which you spread out, and a bed which you lay out (see the explanation of "establishing" (makkana) above, vol. 11, p. 263) = ﴿and made for you therein means of living﴾, by which you live throughout your days, [such as] foods and drinks, as a favor from Me to you and a kindness from Me to you = ﴿little do you give thanks﴾, meaning: and little is your thankfulness for these blessings which I have bestowed upon you, while you worship others than Me and take a god other than Me.

* *

"Ma'ayish" is the plural of "ma'ishah."

* *

The readers differed in its recitation.

The majority of the readers of the major cities recited it: ﴿ma'ayisha﴾ without hamza.

Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj recited it as "ma'a'isha" with hamza.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct recitation in this matter, in our view, is ﴿ma'ayisha﴾ without hamza, because it is a "mafa'il" form from the speaker's saying "'ishta, ta'ish" (you lived, you live). Its mim is an added letter, and the ya' is in the rule (of the pattern) mobile, because its singular is "ma'ishah" (maf'alah), whose ya' is mobile; the movement of the ya' from it was transferred to the 'ayn in its singular. When it was made plural, its movement was returned to it, because what precedes it is quiescent and it is itself mobile. The Arabs do likewise with the ya' and waw when what precedes them is quiescent and they are mobile, in analogous plurals that come in the pattern "mafa'il" as we have described. This differs from what comes as a plural in the pattern "fa'a'il," where the ya' is an added letter and not a root letter. For what comes as a plural in this pattern, the Arabs make a hamza, as in their saying "hadhihi madā'in" (these are cities) and "ṣaḥā'if" (pages) and their analogues, because "madā'in" is the plural of "madīnah," and "madīnah" is "fa'īlah" from their saying "madanat al-madīnah," and likewise "ṣaḥā'if" is the plural of "ṣaḥīfah," and "ṣaḥīfah" is "fa'īlah" from your saying "ṣaḥafat al-ṣaḥīfah." So the ya' in its singular is an added, quiescent letter; when it is made plural, a hamza is made, because in the plural it differs from the ya' that was in its singular, since in its singular it was quiescent and in the plural it is mobile. Had you made "madīnah" a "maf'alah" from "dāna yadīnu" and made its plural "mafā'il," the eloquent form would have been to omit the hamza in it and keep the ya' mobile. The Arabs sometimes make a hamza in the plural of "maf'alah" in the roots with ya' and waw, though the eloquent form of their speech is to omit the hamza in it when it comes in the pattern "mafā'il," by analogy of their plural to the plural of "fa'īlah," just as "maf'al" is likened to "fa'īl," so they say "masīl al-mā'" (water-course) from "sāla yasīlu," then make its plural as the plural of "fa'īl," saying "hiya amsilah" in the plural, likening it to the plural of "ba'īr" which is "fa'īl," since they make its plural "ab'irah." Likewise "al-maṣīr," which is "maf'il," is made plural as "muṣrān," likening it to the plural of "ba'īr," which is "fa'īl," since its plural is "bu'rān." [See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:373–374.] On this basis al-A'raj made a hamza in "ma'ayish." That is not the eloquent form in their speech, and the best recitation of God's Book is in the most eloquent and best-known of dialects, not the strangest and most anomalous.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verse 11:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And We did certainly create you and then We gave you form; then We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and they prostrated, except Iblis; he was not among those who prostrated﴾ (7:11).

Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning the interpretation of this.

Some of them said: The interpretation of that: ﴿And We did certainly create you﴾, in the loins of Adam, O people, ﴿then We gave you form﴾, in the wombs of women: a created creation and a shaped likeness in the form of Adam.

Mentioning those who said that:

14338. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And We did certainly create you, then We gave you form﴾: His saying "created you" means Adam; and as for "gave you form," it means his offspring.

14339. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And We did certainly create you, then We gave you form﴾, the verse: He said: As for "created you," it is Adam. As for "gave you form," it is the offspring of Adam after him.

14340. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi': ﴿And We did certainly create you﴾, meaning Adam; ﴿then We gave you form﴾, meaning in the wombs.

14341. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sa'd narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far al-Razi informed us, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas regarding His saying: ﴿And We did certainly create you, then We gave you form﴾, he says: We created you in the creation of Adam, then We gave you form in the bellies of your mothers.

14342. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿And We did certainly create you, then We gave you form﴾, he says: We created Adam, then We gave form to the offspring in the wombs.

14343. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: ﴿And We did certainly create you, then We gave you form﴾, he said: God created Adam from clay; "then We gave you form", in the bellies of your mothers, creation after creation: a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then bones, then He clothed the bones with flesh, then We brought him into being as another creation. [[Note on the isnad: Bishr ibn Mu'adh al-'Aqadi, who has passed several times; this isnad circulates much in tafsir, but here the manuscript and printed edition have "Bishr ibn Adam", which is an error, beyond doubt.]]

14344. Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, who said: God created Adam, then He formed his offspring after him.

14345. Ibn WakI' narrated to us, saying: 'Umar ibn Harun narrated to us, from Nasr ibn Musharis, from al-Dahhak: ﴿created you, then We gave you form﴾, he said: his offspring. [[Note: 'Umar ibn Harun ibn Yazid al-Balkhi, spoken of and criticised, passed under no. 12389. "Nasr ibn Musharis" or "Nasr ibn Mushayrus" is Abu Musallih al-Khurasani, well known by his kunya, likewise passed under no. 12389. The printed edition had "Mushawish" and the manuscript "Mushawis"; the correct reading is what is recorded here.]]

14346. Narrated to me from al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman informed us, from al-Dahhak, regarding His saying: ﴿And We did certainly create you﴾, meaning Adam; ﴿then We gave you form﴾, meaning his offspring.

* * *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is: ﴿And We did certainly create you﴾, in the loins of your fathers, ﴿then We gave you form﴾, in the wombs of your mothers.

Mentioning those who said that:

14347. Ibn WakI' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sharik, from Simak, from 'Ikrimah: ﴿And We did certainly create you, then We gave you form﴾, he said: We created you in the loins of men, and We gave you form in the wombs of women.

14348. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Hammani narrated to us, saying: Sharik narrated to us, from Simak, from 'Ikrimah, the like of it.

14349. Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Mu'ammal narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, saying: I heard al-A'mash recite: ﴿And We did certainly create you, then We gave you form﴾, and he said: We created you in the loins of men, then We gave you form in the wombs of women.

* * *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that: ﴿We created you﴾, meaning Adam; ﴿then We gave you form﴾, meaning: in his back.

Mentioning those who said that:

14350. Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of God: ﴿And We did certainly create you﴾, he said: Adam; ﴿then We gave you form﴾, he said: in the back of Adam.

14351. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿And We did certainly create you, then We gave you form﴾, in the back of Adam.

14352. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid regarding His saying: ﴿And We did certainly create you, then We gave you form﴾, he said: We gave you form in the back of Adam.

14353. Al-Harith narrated to me, saying: 'Abd al-'Aziz narrated to us, saying: Abu Sa'd al-Madani narrated to us, saying: I heard Mujahid regarding His saying: ﴿And We did certainly create you, then We gave you form﴾, he said: in the back of Adam, for what you will arrive at of reward in the Hereafter.

* * *

Others said: The meaning of that: ﴿And We did certainly create you﴾, in the wombs of your mothers, ﴿then We gave you form﴾ in them.

Mentioning those who said that:

14354. Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from one he mentioned, who said: ﴿created you, then We gave you form﴾: God created the human in the womb, then formed him, and split his hearing, his sight and his fingers.

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the sayings is the saying of the one who said: its interpretation: ﴿And We did certainly create you﴾ means: We did certainly create Adam, ﴿then We gave you form﴾ means: by Our giving form to Adam, as we have already explained earlier in the Arabic manner of addressing a person with actions that you attribute to him while the intended meaning is his forefathers, and as He, glorified be His praise, said to those among the believers of the Jews in the time of the Messenger of God: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mount above you: "Take what We have given you with strength"﴾ (2:63). And the like of that is address directed to a living existing people while the intended are their absent predecessors; so likewise in His saying: ﴿And We did certainly create you, then We gave you form﴾, its meaning is: And We did certainly create your father Adam, then We gave him form.

We have said this is the most correct of the sayings on this because what follows it is His saying: ﴿Then We said to the angels: "Prostrate to Adam"﴾, and it is known that God, blessed and exalted, commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam before He formed his offspring in their mothers' wombs, indeed before He created their mothers.

And "thumma" in the speech of the Arabs only comes to indicate the severance of what follows from what precedes it. Such as the speaker's saying: "I stood, then I sat," the sitting cannot be, when joined by "then" to his saying "I stood," except after the standing. And so it is in all speech. Had the conjunction been with "wa" (and), it would be permissible that what follows had been before what precedes, as in the speaker's saying: "I stood and I sat," where it is possible that the sitting in this utterance was before the standing, because "wa" enters speech as a conjunction to require for what follows the same meaning as for what precedes, without any indication in itself that this occurred at one time or at two different times, or, if at two times, which is earlier and which later. Since we have described this, we say that His saying: ﴿And We did certainly create you, then We gave you form﴾ cannot be correctly interpreted except as we have mentioned.

If someone supposes that the Arabs, since they sometimes use "thumma" in place of "wa" out of poetic necessity, as one of them said:

I asked Rabi'ah: who is best of them / in father, then in mother? She said: "Why?" [[I have not identified its speaker.]]

meaning: in father and in mother, then that is permissible to be its like — that supposition is contrary to what he thinks. For the Book of God, glorified be His praise, was revealed in the most eloquent of the Arabic dialects, and it is not permissible to direct any part of it toward the rare of their dialects, while in the most eloquent and most famous usage it has a clear meaning and a known sense.

* * *

Some who had weak knowledge of the Arabic language directed this to being one of the postponed (mu'akhkhar) whose meaning is advanced, and claimed that the meaning is: "And We did certainly create you, then We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam, then We gave you form." This is not permissible in the speech of the Arabs, for they do not place "thumma" in speech intending that it precede what came before it in the report, although they may place it earlier in speech when there is evidence that its meaning is delay, as in their saying: "Stood then 'Abd Allah 'Amr," but when it is said: "'Abd Allah stood, then 'Amr sat," it is not permissible that the sitting of 'Amr occurred except after the standing of 'Abd Allah, if the report is true. So the saying of God, blessed and exalted: ﴿And We did certainly create you, then We gave you form, then We said to the angels: Prostrate﴾ is like the saying of the speaker: "'Abd Allah stood, then 'Amr sat," in that it is not permissible that God's command to the angels to prostrate to Adam occurred except after the creation and the giving of form, for what we have described before.

* * *

As for His saying to the angels: ﴿Prostrate to Adam﴾, He, glorified be His praise, says: When We gave form to Adam and made him a proportioned creation, and breathed into him of Our spirit, We said to the angels: "Prostrate to Adam," as a trial and test from Us for them by the command, so that He might know the obedient among them from the disobedient. ﴿So they prostrated﴾, that is: the angels prostrated, ﴿except Iblis; he was not among those who prostrated﴾ to Adam, when God commanded him together with whoever among the other angels He commanded to prostrate.

* * *

We have already explained earlier the reason for which God, great is His majesty, tested His angels with prostrating to Adam, and the command to Iblis and his account, with what is sufficient to dispense with repeating it in this place.

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿He said, "What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?" He said, "I am better than him; You created me from fire and created him from clay."﴾ (7:12)

Abu Ja'far said: This is a report from God, may His remembrance be exalted, about what He said to Iblis when Iblis disobeyed Him by not prostrating to Adam when He commanded him to prostrate to him. He means: God said to Iblis: ﴿What prevented you﴾, what thing kept you from ﴿prostrating﴾, from abandoning prostration to Adam, ﴿when I commanded you﴾, to prostrate? ﴿He said, "I am better than him"﴾, meaning Iblis said: I am better than Adam, ﴿"You created me from fire and created him from clay."﴾

* *

If someone says: Tell us about Iblis. Was he blamed for prostrating, or for not prostrating? If he was blamed for not prostrating, how was it said to him, ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ And if the rebuke was for prostrating, that contradicts what the revelation brings throughout the Qur'an and what Muslims know! It is said: Iblis was only blamed for his disobedience to his Lord, by abandoning prostration to Adam when He commanded him to prostrate to him.

However, there is disagreement among those knowledgeable in the speech of the Arabs regarding the interpretation (ta'wil, meaning the explanation of the text) of His saying: ﴿What prevented you from not prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ I will begin by mentioning what they said, then mention what is most correct.

Some of the grammarians of Basra said: The meaning is: What prevented you from prostrating? Here "la" (not) is superfluous, as the poet said, whose speaker is unknown:

*His generosity refused, not stinginess, and it hastened him,*
*Yes, from a youth who does not prevent hunger from its killer.* [Source: Lisan al-Arab (nu'm); Amali Ibn al-Shajari 2:228, 231; Sharh Shawahid al-Mughni 217. In the manuscript and printed edition it read "does not prevent hunger," as I have established, and likewise it appears from al-Farisi in Lisan. In other sources its reading is "does not prevent generosity."]

He said: The Arabs explained it as "his generosity refused stinginess," and they made "la" an inserted superfluous particle here, and connected the speech with it. He said: Yunus claimed that Abu 'Amr used to put "stinginess" in the genitive and make "la" attached to it, meaning: his generosity refused the "la" which belongs to stinginess; and he made "la" attached, because "la" can belong to both generosity and stinginess, since if someone said to him, "Withhold the right and do not give to the poor," and he said "la" (no), this would be generosity from him.

* *

Some of the grammarians of Kufa said similarly to what we mentioned from the Basrans regarding its meaning and interpretation, except that he claimed the reason for the entry of "la" in His saying ﴿that you not prostrate﴾ is that at the beginning of the speech there is a negation, meaning His saying ﴿he was not among the prostrators﴾. The Arabs often repeat the negation within speech that contains a negation, for confirmation and emphasis. He said: This is like their saying:

*We have not seen the like of them among a people with black heads, camels with two humps and elephants.* [Source: Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1:176, 374. "Al-fawalij" is the plural of "falij," a two-humped camel brought from Sind for stallion breeding. "Al-fuyul" is the plural of "fil" (elephant).]

So he repeated a negation upon the negation which is "ma," that is "in," and combined them for emphasis.

* *

Another of them said: "La" is not superfluous in this place nor an insertion (silah, meaning an added particle, as previously explained; see the glossary of terms), but "al-man'" (prevention) here means "al-qawl" (saying). The meaning of the speech is: Who said to you, "Do not prostrate when I commanded you to prostrate?" The particle "an" entered the speech because "al-man'" carries the sense of "al-qawl," not its wording, as is done in all speech that resembles saying while differing from it in wording, such as their saying "I called out that you should not stand," and "I swore that you should not sit," and what is similar to that. He said: "Stinginess" is in the genitive for the one who transmitted "his generosity, not stinginess," meaning: the word of stinginess, because "la" is the word of stinginess, so it is as if he said: the word of stinginess.

* *

Some of them said: The meaning of "al-man'" is hindering a person between himself and what he wants. He said: The one who is prevented is compelled toward the opposite of what he was prevented from, like one prevented from standing while wanting to stand; he is compelled from the act toward what is opposite to standing, since the one who chooses the act is the one who has the path to it and to its opposite, so he prefers one over the other and does it. He said: Since the nature of "prevention" is that, and Iblis was addressed with "prevention," saying to him ﴿What prevented you from not prostrating?﴾, the meaning was as if it were said to him: What thing compelled you to not prostrate?

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on this, in my opinion, is to say that there is an ellipsis in the speech, the indication of the apparent meaning being sufficient for it. Its meaning is: What prevented you from prostrating, so that it compelled you to not prostrate? So the mention of "compelled you" was omitted, relying on the listeners' knowledge of His saying ﴿except Iblis, he was not among the prostrators﴾, that this is the meaning of the speech, from its mention. Then His saying ﴿What prevented you﴾ takes effect on "an" as it would have taken effect before "compelled you" if it were manifest, since it has substituted for it.

We said this view is closer to correct because of what has already passed in our earlier argument, that it is impermissible for there to be in the Book of God something without meaning, and that every word has a sound meaning. Thus the corruption of the view of those who said "la" is an insertion with no meaning became clear.

As for the view of those who said the meaning of "al-man'" here is "al-qawl," and that therefore "la" entered with "an": although "al-man'" may be speech and act, the known usage among people is not to use "al-man'" in commanding the abandonment of something, because the one commanded to abandon an act, when he is able to do it and to abandon it, and does it, is not said to have "done it" while being prevented from doing it, except as a strained use of speech. That is because prevention from an act is a barrier placed between him and it, so it is impermissible for him to be doing it while a barrier is placed between him and it, since if that were permissible, it would have to be that he is barred from it and not barred, and prevented and not prevented. [Meaning that he combines both attributes: barred between him and it, and not barred, prevented and not prevented, which is a contradiction.]

Moreover, Iblis did not obey God's command to prostrate to Adam out of arrogance, so how would he obey someone else in abandoning God's command and obedience by abandoning prostration to Adam? So it would be permissible to say to him, "What did someone say to you: Do not prostrate to Adam when I commanded you to prostrate to him?" Rather, its meaning, God willing, is what I said: "What prevented you from prostrating to him so that it compelled you, or drove you out, or forced you to not prostrate to him," as I have explained.

* *

As for His saying ﴿"I am better than him; You created me from fire and created him from clay."﴾ This is a report from God, majestic is His praise, about Iblis's answer to Him when He asked him what prevented him from prostrating to Adam, so that it compelled him to not prostrate to him and forced him to oppose His command and abandon obedience to Him. The reply was that the barrier that prevented him from prostrating, and the motive that drove him to oppose his Lord's command in this, was that he is more powerful than him, stronger in strength, and more excellent than him in excellence, because of the excellence of the element from which he was created, which is fire, over that from which Adam was created, which is clay. The enemy of God was ignorant of the face of truth and erred from the path of correctness. For it is known that the essence of fire is lightness, recklessness, agitation, and rising high. What is in its essence of that is what carried the wicked one, after the wretchedness that God had already decreed for him in the previous Book, to arrogance against prostrating to Adam, and to belittling his Lord's command, so that it brought him ruin and destruction. And it is known that the essence of clay is steadiness, deliberation, forbearance, modesty, and carefulness; and that which is in its essence of that was what called Adam, after the happiness that his Lord had already decreed for him in the previous Book, to repent of his sin, and to ask his Lord for pardon and forgiveness. Therefore al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin used to say: "The first to employ analogy (qiyas, reasoning by analogy) was Iblis," meaning by this faulty analogy, which is this that we have mentioned of the error of his speech, and its distance from hitting the truth, regarding the excellence which God specially gave to Adam over the rest of His creation: that He created him with His own hand, breathed into him from His spirit, made the angels prostrate to him, taught him the names of everything, along with the rest of the honor He specially bestowed on him. The ignorant one disregarded all of that, and aimed to argue that he was created from fire and Adam was created from clay!! [In the printed edition: "that he created him from fire." The manuscript reading is what is here.] And in this he was also unequal, even if Adam had no honor from God, majestic is His remembrance, other than this; so how, when the excellence He specially gave him is abundant in enumeration and wearisome to count?

14355 - Amr ibn Malik narrated to me, saying: Yahya ibn Sulaym al-Ta'ifi narrated to us, from Hisham, from Ibn Sirin, who said: "The first to employ analogy was Iblis, and the sun and moon were not worshipped except through analogies." [Report 14355: Amr ibn Malik al-Rasibi al-Ghubari, Abu 'Uthman al-Basri, the teacher of al-Tabari. Ibn 'Adi said: "He is a rejected narrator from trustworthy narrators, and he steals hadith." Ibn Abi Hatim said: "My father abandoned narrating from him." He is biographed in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/259. Yahya ibn Sulaym al-Ta'ifi is trustworthy; the group narrated from him; he has passed as numbers 4894 and 7831.]

14356 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Kathir narrated to us, from Ibn Shawdhab, from Mutar al-Warraq, from al-Hasan regarding His saying: ﴿You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾, he said: "Iblis analogized, and he was the first to analogize."

* *

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said things in accordance with what we have said on this matter.

Mentioning those who said that:

14357 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umara narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When God created Adam, He said to the angels who were with Iblis specifically, not the angels who were in the heavens: "Prostrate to Adam." So they all prostrated together, except Iblis, who was arrogant, because of what he had been saying to himself, of his pride and self-deception. He said: "I will not prostrate to him, and I am better than him, and older than him, and stronger in creation. You created me from fire and created him from clay!" He means: fire is stronger than clay.

14358 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid regarding His saying: ﴿You created me from fire﴾, he said: "Then He made his descendants from water."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: What this enemy of God said is not an answer to what he was asked about. That is because God, may His remembrance be exalted, said to him: What prevented you from prostrating? He did not answer that what prevented him from prostrating was that he was created from fire and Adam was created from clay [in the printed edition: "that He created him from fire"; the correct reading is in the manuscript], but he began a statement about himself, which contains an indication of the point of the answer, so he said: ﴿I am better than him; You created me from fire and created him from clay.﴾

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿He said, "Then descend from it, for it is not for you to be arrogant therein, so get out; indeed, you are of the debased"﴾ (13)

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His mention be exalted, is meant: God said to Iblis at that moment: ﴿Then descend from it.﴾

We have already explained the meaning of "descent" (al-hubut) earlier, in a way that makes repeating it unnecessary. [[See the explanation of "descent" (al-hubut) above: 1:534, 548; 2:132, 239.]]

* *

= ﴿So it is not for you to be arrogant therein﴾: may His mention be exalted, says: God said to him, "Descend from it," meaning: from the Garden, ﴿so it is not for you﴾, meaning: it is not for you to be proud in the Garden against My obedience and My command.

* *

If someone says: Is it possible for anyone to be arrogant in Paradise? It is said: The meaning of that is contrary to what you have understood. Rather, the meaning is: Descend from the Garden, for no one who is arrogant toward God's command dwells in the Garden. As for other than it, the one arrogant toward God's command may dwell there, and so may the one who humbles himself to His obedience.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿So get out; indeed, you are of the debased﴾, it means: get out of the Garden, for you are among those upon whom God has brought humiliation (al-sighar), abasement and disgrace (al-dhull wa al-mahanah).

* *

It is said from this: "ṣaghira yaṣghar ṣaghaaran wa ṣighaaran wa ṣughraanan," and it has been said: "ṣaghura yaṣghur ṣaghaaran wa ṣaghaarah." [[See the explanation of "al-ṣighar" (humiliation) above: p. 96.]]

* *

And al-Suddi said something similar to that. [[In the printed edition: "wa-bi-naḥw al-ladhi qulna qal al-Suddi," and I have adopted what is in the manuscript.]]

14359- Musa narrated to us, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿So get out; indeed, you are of the debased﴾, and "al-ṣighar" is humiliation.

**Commentary on the Words of Allah Most High (Ta'wil, interpretation): ﴿He said: "Respite me until the day they are raised." (14) He said: "Indeed, you are among those given respite."﴾ (15)**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: This is another of Iblis's wicked ignorances. He asked his Lord for something that he knew no one among Allah's creatures could attain. He asked for respite until the Hour rises, which is the day on which creation is raised. Had he been granted the respite he asked for, he would have been granted eternal life, with no death after it, since there is no death after the resurrection. So Allah, exalted is His praise, said to him: ﴿Indeed, you are among those given respite until the day of the appointed time﴾ [Surah al-Hijr: 37-38; Surah Sad: 80-81]. That is until the day on which Allah has decreed destruction, death, and annihilation for him, because nothing remains and does not perish except our Lord, the Living who does not die. Allah, remembered is His mention, says: ﴿Every soul will taste death﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 185; Surah al-Anbiya': 35; Surah al-'Ankabut: 57].

* *

In the speech of the Arabs, *al-inzar* (respite) means delay. It is said: "I gave him respite regarding his debt (anzartuhu bi-haqqi 'alayhi), I grant him respite, inzaran."[[See the explanation of "al-inzar" in what has passed before: 2:467-468; 3:264; 6:577; 11:267.]]

* *

If someone says: Allah said to him, when he asked for respite until the day they are raised, ﴿You are among those given respite﴾ in this place, so has He not granted him what he asked?

It is said to him: The matter is not so. He would have been granted what he asked only if He had said to him: "You are among those given respite until the time you asked for," or "until the day of resurrection," or "until the day they are raised," or something similar, which indicates that his request for respite had been granted. But as for His saying ﴿You are among those given respite﴾, there is no proof in it, were it not for the other verse in which He specified the duration of the respite up to which He granted it, namely His saying: ﴿So indeed, you are among those given respite until the day of the appointed time﴾ [Surah al-Hijr: 37-38; Surah Sad: 80-81]. This shows the length of the period up to which He granted him respite.[[In the printed edition: "on the period" ; I have kept what is in the manuscript.]] For if He had granted him respite for one day, or less, or more, he would have entered the ranks of those given respite, and Allah's true promise would have been fulfilled regarding him. But He has specified the extent of that period with what we have mentioned, and thus the time up to which he was given respite became known.

* *

Al-Sudi used to say something similar to this.

14360. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Sudi, regarding ﴿He said: "My Lord, respite me until the day they are raised." He said: "Indeed, you are among those given respite. Until the day of the appointed time"﴾ [Surah al-Hijr: 36-38; Surah Sad: 80-81]. He did not grant him respite until the day of resurrection, but granted him respite until the day of the appointed time, which is the day when the first blast is blown into the Horn, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth swoons and dies.[[Narration 14360: Musa ibn Harun al-Hamdani, who has appeared many times before. In the manuscript and printed edition it was "Yunus ibn Harun," which is a plain error, since this is a chain that recurs in the tafsir.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of the speech is: Iblis said to his Lord: "Respite me" (anzirni), that is, delay me, grant me a term, extend my life, and do not cause me to die, "until the day they are raised," meaning until the day creation is raised. Then Allah, remembered is His mention, said: ﴿Indeed, you are among those given respite﴾ until the day the Horn is blown, when whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth swoons, except whom Allah wills.

* *

If someone says: Is there anyone other than Iblis who is given respite until that day, so that it can be said to him, "You are among them"?

It is said: Yes. Everyone whose soul Allah has not taken from among His creatures until that day, from among those upon whom the Hour will rise, is among those given respite by their appointed terms until then. That is why it was said to Iblis: ﴿You are among those given respite﴾, meaning: you are among those whom Allah will not cause to die until that day.
