He also held that the comparison that was made between His words "Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good" and His words "And if a group of you believed" is not a valid comparison. That is because "a group" (ṭāʾifa), in his opinion, is a verbal noun meaning "a phantom" (ṭayf), just as "a shriek" (ṣayḥa) and "a clamor" (ṣiyāḥ) have the same meaning, and for this reason it was said: ﴿And the shriek seized those who had done wrong﴾ [Qur'an 11:67].

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verse 57:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And it is He who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy, until, when they carry heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land, and send down water therefrom, and bring forth with it fruits of every kind. Thus We bring forth the dead; perhaps you will remember.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is His remembrance, says: Indeed your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth, and the sun, the moon and the stars, subjected by His command. It is He who sends the winds *nushran* (as spreaders) before His mercy. [[The reading that Abu Ja'far adopted in the interpretation of the verse is *nushran*, but in the verse I adopt the reading of our own codex, and I will adopt it in all the other places, with the reading of Abu Ja'far with the *nun*.]]

* *

*Al-nashr* (with a *fatha* on the *nun* and a *sukun* on the *shin*) in the speech of the Arabs refers to winds that are pleasant and gentle in their blowing, which produce clouds. Likewise, every pleasant wind among them is *nashr*. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*As if the wine and the falling of the cloud… and the scent of the *khuzama* flower and the *nashr* of the *qutr*.* [[From his Diwan, p. 79, and Lisan al-Arab (n-sh-r), from a long poem of his. This verse is in the description of his beloved, and this verse describes the fragrance of her mouth at dawn, when people's mouths change. He says after it: "Its cold teeth are refreshed by it, when the bird that crows at dawn sings."

*Al-qutr* (with two *damma*s) is the aloe wood by which one fumigates. *Sawb al-ghamam* means its falling where it falls. *Yu'all* means it is given to drink with wine again and again. *Al-ta'ir al-mustahir* is the rooster when it crows before dawn. He describes her by the pleasantness of the scent of her mouth, when mouths change after sleep.]]

* *

Most of the readers of Kufa read it in this way, except 'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, who read it *bushran* (with a *ba'* and its damma, and a *sukun* on the *shin*), according to a difference reported from him.

* *

Some of them narrated from him: *bushran*, with the *ba'* and its *damma* and a *sukun* on the *shin*.

And some: with the *ba'* and its *damma* and the *shin* also with a *damma*.

He interpreted his reading of it in this way by the saying of Allah: ﴿And among His signs is that He sends the winds as bearers of glad tidings﴾ [Surah al-Rum: 46], that they bring glad tidings of rain, and that it is the plural of *bashir* (one who brings glad tidings), which brings glad tidings of rain, pluralized as *bushran*, just as *nadhir* (warner) is pluralized as *nudhran*. [[In the printed edition: "and that it is the plural of *bashir*, *bashran*, just as *nadhir* is pluralized as *nadhran*," and I have adopted what is in the manuscript.]]

* *

As for the readers of Madina and the majority of the Meccans and Basrans, they read it: ﴿And it is He who sends the winds *nushuran*﴾, with a *damma* on the *nun*, and the *shin* with the meaning of the plural of *nashur* (spreader), pluralized as *nushran*, just as *al-sabur* (the patient) is pluralized as *subur*, and *al-shakur* (the grateful) as *shukur*.

* *

Some of the people of knowledge of the speech of the Arabs said: its meaning when it is read in this way is that it is the wind which blows from every direction and comes from every side. [[See Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubayda, 1:217.]]

* *

Some of them said: when it is read with a *damma* on the *nun*, its *shin* must be given a *sukun*, because that is a dialect with the meaning of *al-nashr* with a *fatha*. He said: the Arabs sometimes put a *damma* on the *nun* of *al-nushr* and sometimes a *fatha*, with one meaning. He said: the difference of the readers in this is according to the difference of their dialects in it. He used to say: it is similar to *al-khasf* and *al-khusf* (with a *fatha* and a *damma* on the *kha'*).

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct statement on this matter is to say: the reading of the one who read it as ﴿*nashran*﴾ and ﴿*nushuran*﴾, with a *fatha* on the *nun* and a *sukun* on the *shin*, and with a *damma* on the *nun* and the *shin*, are two well-known readings among the readers of the cities.

.. ... .... ...... ..... ..... ...... ...... ...... ..... ..... ... ... ...... ..... ..... ... ... [[There is undoubtedly a lacuna at the place of these dots, in which he mentioned the reason that he will refer to later. I have not been able to find a transmission from Abu Ja'far that leads to something that fills this gap.]] .

So I do not prefer reading with it, although it has a correct meaning and an understandable aspect in meaning and grammatical analysis (*i'rab*), because of the reason we have mentioned.

* *

As for His saying: "before His mercy," he means: in front of His mercy and before it.

* *

The Arabs similarly say, for anything that happens in front of or before something: "he came between his hands" (*bayn yadayh*), because that is among their speech that occurred in their reports about the children of Adam, and its use became frequent among them, until they said this about other than the son of Adam and that which has no hand. [[See the interpretation of "bayn yadayh" in what has preceded, 6:160, 438.]]

* *

The "mercy" that He, may His praise be exalted, mentioned in this place is the rain.

* *

So the meaning of the speech, then: And Allah is the one who sends the winds, gentle in their blowing and pleasant in their breeze, before His rain, which He drives by them to His creation, so that by them He produces heavy clouds, until when they carry them, — and *al-iqlal* with them is carrying them, as one says: "the camel rose with its load" (*istaqalla*) and "lifted it" (*aqalla*), when he carries it and stands up with it — He drives them, Allah, to give life to a dead land, whose fields have become desolate, whose watering places have been effaced, and whose people have become barren, so He sends down rain upon it, and brings forth with it all kinds of fruits.

* *

The people of interpretation have said in accordance with what we have said in this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

14782 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿And it is He who sends the winds as spreaders before His mercy﴾ to His saying: ﴿perhaps you will remember﴾. He said: Indeed Allah sends the wind, and it brings the clouds from between the two horizons, the edge of the sky and the earth from where they meet, and He brings it out from there, then He spreads it and extends it in the sky as He wills, then He opens the gates of the sky, and the water flows over the clouds, then the clouds rain after that. As for "His mercy," it is the rain.

* *

As for His saying: "Thus We bring forth the dead; perhaps you will remember," He, exalted is His remembrance, says: Just as We give life to this dead land by what We send down of water which We send down from the clouds, and We bring forth from it fruits after its death and dryness and the barrenness of its people, so We bring forth the dead from their graves, alive, after their perishing and the effacement of their traces, "perhaps you will remember." Exalted is His remembrance, says to the polytheists who worship idols, who deny the resurrection after death, who reject reward and punishment: I have struck for you, O people, this parable that I have mentioned to you, of the revival of the dead land by the drops of rain which the cloud brings, which the winds spread, whose attributes I have described, so that you may take heed, and remember, and know that the one who has this power, it is easy within His power to revive the dead after their perishing, and to restore them as a proper creation after their effacement. [[See the interpretation of "remembrance" in what has preceded, p. 299, footnote 1, and the references there.]]

* *

The people of interpretation have said in accordance with what we have said in this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

14783 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding His saying: "Thus We bring forth the dead; perhaps you will remember": Thus you will be brought forth, and thus is the resurrection (*nushur*), just as We bring forth the crops by water.

* *

14784 - Abu Hurayra said: Indeed, when people die at the first blast, rain will fall upon them from water beneath the Throne called "the water of life" for forty years, and they will grow as plants grow from water. Until their bodies are complete, the spirit is blown into them, then a sleep is cast upon them, and they sleep in their graves. When the Trumpet is blown a second time, they will live, and they will find the taste of sleep in their heads and eyes, as the sleeper finds when he wakes from his sleep. At that point they will say: ﴿O woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place?﴾ The caller will call out to them: ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke truly﴾ [Surah Ya-Sin: 52]. [[The report: 14784 - This report from Abu Hurayra was transmitted without a chain of narration, and I used to think it was from al-Suddi's narration in the previous report, but I doubted that, so I preferred to give it a separate number. In any case, I have not found the text of this report in any of my sources. The hadith of Abu Hurayra about resurrection was narrated by Muslim in his Sahih, 18:91, who said:

"The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Between the two blasts is forty. They said: O Abu Hurayra, forty days? He said: I refuse. They said: forty months? He said: I refuse. They said: forty years? He said: I refuse. Then Allah will send down water from the sky, and they will sprout as herbs sprout. There is nothing of the human being that does not decay, except one bone, which is the coccyx, and from it the creation will be reassembled on the Day of Resurrection."]]

* *

14785 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the words of Allah: "Thus We bring forth the dead," he said: When Allah wants to bring forth the dead, He sends rain upon the sky until the earth splits open for them, then He sends the spirits, and each spirit returns to its body. Thus Allah gives life to the dead by rain, as His giving life to the earth.

The commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 7, verse 58:

On the exegesis (ta'wil) of His words: ﴿The good land - its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord, and that which is bad comes forth only sparsely. Thus do We vary the signs for a people who give thanks.﴾ (7:58)

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The Exalted says: "The good land," whose soil is good and whose water is sweet, "its vegetation comes forth" when God sends down rain and its abundant showers fall upon it, "by His permission," with its fruit good in its season and its time. "And that which is bad," whose soil is corrupted and whose water is salty, "does not bring forth its vegetation except sparsely" - that is, "except with difficulty and hardship," as the poet said: [[I do not know who the poet is.]]

*"He does not fulfil the promise, if he promises, and if he gives, he gives something trivial and meagre."* [[Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubayda, 1:217, and Lisan al-Arab (tafh).]]

By "al-tafih" (trivial) is meant little, and by "al-nakad" is meant hardship. It is said of it: "nakida yankadu nakadan, nakdan" - so he is "nakad" and "nakid," and "al-nukd" is the verbal noun. Among their proverbs: "nakdan wa jahdan" and "nukdan wa juhdan." "Al-juhd" means severity and constriction. It is said: "When a man is pressed (shuffiha) and asked [[shuffiha al-rajul," in the passive, means when people's requests to him increase, so he gives until what he has is exhausted and his wealth is destroyed. He is "mashfuh." Similar to it are "mankud," "mathmud," "ma'ruk," "ma'jūz," "masfūf," and "makthūr 'alayh." It is said: "ma' mashfuh," meaning water much drunk from, and likewise water and food.]] They have "nakadūhu, yankadūnahu, nakdan," as the poet said: [[I do not know who the poet is.]]

*"Give what you have given, in goodness; there is no good in the one who is harmed (mankud) or the one who is afflicted (nakid)."* [[Lisan al-Arab (nakad), and I have already cited this verse above, 1:442, note 1.]]

* * *

The readers differed regarding the recitation of this.

Some of the people of Medina recited it: ﴿إلا نَكَدًا﴾ (illa nakadan), with a fatha on the kaf.

* * *

Some of the Kufans recited it with a sukun on the kaf: ﴿نَكْدًا﴾ (nakdan).

* * *

Apart from these two, the rest of the readers in the cities differed from them and recited it: ﴿إلا نَكِدًا﴾ (illa nakidan), with a kasra on the kaf.

* * *

It seems that whoever recited "nakadan" with a fatha on the kaf intended the verbal noun.

And it seems that whoever recited it with a sukun on the kaf intended the kasra but made it sukun, according to the dialect of those who say "hadhihi fakhdh wa kibd" (this is a thigh and a liver). Whoever wanted that should, by analogy, have vocalized the nun of "nakad" with a kasra.

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct recitation in this matter, in our view, is the recitation of the one who recited ﴿نَكِدًا﴾ with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the kaf, due to the consensus (ijma') of the authoritative readers of the cities upon it.

* * *

As for His words: "Thus do We vary the signs for a people who give thanks," He means: Thus do We make clear one sign after another, and We bring forth one proof after another, and We strike one parable after another, for a people who give thanks to God for His favour upon them in guiding them, and in making clear to them the path of the people of misguidance, by their following what He commanded them to follow, and their avoiding what He commanded them to avoid of the paths of misguidance. This is a parable which God struck for the believer and the disbeliever: the good land whose vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord is a parable for the believer, and that which is bad, whose vegetation comes forth only sparsely, is a parable for the disbeliever.

* * *

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said something similar to what we have said regarding this.

Those who said that:

14786 - Al-Mathna narrated to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: "The good land - its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord, and that which is bad does not come forth except sparsely." He said: This is a parable which God struck for the believer. He says: He is good, and his deed is good, just as the good land's fruit is good. Then He struck the parable of the disbeliever as the salty, brackish land from which seepage (nazz) comes forth [[In the printed edition: "from which the blessing (al-barakah) comes forth," with an added "la" which is not in the manuscript, following what is in al-Durr (3:93). In the manuscript, similarly, the copyist wrote "al-nazlah" without dots, which is not understood if read as "the blessing comes forth from it." The description of "al-sabakhah" land is that it is land with salt and seepage, which is water that the earth exudes, so it becomes pools. For this reason it has become more probable to me that what I have established is correct, and that what is in the manuscript is an error of the copyist.]] So the disbeliever is the bad one, and his deed is bad.

14787 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding God's words: "The good land" and "that which is bad." He said: All of that, from salt-marshes and other lands, is like Adam and his offspring: among them there is good and bad.

14788 - Al-Mathna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly.

14789 - Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada: "The good land - its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord, and that which is bad does not come forth except sparsely." He said: This is a parable which God struck for the disbeliever and the believer.

14790 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad - meaning Ibn al-Mufaddal - narrated to me, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "The good land - its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord, and that which is bad" - it is the salt-marsh whose vegetation does not come forth except sparsely. And "al-nakad" is the little thing that is of no benefit. Thus with hearts when the Qur'an was sent down: the believing heart, when the Qur'an entered it, believed in it and faith was established in it, and the disbelieving heart, when the Qur'an entered it, did not take hold of anything that would benefit it, and there was not established in it of faith anything except what is of no benefit, just as this land brings forth only what is of no benefit of vegetation.

14791 - Al-Harith narrated to me, saying: Abd al-Aziz narrated to us, saying: Abu Sa'd narrated to us, from Mujahid: "The good land - its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord, and that which is bad does not come forth except sparsely." He said: The good land - rain benefits it and it grows, and "that which is bad" is the salt-marsh, which rain does not benefit; its vegetation does not come forth except sparsely. He said: This is a parable which God struck for Adam and all his offspring, for they were only created from a single soul. Among them is the one who believed in God and His Book, and he became good; and among them is the one who disbelieved in God and His Book, and he became bad.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verse 59:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah to his people, and he said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day."﴾

Abu Ja'far said: Our Lord, glorified is His praise, swears to those addressed by this verse that He sent Noah to his people, warning them of His punishment and frightening them with His wrath for their worship of other than Him. He said to those among them who disbelieved: "O my people, worship Allah, to whom worship is due, submit to Him in obedience, and humble yourselves before Him in lowliness, and abandon the worship of what is other than Him of rivals and deities, for there is no deity for you deserving of worship other than Him. Indeed, I fear for you, if you do not do that, ﴿the punishment of a tremendous day﴾," meaning: the punishment of a day in which your affliction will be great by its coming upon you with the wrath of your Lord.

* *

The reciters have differed concerning the reading of His saying "ghayrihi" (other than Him).

Some of the people of Medina and Kufa read it: ﴿mā lakum min ilāhin ghayrihi﴾, with the genitive "ghayr" (ghayrihi, "other than Him") as a qualifier of "ilāh" (deity).

* *

Others among the people of Medina, Basra and Kufa read it: ﴿mā lakum min ilāhin ghayruhu﴾, with the nominative "ghayr" (ghayruhu), taking it back to the position of "min" (min, the preposition), since its position is nominative: if you removed it from the sentence, the sentence would still be nominative, and it is said: "You have no deity other than Allah" (mā lakum ilāhun ghayru Allāh). [[See Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1: 382, 383.]] The Arabs, [since what is described by the speech] [[The phrasing is as it appears in the printed and manuscript texts; there is undoubtedly a lacuna in the sentence which I was unable to restore to its original form, and so I have placed this phrase between brackets. The lacuna appears to be lengthy, since Abu Ja'far here departs from his usual practice in this context of mentioning the more correct of the two readings.]] they insert "min" into it or omit it, and sometimes they include it in such speech and sometimes omit it, returning what the noun is described with to the wording of the noun on which it operates. When one reads it with the genitive, it is one continuous statement, since it qualifies "ilāh." When one reads it with the nominative, it is two statements: "mā lakum ghayruhu min ilāh" (you have no other deity besides Him), and this is a view that the grammarians consider weak.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verse 60:

The exposition of His saying: ﴿The eminent ones (al-mala') among his people said, "Indeed, we see you in manifest error."﴾

Abu Ja'far said: This is an account from God, may His praise be exalted, concerning the reply of the polytheists of the people of Noah to Noah, and they are "al-mala'" (the eminent ones; the assembly of men, with no women among them) [[See the explanation of "al-mala'" above, 5:291, where it was explained according to what the lexicographers explained: that they are the notables, leaders and nobles of the people. As for the explanation given here, it has not been reported there, and it is something that should be qualified. This is the text of al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:383.]] = that they said to him when he invited them to worship God alone, without partner: "Indeed, we see you," O Noah, "in manifest error," [[See the explanation of "al-dalal" (error) and "mubin" (manifest) above in the lexical indexes under (d-l-l) and (b-y-n).]] meaning: in a matter that has departed from the truth, its departure from the aim of truth being clear to anyone who considers it.

[[In the printed edition: "ʿan qasd al-hadd" (from the aim of the limit), which has no meaning. In the manuscript the writing is poor, and this is the correct reading of it. See the explanation of the following verse.]]

The commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 7, verses 61–62:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿He said: "O my people, there is no misguidance in me, but I am a Messenger from the Lord of the worlds"﴾ (61)

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The Exalted says: Noah said to his people, responding to them: "O my people, I did not command you with what I have commanded you, namely the sincere monotheism of God and devoting worship to Him alone, to the exclusion of rivals and deities, out of any deviation on my part from the path of truth or straying from the way of what is right. There is no misguidance in me of the kind you suppose. Rather, I am a messenger to you from the Lord of the worlds, with what I have commanded you: devoting worship to Him alone, affirming His oneness, and disavowing rivals and deities."

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I give you sound advice, and I know from God what you do not know﴾ (62)

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: This is a report from God, may His praise be mentioned, concerning His prophet Noah, peace be upon him, that he said to his people who disbelieved in God and denied him: ﴿But I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds﴾, sent to you. So I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I give you sound advice in my warning you of God's punishment for your disbelief in Him, your denial of me, and your rejection of my counsel. ﴿And I know from God what you do not know﴾, namely that His punishment will not be turned back from the wrongdoing people.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verse 63:

On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, so that he may warn you, and that you may fear God, and that perhaps you may receive mercy?﴾ (63)

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: This is also a report from God, exalted is His mention, about what Noah said to his people, when they rejected his counsel concerning God and denied that God had sent him as a prophet, and said to him: ﴿We see you only as a human like ourselves, and we see none following you except those who are the lowest of us in judgment at first glance, and we see in you no superiority over us; rather, we think you are liars.﴾ [Surah Hud: 27] He said: "Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you" — meaning: do you wonder that there has come to you a admonition and exhortation from God, reminding you of what your Lord has sent down; "through a man from among you" — it was said that the meaning of His saying "through a man from among you" is "together with a man from among you" [see al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 383]; "so that he may warn you" — meaning: so that he may warn you of God's punishment and threaten you with His retribution for your disbelief in Him; "and that you may fear God" — meaning: so that you may fear God's punishment and His retribution, by affirming His oneness and sincerely believing in Him, and acting in obedience to Him; "and that perhaps you may receive mercy" — meaning: and that your Lord may show you mercy if you fear God, and dread Him, and beware of His retribution.

* *

The "wa" (و) in His saying "awa ʿajibtum" was given a fatḥah (vowel), because it is a conjunctive wāw (wāw of ʿaṭf) to which the interrogative alif has been prefixed. [see al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 383.]

**The meaning of His words: ﴿So they denied him, and We saved him and those with him in the ship, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. Indeed, they were a blind people.﴾ (7:64)**

Abu Ja'far said: Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: His people denied Nuh when he informed them that he was a messenger of Allah to them, commanding them to renounce rivals (al-andad) and to affirm the oneness of Allah and to act in obedience to Him. They opposed the command of their Lord and persisted in their rebellion, wandering blindly. So Allah saved him in the ship, along with those who were with him of the believers. With Nuh, peace be upon him, there were ten souls.[[The manuscript has what I have recorded, but the editor of the printed edition took it upon himself to write "with Nuh, peace be upon him, there were thirteen," which is a faulty alteration. The report of Ibn Ishaq on this matter will come in the commentary on Surah Hud (12:26, Bulaq edition), where it says: "They were ten persons with Nuh, his sons and their wives." Nuh and his sons were four, and six people, which makes ten. As for the wives, he did not include them in the count, as you can see, and he meant only the number of men, not women.]] Concerning this:

14792 - Ibn Humayd narrated to me, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq: Nuh, and his three sons Sam, Ham and Yafith, and their wives, and six people of those who had believed in him.

* *

He took with him in the ship of every kind two of each, as Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And none believed with him except a few﴾ (11:40).

* *

And "al-Fulk" is the ship.

* *

"And We drowned those who denied Our signs": He says, Allah drowned those who denied His proofs, who did not follow His messengers and did not accept their counsel concerning Allah, by the flood.

"Indeed, they were a blind people": He says, blind to the truth. As follows:

14793 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the words of Allah "blind": he said, "blind to the truth."

14794 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words "a blind people": he said, "Al-'Ama, the one who is blind to the truth." [[See the explanation of "al-'ama" (blindness) above, 11:372, footnote 1, and the references there.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 7, verses 65–67:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And to ʿĀd [We sent] their brother Hūd. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. Will you not then fear Him?"﴾ (7:65)

Abu Jaʿfar said: The Exalted says: "And We certainly sent to ʿĀd their brother Hūd." The word "Hūd" is in the accusative case because it is conjoined (maʿṭūf) to "Nūḥ," peace be upon them both. Hūd said: "O my people, worship Allah," so single Him out in worship, "and do not associate with Him any other deity, for there is no deity for you other than Him," "Will you not then fear" your Lord, "so that you beware of Him and fear His punishment by worshipping other than Him, when He is your Creator and your Provider, apart from all that is other than Him."

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿The eminent ones who disbelieved among his people said, "Indeed, we see you in foolishness, and indeed, we think you are among the liars." He said, "O my people, there is no foolishness in me, but I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds."﴾ (7:66–67)

Abu Jaʿfar said: The Exalted says, reporting what his people who disbelieved in Allah answered Hūd with: "The eminent ones who disbelieved," meaning those who denied the oneness of Allah and rejected His messengership to them. [[See the explanation of "al-Malaʾ" (the eminent ones/chiefs) above, p. 499, note 3, and the references there.]]

"Indeed, we see you, O Hūd, in foolishness," meaning: in error, away from the truth and rightness, by your abandoning our religion and worship of our deities. [[See the explanation of "al-Safāha" (foolishness) above, p. 153, note 4, and the references there.]] "And indeed, we think you are among the liars" in your saying, "Indeed, I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds." He said: "O my people, there is no foolishness in me," meaning: no error away from truth and rightness. "But I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds," who has sent me, so I convey to you the messages of my Lord and deliver them to you as He commanded me to deliver them.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verses 68–69 (part 1 of 3):

The explanation of His saying: ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I am a sincere and trustworthy adviser to you. (68) Are you surprised that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, so that he may warn you? And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah, and increased you in stature and bodily strength. So remember the favours of God, that you may prosper.﴾ (69)

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, "I convey to you the messages of my Lord," he means: I deliver them to you, O people [[See the explanation of "al-balagh" (conveying) above, 10:575 / 11:9.]]. "And I am a sincere adviser to you" means: and in my command to you to worship God alone, rather than the rivals and deities besides Him, and in my calling you to believe what I have brought you from God, I am a sincere adviser to you. So accept my counsel, for I am trustworthy regarding the revelation of God and regarding what God has entrusted me with of the message. I do not lie in it, add to it, or alter it; rather, I convey what I have been commanded, as I have been commanded. "Are you surprised that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, so that he may warn you?" means: Are you astonished that God has sent down His revelation, to remind and admonish you, through a man from among you, concerning your state of error in which you remain, so that he may warn you of God's punishment and frighten you with His retribution? [[See the explanation of a similar verse above, p. 501.]] "And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah" means: Fear God regarding yourselves, and remember what befell the people of Noah of punishment when they disobeyed their messenger and disbelieved in their Lord. Indeed, your Lord made you successors in the earth after them; when He destroyed them, He replaced them with you in it [[See the explanation of "khalifah" (successor) above, 1:449 / 12:288.]]. So fear God lest there befall you the like of the punishment that befell them, and He destroy you and replace you with others, in keeping with His practice regarding the people of Noah before you, for your disobedience to Him and your disbelief in Him. "And increased you in stature" means: He increased your bodies in height and largeness over the bodies of the people of Noah [[See the explanation of "bastah" (expansion) above, 5:313.]], "and in strength over their strength" [[In the printed edition: "qawāmakum 'alā qawāmihim," which is an error; the correct reading is what is in the manuscript.]], as a favour from Him upon you. So remember His favours and His bounty by which He preferred you over them in your bodies and your strength [[In the printed edition also: "wa-qawāmakum"; the correct reading is from the manuscript.]], and thank God for that by sincerely worshipping Him, abandoning associating others with Him, and forsaking idols and rivals. "That you may prosper" means: so that you may prosper, attaining eternal life and abiding in blessings in the Hereafter, and succeed in your requests from Him. [[See the explanation of "al-falah" (prosperity) above, p. 312, note 1, and the references there.]]

* *

In the same sense as what we have said regarding the interpretation of His saying, "And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah," the people of interpretation (ta'wil) said:

Those who said that:

14795 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah": he means: He destroyed the people of Noah and made you successors after them.

14796 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq: "And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah": i.e., inhabitants of the earth after the people of Noah.

* *

In the same sense as what we have said, they also said regarding His saying, "bastah" (expansion):

Those who said that:

14797 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And increased you in stature": he said: [in strength] like the strength of the people of 'Ad. [[In the printed edition: "li-qawām qawm 'Ād," and the correct reading is what is in the manuscript.]]

* *

As for "al-ala'" (favours), it is a plural whose singular is "ilan" (with a kasrah on the alif), in the pattern of "mi'an," and it is said "alan" (with a fathah on the alif) in the pattern of "qafan." And it has been transmitted from the Arabs as "ilj" like "hisy." "Al-ala'" means blessings.

* *

Likewise the people of interpretation said:

Those who said that:

14798 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: "So remember the favours of God": i.e., the blessings of God.

14799 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: As for "the favours of God," they are the blessings of God.

14800 – Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: "So remember the favours of God," he said: His favours are His blessings.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: As for "'Ad," these are the people whose description God mentioned, and to whom He sent Hud, calling them to the oneness of God and to following what he brought them from Him. Regarding them, it is reported:

14801 – Ibn Humayd narrated this to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq: The descendants of 'Ad ibn Iram ibn 'Awṣ ibn Sam ibn Noah.

* *

Their dwellings were al-Shihr, in the land of Yemen, and the regions adjoining Hadramawt up to 'Uman, as reported:

14802 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: That 'Ad was a people who lived in Yemen, in al-Ahqaf.

14803 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sa'id al-Khuza'i, from Abu al-Tufayl 'Amir ibn Wathilah, who said: I heard 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) say to a man from Hadramawt: "Have you seen a reddish sand dune mixed with red clay [["al-madarah" is clay that is sticky and has no sand in it.]], with arak and much sidr (lote) trees in such-and-such a region of the land of Hadramawt? [["al-Arak" and "al-Sidr" are plants.]] Have you seen it?" He said: "Yes, O Commander of the Faithful! By God, you describe it as one who has seen it!" He said: "No, but I have been told about it." The Hadrami said: "What about it, O Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "In it is the grave of Hud, may God's blessings be upon him." [[Report 14803: "Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sa'id al-Khuza'i" was biographed by al-Bukhari in al-Kabir 1/1/135, who related the report, in a similar but longer form, and mentioned no criticism of him. Also Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/297.
"Abu al-Tufayl," "'Amir ibn Wathilah al-Kinani," saw the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was a youth; his seeing the Messenger of God is established, but his hearing from him is not established. They said he was the last of the Companions to die, in the year 100 or after.]]

14804 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: The dwellings of 'Ad and their community, when God sent Hud among them, were al-Ahqaf. He said: "Al-Ahqaf" means the sand, the area between 'Uman and Hadramawt, and all of Yemen. [[In the printed edition: "bi-l-Yaman," omitting "kullahu"; I have restored what is in the manuscript.]] They, moreover, had spread throughout the whole earth, and subdued its inhabitants through the excess of the strength that God had given them. They were worshippers of idols besides God: an idol called "Sada'," an idol called "Samud," and an idol called "al-Haba'." So God sent to them Hud, who was of the most central of them in lineage and the most excellent in position. He commanded them to worship God alone and not to set up any other god alongside Him, and to refrain from wronging people. He did not command them, as is reported, and God knows best, in anything other than that. But they refused him and denied him, and said: "Who is stronger than us in power!" Some of them followed him, but they were few, concealing their faith. Among those who believed in him and affirmed him was a man of 'Ad called "Murthid ibn Sa'd ibn 'Ufayr," who concealed his faith. [[In the printed edition: "yaktumūn īmānahum"; I have restored what is in the manuscript.]] When they transgressed against God, may He be blessed and exalted, and denied their Prophet, and multiplied corruption in the earth, and became tyrannical, and built on every high place a landmark in vain, without benefit, Hud addressed them, saying: ﴿Do you build on every high place a monument, playing? And you take fortresses, perhaps you will abide forever? And when you strike, you strike as tyrants. So fear God and obey me.﴾ [Surah al-Shu'ara: 128–131]. They said: ﴿O Hud, you have brought us no clear proof, and we will not abandon our gods on your word, nor will we believe in you. We say only that some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾ — meaning: what you have brought us is nothing but madness that some of these gods of ours, whom you revile, have afflicted you with. ﴿He said: "I call God to witness, and bear witness yourselves that I am free of what you associate besides Him. So plot against me all together, then give me no respite. Indeed, I have put my trust in God, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path"﴾ [Surah Hud: 53–56], up to His saying: ﴿on a straight path﴾. When they did that, God withheld the rain from the sky from them for three years, so it is claimed, until that hardship afflicted them. In that time, when affliction or hardship befell people and they sought relief from God, they would make their petition to God at His Sacred House in Mecca, Muslim and polytheist alike; so many people of various and differing religions would gather in Mecca, and all of them would revere Mecca, knowing its sanctity and its place with God.

= Ibn Ishaq said: The House in that time was known in its location, and the sanctuary (haram) was standing, as they report. The people of Mecca at that time were the 'Amaliq [[They were named "'Amaliq" because their forefather was "'Amlik ibn Lawdh ibn Sam ibn Noah."]]. The chief of the 'Amaliq at that time in Mecca, it is claimed, was a man called Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr. His father was still alive at that time, but he had grown old, and his son led his people. Leadership and nobility among the 'Amaliq, it is claimed, belonged to the people of that House. The mother of Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr was Kalhadah, daughter of al-Khaybari, a man of 'Ad. When the rain was withheld from 'Ad and they were afflicted, they said: "Send from among you a delegation to Mecca, so that they may seek rain for you, for you are surely destroyed!" So they dispatched Qayl ibn 'Anz [[In the printed edition: "ibn 'Anz"; in the manuscript: "'Atar"; in the History: "'Athar," and later in the History: "'Anz."]] and Luqaym ibn Hazzal ibn Hazil [[In the printed edition: "min Hudhayl"; I have restored what is in the manuscript, which agrees with the History of al-Tabari.]] and 'Utayl ibn Sadd ibn 'Ad al-Akbar [[In the printed edition: "wa-'Aqil ibn Sadd"; I have restored what is in the manuscript, agreeing with the History, though what is in the History reads: "wa-Luqaym ibn Hazzal ibn Hazil ibn 'Utayl ibn Dadd ..." with "Dadd" spelled with a dad, and I think the sad is more correct.]] and Murthid ibn Sa'd ibn 'Ufayr, who was a Muslim concealing his Islam, and Juhaymah ibn al-Khaybari, the maternal uncle of Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr, his mother's brother. Then they sent Luqman ibn 'Ad ibn so-and-so ibn so-and-so ibn Sadd ibn 'Ad al-Akbar. So each man of these people set out with a company of his folk, until the number of their delegation reached seventy men. When they came to Mecca, they stayed with Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr, who was outside Mecca, outside the sanctuary, and he hosted them and honoured them, for they were his maternal relatives and in-laws. [[In the printed edition: "wa-asbāruh"; I have restored what is in the manuscript, which agrees with the History.]]

= When the delegation of 'Ad stayed with Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr, they remained with him for a month, drinking wine, while two singing-girls, al-Jaradatan (the two locusts), who were Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr's slave-girls, sang to them. Their journey had lasted a month, and their stay was a month. When Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr saw how long they stayed, and that their people had sent them to seek refuge with them from the affliction that had befallen them [[In the printed edition and History: "yatghawwathūn" (seeking relief); in the manuscript: "yata'awwadhūn" (seeking refuge), unpointed, which is correct, so I have adopted it.]], it grieved him, and he said: "My maternal relatives and in-laws are destroyed! And these are staying with me, my guests, lodging with me! By God, I do not know what to do with them! I am ashamed to order them to leave for what they were sent for [[In the printed edition: "in amartuhum bi-l-khurūj"; in the manuscript: "in āmuruhum bi-l-khurūj," so it is clear that a phrase has dropped from the text, which I have supplied from the History.]], lest they think I am weary of their staying with me, while those behind them of their people have perished of hardship and thirst!" Or as he said. So he complained of their affair to his two singing-girls, the two locusts, and they said: "Compose a poem for us to sing to them, which they will not know who said it; perhaps it will stir them!" So Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr, when they advised him to do so, said:

Ah, O Qayl! Woe to you! Rise and make a sound, perhaps God will bring us a cloud [[The verses are in the History and in al-Bidayah wa-l-Nihayah 1:126. In the History: "yasqīnā al-ghamāmā" (give us to drink the clouds), as it was in the printed edition; I have adopted what is in the manuscript; in al-Bidayah: "yamnahunā" (grant us).]]
that will water the land of 'Ad, for 'Ad
have become such that they cannot speak clearly
from the severe thirst; we hope from it
neither the old shaykh nor the youth.
Their women were once in goodness,
but now their women have become widows [[In the manuscript: "nisā'uhum 'irāman," and the correct reading is what is in the History and the printed edition: "'ayāmā" (barren/without milk), since "a'āma al-qawm" means their camels died and they found no milk. "Al-'ayma" is the intense craving for milk, and "'āma al-qawm" means their milk became scarce from drought. "A man 'umān and a woman 'ayma" ... the plural being "'iyām" and "'iyāmā." In al-Bidayah: "nisā'uhum ayāmā," the plural of "ayyim," the woman whose husband has died.]].
And the wild beasts come to them openly
and do not fear the arrows of the 'Adites.
And you are here, in what you desire,
your day and your night in full.
So shameful is your delegation, from a people's delegation,
and may they never be greeted with greeting or peace.

When Mu'awiyah recited that poem, the two locusts sang it to them. When the people heard what the two girls sang, some of them said to others: "O people, your people only sent you to seek refuge with you from this affliction which has fallen on them, and you have been slow with them! Enter this sanctuary and seek rain for your people!" Murthid ibn Sa'd ibn 'Ufayr said to them: "By God, you will not be watered by your supplications, but if you obey your Prophet and turn in repentance to Him, you will be watered!" Thereupon he made his Islam manifest. Juhaymah ibn al-Khaybari, the maternal uncle of Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr, said to them, when he heard his words and knew that he had followed the religion of Hud and believed in him:

Abu Sa'd, you are of a tribe
of nobility, and your mother is from Thamud.
[[The verses are in the History of al-Tabari 1:112.]]
We will not obey you as long as we live,
and we will not do what you desire.
Do you command us to abandon the religion of Rifd
and Ramal and the family of Sadd and al-'Ubud? [[In the printed edition: "lā nuṭī'uka" (we do not obey you); I have restored what is in the manuscript, which agrees with the History. In the manuscript: "a-ta'murunā bi-l-sark" (unpointed, with a "ṭ" written above it indicating doubt and error); the correct reading is what is in the printed edition, agreeing with the History. In the printed edition: "dīn wafd, wa-ramal wa-l-ṣadā' ma'a al-ṣamūd," differing completely from the manuscript. What I have adopted from the manuscript agrees with the History.
Abu Ja'far said concerning this report, after these verses, in his History: "Rifd, Ramal, Dadd, are tribes of 'Ad, and al-'Ubud among them."]]
And that we abandon the religion of noble fathers
who have judgment, and follow the religion of Hud.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verses 68–69 (part 2 of 3):

Then they said to Mu'awiya ibn Abi Bakr and his father Bakr: "Detain Murthid ibn Sa'd for us, so that he does not come with us to Makkah, for he has followed the religion of Hud and abandoned our religion!" Then they set out for Makkah to seek rain through it for 'Ad. When they had turned toward Makkah, Murthid ibn Sa'd left the abode of Mu'awiya ibn Bakr and caught up with them there, before they had asked Allah for anything of what they had come out for. [[In the printed edition: "He said: I will not ask Allah for anything of what they came out for," adding what is not permissible for him to add. In the manuscript: "He said: that he would ask Allah for anything of what they came out for," and the correct reading is from Tarikh al-Tabari.]] When he reached them, he stood and prayed to Allah in Makkah, and there was the delegation of 'Ad gathered, calling upon Allah. He said: "O Allah, give me my request alone, and do not include me in anything for which the delegation of 'Ad calls upon You!" Qayl ibn 'Anz was the leader of the delegation of 'Ad. The delegation of 'Ad said: "O Allah, give Qayl what he asks of You, and make our request along with his request!" Luqman ibn 'Ad, who was the chief of 'Ad, had remained behind from the delegation of 'Ad when they prayed. When they had finished their supplication, he stood and said: "O Allah, I have come to You alone with my need, so give me my request!" And Qayl ibn 'Anz, when he prayed, said: "O our God, if Hud is truthful, then give us water, for we have perished!" So Allah brought forth for them three clouds: a white one, a red one, and a black one. Then a caller called out to him from the cloud: "O Qayl, choose for yourself and your people from these clouds." He said: "I have chosen the black cloud, for it is the most abundant in water!" The caller called out: "You have chosen ramadan ramdad [[Ramad ramdad: intensified in burning and fineness. It is said: "ramad aramad" and "ramdad," with the ra' vowelled with kasra, the mim sukun, and the dal kasra, and "ramdad" (with the ra' kasra, the mim sukun, and the dal fatha).]], which will leave none of the family of 'Ad alive, neither a parent who remains nor a child, but will make them all hamidan [[Hamid, hamad, and hamid: dead, perished. "Hamad, hamudan": died and perished.]], except the Banu al-Ludhiyya al-Muhadda," meaning: the Banu al-Ludhiyya are the descendants of Luqaym ibn Hazzal ibn Hazila ibn Bakr. [[In Tarikh: "... Hazal ibn Hazil ibn Hazila ibn Bakr," which is probably the correct reading.]] They were residents of Makkah with their maternal uncles, and they were not with 'Ad in their land. They are the later 'Ad, and whoever was of their lineage who remained of 'Ad.

And Allah drove the black cloud, as they relate, with the punishment it contained toward 'Ad, until it came upon them from a valley called "al-Mughith." When they saw it, they rejoiced at it and said: ﴿This is a cloud bringing us rain﴾. Allah says: ﴿Rather, it is that for which you were impatient: a wind in which is a painful punishment, destroying everything by the command of its Lord﴾ [Surat al-Ahqaf: 24–25], meaning: everything it was commanded to destroy. The first to perceive what was in it and to recognize that it was a wind, as they relate, was a woman of 'Ad called "Mahdad." When she became certain of what was in it, she cried out, [[In Tarikh: "When she clearly saw," and this is likely more correct.]] then she fell unconscious. When she regained consciousness, they said: "What did you see, O Mahdad?" She said: "I saw a wind in which were sparks of fire, and before it were men leading it!" So Allah subjected it upon them for seven nights and eight days, continuously [as Allah said], [[Surat al-Haqqa: 7.]] and "husum" means continuous. So it left none of 'Ad alive except that they perished.

Hud, as was mentioned to me, and those who were with him of the believers, withdrew into an enclosure. What afflicted him and those with him of the wind was nothing more than what was soft upon the skin and pleasant to the souls. [[In the printed edition: "and pleasant to it," adding what is not in the manuscript or in Tarikh.]] Indeed, the wind passed over 'Ad, striking between the sky and the earth, and pelting them with stones. The delegation of 'Ad left Makkah until they passed by Mu'awiya ibn Bakr and his father, [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "and his son," and the correct reading is from Tarikh and from the beginning of the report.]] and they stayed with him. While they were with him, a man came riding a she-camel on a moonlit night, in the third evening after the calamity of 'Ad. [["Al-Misy" (with a damma and then sukun): evening, like "al-subh" and "al-sabah." In the printed edition and Tarikh: "the evening of the third," and what is in the manuscript is preferred.]] He informed them of the news, and they said to him: "Where did you leave Hud and his companions?" He said: "I left them on the seashore." They seemed to doubt what he told them, so Hudhayla bint Bakr said: "He speaks the truth, by the Lord of the Ka'ba!" [[In the printed edition: "Hudhayla," and the correct reading is from the manuscript and Tarikh.]] [[The report: 14804. This report was related by al-Tabari in his History, abridged at its beginning and expanded later at its end, 1: 111–113.]]

14805 – Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash narrated to us, he said: 'Asim narrated to us, from al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri, who said: I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I passed by a woman at al-Rabadha. [[In the printed edition: "upon a woman," and what is in the manuscript is preferred.]] She said: "Will you carry me to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?" I said: "Yes!" So I carried her until we reached Madina, and I entered the mosque, and there was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the minbar, and Bilal was wearing a sword, and there were black banners. I said: "What is this?" They said: "'Amr ibn al-'As has returned from his expedition." When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) descended from his minbar, I went to him and asked permission, and he permitted me. I said: "O Messenger of Allah, at the door is a woman from the Banu Tamim, and she asked me to carry her to you." He said: "O Bilal, let her in." She entered, and when she sat down, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "Is there something between you and Tamim?" I said: "Yes! And the defeat was against them," [[In the printed edition: "and the victory was for us against them," an addition beyond the manuscript which distorts the text; the correct reading is from the manuscript. "Al-Dabara" (with fatha of the dal and sukun or fatha of the ba'): defeat for them, and dominance and victory for the others.]] so if you see fit to place Dahna' between us and them as a barrier, you may do so!" He said: The woman said: "Then where will your Mudar go, O Messenger of Allah?" [[In the printed edition: "Then where will the one who is compelled be compelled, O Messenger of Allah," which is a faulty and reprehensible alteration and an extreme distortion. The correct reading is that of the manuscript. "Mudar" is the root of the Arabs, namely "Mudar ibn Nizar ibn Ma'add ibn 'Adnan," from whom Quraysh and Banu Tamim branched. This is why the woman from Tamim said "your Mudar" to the Messenger of Allah, because he was her grandfather and his.]] I said: "My likeness is that of a goat that carried its death!" [[In the printed edition: "My likeness is like what the first one said: a goat that carried its death," adding from another narration, which is a severe distortion, and changing "hatfan" to "hatfuha." I have preferred what matches the narration in Tarikh. And his saying: "a goat that carried its death," means it carried its fate; it is a proverb for one who carries what will destroy him. It is not found in the books of proverbs.]] I said: "And I have carried you, you will be an adversary to me! I seek refuge in Allah that I become like the delegation of 'Ad!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "And what is the delegation of 'Ad?" I said: "You have fallen upon one who knows! 'Ad suffered drought, so they sent someone to seek rain for them. They sent men who passed by Bakr ibn Mu'awiya, and he gave them wine to drink, and two singing girls entertained them for a month. Then he sent a man from among them until he reached the mountains of Mahra, [["Mahra" (with fatha then sukun): a great tribe, and the ancestor of a tribe: "Mahra ibn Haydan ibn 'Amr ibn al-Haf ibn Qudha'a." The lands of Mahra are in the region of Shihr in Yemen, in the lands of al-'Anbar on the seashore. In the printed edition and the manuscript it reads: "Then they departed from his presence until they came to the mountains of Mahra," and this sentence badly disrupts the flow of the report, the pronouns shift, and the report has no coherent thread. It seems to be a scribal error, for Abu Ja'far related this report in Tarikh with its chain and wording, so I have adopted from it the text of the report, as it is what makes the speech coherent.]] and they prayed, and clouds came. He said: Whenever a cloud came, he would say: "Go to such and such," until a cloud came, and a call came from it: "Take it, ramadan ramdad, * which leaves none of 'Ad alive." He said: He heard it, and he concealed it from them until the punishment came upon them. [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "He heard them and spoke to them," and the correct reading is from Tarikh.]]

Abu Kurayb said: Abu Bakr said after that in the report about 'Ad: He said: Then the one who had come to them came, and he came to the mountains of Mahra, [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "the ones who came to them," and the correct reading is from Tarikh.]] and he climbed up and said: "O Allah, I have not come to You to free a captive so that I may ransom him, nor for a sick person so that I may cure him. So give 'Ad drink as You used to give them to drink!" He said: Clouds were raised for him, and a call came from them: "Choose!" He said: He began to say: "Go to the Banu so-and-so, go to the Banu so-and-so." He said: Then the last of them passed, a black cloud, and he said: "Go to 'Ad!" A call came from it: "Take it, ramadan ramdad, which leaves none of 'Ad alive." He said: And he concealed it from them, [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "and he spoke to them," and the correct reading is from Tarikh.]] while the people were with Bakr ibn Mu'awiya, drinking. He said: Bakr ibn Mu'awiya disliked telling them, because they were his guests and were eating his food. He said: So he began to sing and reminded them. [[Report 14805: "Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash," a trustworthy narrator, one of the devout and precise memorizers, but when he grew old his memory deteriorated, so he would err when narrating. Error and mistake are two things that no human being is free from, and whoever does not commit them frequently does not deserve to have his narrations abandoned, once his probity is established. Thus said Ibn Hibban, and he spoke truly. It has passed under numbers 2150, 3000, 5725, 8098.

And "'Asim" is "'Asim ibn Bahdala," "'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud," a trustworthy, eminent, well-known narrator, who has passed many times.

As for "al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri," it is said of him: "al-Harith ibn Yazid al-Bakri," and it is said his name is "Hurayth." Ibn 'Abd al-Barr affirmed that his name is "al-Harith ibn Hassan," saying: "Most say al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri, and this is the sound one, God willing." But it is strange that al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in al-Tahdhib: "Ibn 'Abd al-Barr affirmed that his name is Hurayth," and he erred a great error, for what I quoted is the text of Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in al-Isti'ab!! So let what is in al-Tahdhib be corrected.

"Al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri" is biographed in Ibn Sa'd 6: 22, al-Kabir of al-Bukhari 1/2/259, al-Isti'ab: 109, Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/71, Usd al-Ghaba 1: 323, al-Isaba in his biography, and al-Tahdhib. Abu Wa'il and Sammak ibn Harb related from him.

The report of "al-Harith al-Bakri" will come with another chain: "from 'Asim, from Abu Wa'il, from al-Harith ibn Yazid al-Bakri."

As for this chain, "'Asim, from al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri," with no "Abu Wa'il" between them, Ibn al-Athir said in Usd al-Ghaba in the biography of "al-Harith": "Ahmad ibn Hanbal also related it, and Sa'id al-Umawi, Yahya al-Himmani, 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Sala, and Abu Bakr ibn Shayba, all of them from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash, from 'Asim, from al-Harith, without mentioning Abu Wa'il." Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in al-Tahdhib in the biography of "al-Harith": "'Asim ibn Bahdala related from him," and the correct version is: from him, from Abu Wa'il, from al-Harith.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said in al-Isti'ab: "There is disagreement regarding his narration: some make it from 'Asim ibn Bahdala, from al-Harith ibn Hassan, without mentioning Abu Wa'il, while the correct version is: from 'Asim, from Abu Wa'il, from al-Harith ibn Hassan." Others said likewise.

This report with this chain was related by Abu Ja'far again in his History 1: 110. Ahmad in his Musnad 3: 481 related its beginning: "from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash, who said: 'Asim ibn Abi al-Fazr (??) narrated to us, from al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri," abridged, and it is the beginning of the report. As for what came in the printed Musnad, "'Asim ibn Abi al-Fazr," I deem it likely to be a distortion of "'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud," for the narration is his, and I have not known that he is called "'Asim ibn Abi al-Fazr."

Ibn Maja also related it in abridged form through this same route in his Sunan, p. 941, no. 2816, with wording similar to Ahmad's.

The takhrij of this report of "al-Harith" will come in the following report.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 7, verses 68–69 (part 3 of 3):**

14806. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Zayd ibn al-Habbab narrated to us, saying: Salam Abu al-Mundhir al-Nahwi (the grammarian) narrated to us, saying: 'Asim narrated to us, from Abu Wa'il, from al-Harith ibn Yazid al-Bakri, who said: "I set out to complain about al-'Ala' ibn al-Hadrami to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). I passed by al-Rabadhah and found an old woman who had been cut off there [[“Munqati‘ bihā” (with the *mīm* vowelled, and the *qāf* and *ṭā’* with fatḥa). It is said: “qutiʿa bi-l-rajul, fa-huwa maqṭūʿ bihi,” and “inqaṭaʿa bihi, fa-huwa munqaṭiʿ bihi” (all in the passive form), when a traveller’s mount has perished and his provisions and wealth are gone, or when a matter befalls him that prevents him from moving.]] from the Banu Tamim. She said: 'O servant of God, I have a need of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Will you convey me to him?' He said: 'So I carried her and we reached Medina. Then I saw banners [[At this point Abu Ja‘far said, in his narration in the *Tarikh*: “Abu Ja‘far said: I think he said: ‘Then I saw black banners.’”]] and said: "What is the matter with the people?" They said: "He wishes to dispatch ‘Amr ibn al-‘As on an expedition." [[In the printed edition: “‘Amr ibn al-‘As”, with the *bāʾ* omitted; it is established in the manuscript and in the narration of this report in the *Tarikh*.]] He said: 'So I sat until he had finished. Then he entered his dwelling, or he said: his camel-saddle, and I asked permission to see him, and he permitted me. I entered and sat, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to me: "Was there any dispute between you and Tamim?" I said: "Yes! And we had the upper hand over them, [[In the printed edition: “wa-kānat lanā al-dārah ʿalayhim”; in the manuscript: “wa-kānat al-dāʾirah ʿalayhim”, undotted. The narration of Abu Ja‘far in the *Tarikh* and the narration of Ahmad in his *Musnad* are preferred. See the note above, p. 514, n. 1.]] and I passed by al-Rabadhah, where there was an old woman from them, cut off there, who asked me to carry her to you, and here she is at the door." So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) permitted her, and she entered. I said: "O Messenger of God, make between us and Tamim a barrier of al-Dahna." The old woman grew angry and became agitated [[“Ḥamiyat”: she became angry, seized by zeal, pride and rage. “Istawfaza al-rajul fi qaʿdatihi”: when a man sits upright without settling down, not standing fully, like one readying to leap up; this occurs at times of evil, quarrel, dispute and contention.]] and said: "Then where will you take your Mudar, O Messenger of God?" [[In the printed edition: “fa-ila ayna yuḍṭarru muḍṭarraka”, which is a change from what is in the manuscript and an addition to it, as was done in the earlier report, p. 514, n. 2.]] He said: I said: "I am as the first one said: 'A goat that carried its own death!' [[In the printed edition: “ḥatfahā”, which agrees with Ahmad’s narration in his *Musnad*; but what I have established is what is in the manuscript and the *Tarikh*, except that in the *Tarikh* it reads “ḥayfan”, which is an error; the correct reading is what I have given. See above, p. 514, n. 3.]] I carried this one and did not realise that she would be an adversary to me! I seek refuge in God and His Messenger from being like the envoy of ‘Ad!" He said: "And what is the envoy of ‘Ad?" I said [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: “He said: ‘You have fallen upon one who knows’”; I have established what is in the *Tarikh*.]] "You have fallen upon one who knows!" He said: and he was asking me for the story [[“Istaṭʿamahu al-ḥadith”: he tempted him to narrate to him, as if he wanted to let him taste the flavour of his narration. This is said when he lures him into it while knowing the narration better than him. Its explanation is found in Ahmad’s *Musnad*: “and he knew the narration better than him, but he was asking him to tell it.” The explanation of this expression in the lexicographical books is not sufficient, so I have qualified it there.]]. I said: "Indeed ‘Ad suffered drought, so they sent Qayl as an envoy. He stayed with Bakr and they gave him wine for a month, and two slave-girls who were called ‘al-Jaradatan’ sang to him, [[In the printed edition: “wa-ghannathu jāriyatān”, different from the manuscript, and it agrees with the *Tafsir* and the *Musnad* of Ahmad.]] Then he went out to the mountains of Mahrah and called out: 'I have not come to a sick man that I might treat him, nor to a captive that I might ransom him. O God, give drink to ‘Ad as much as they used to give drink to you!' [[In the printed edition and the *Tarikh* of al-Tabari: “Allahumma asqi”; I have established what is in the manuscript. The rest of the sentence is displaced from its place in the manuscript, namely his saying: “mā kunta tusqīhi”, which is established in the *Tarikh*. But in the printed edition and the manuscript it reads “musqīhi”, as in the earlier report; yet “tusqīhi” is the narration of Abu Ja‘far in the *Tarikh* and also of Ahmad.]] Then dark clouds passed over him, and a voice called out from them: [[After his saying “a voice called out from them”, the words “mā kunta musqīhi” are placed, as I mentioned in the previous note.]] "Take it as ashes, scattering, leaving none of ‘Ad alive." He said: So the woman used to say: "Do not be like the envoy of ‘Ad!" And it did not reach me, O Messenger of God, that God sent upon them any wind except as much as flows through my ring." [[In the printed edition: “fa-fīmā balaghanī”; I have established what is in the manuscript, which agrees with Abu Ja‘far’s narration in the *Tarikh* and Ahmad’s narration in the *Musnad*.]] He said: Abu Wa'il said: "So it reached me too."] [[The report: No. 14806. This is another chain for the earlier report, the chain in which I pointed out that “Abu Wa’il” appears between “‘Asim ibn Bahdalah” and “al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri”, and that this is the correct one.

“Al-Harith ibn Yazid al-Bakri” is “al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri”, which is disputed, as I stated in the note on no. 14805.

“Salam Abu al-Mundhir al-Nahwi” is “Salam ibn Sulayman al-Muzani”. Yahya ibn Ma‘in said: “He is nothing.” Abu Hatim said: “Truthful, good in narration.” Al-Saji said: “Truthful, makes mistakes, not precise in narration.” Ibn Ma‘in said again: “His truthfulness is tolerated.” He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/2/135, Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/259, and Mizan al-I‘tidal 1:400.

As for “Abu Wa’il”, he is “Shaqiq ibn Salamah al-Asadi”, a trustworthy imam, who has been mentioned many times before.

As for the woman mentioned in this report and the earlier report, she is: “Qaylah bint Makhramah al-Tamimiyyah”, from the Banu al-‘Anbar ibn ‘Amr ibn Tamim. In some books she is mentioned as “al-Ghanawiyyah”, which is a misreading of “al-‘Anbariyyah”. The narration of Qaylah is a long narration, containing much that is strange; Ibn Hajar mentioned it in her biography in al-Isabah.

Investigating her report and the report of “al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri” or “Huraith ibn Hassan al-Shaybani”, the envoy of Bakr ibn Wa’il (as in her biography in Ibn Sa‘d 8:228), requires discussion beyond the scope of this place.

This report was narrated by Abu Ja‘far in his *Tarikh* with this same chain. Ahmad narrated it in his *Musnad* 3:481, 482, by two routes: from the route of ‘Affan, from Salam Abu al-Mundhir, from ‘Asim; then from the route of Zayd ibn al-Habbab, from Abu al-Mundhir Salam ibn Sulayman al-Nahwi, from ‘Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, in similar wording.

Ibn Sa‘d narrated it in *al-Tabaqat* 6:22, from the route of ‘Affan, from Salam Abu al-Mundhir, in abridged form.

Al-Bukhari narrated its beginning in *al-Kabir* 1/2/259.

Ibn al-Athir narrated it in the biography of “al-Harith” in *Usd al-Ghabah*, Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr in *al-Isti‘ab* in abridged form, and Ibn Hajar in *al-Isabah*. Ibn Kathir narrated it in his *Tafsir* 3:502 / 7:470, from the route of Ahmad’s *Musnad*. He also narrated it in *al-Bidayah wa-l-Nihayah* 1:127, 128, and said: “Ibn Jarir narrated it from Abu Kurayb, from Zayd ibn al-Habbab, with it. In his version it reads: ‘from al-Harith ibn Yazid al-Bakri’, and he narrated it. He also narrated it from Abu Kurayb, from Abu Bakr ibn ‘Ayyash, from ‘Asim, from al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri, and he narrated it. I did not find in the copy ‘Abu Wa’il’, and God knows best.” I say: He means the earlier report; see the note there.

Ibn Kathir also said in *al-Bidayah wa-l-Nihayah*: “al-Tirmidhi narrated it from ‘Abd ibn Humayd, from Zayd ibn al-Habbab, with it. Al-Nasa’i narrated it from the hadith of Salam Abu al-Mundhir, from ‘Asim ibn Bahdalah, and Ibn Majah narrated it through him. Likewise, this hadith and this story have been cited by more than one exegete when interpreting this story, such as Ibn Jarir and others. This context may be for the destruction of the later ‘Ad, for what Ibn Ishaq and others mentioned contains no mention of Mecca, which was not built until after Abraham the Friend, when he settled Hagar and his son Ishmael there, and the Jurhum people settled with them, as will come. The first ‘Ad was before the Friend. It contains mention of ‘Mu‘awiyah ibn Bakr’ and his poetry, and this is poetry later than the time of the first ‘Ad, not resembling the speech of earlier people. It also states that in that cloud there were sparks of fire, whereas the first ‘Ad were only destroyed by a violent, roaring wind.”

This is a very good critique of all these earlier reports and the report that follows.]]

14807. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding God’s words: “And to ‘Ad their brother Hud, he said: O my people, worship God; you have no god other than Him”: that Hud came to ‘Ad, admonished them, and reminded them of what God recounted in the Qur’an, but they denied him and disbelieved, and they asked him to bring them the punishment. So he said to them: ﴿The knowledge is only with God, and I convey to you that with which I have been sent﴾ [Surah al-Ahqaf: 23]. When ‘Ad disbelieved, they were struck by a drought of rain [[In the *Tarikh*: “qaḥṭ min al-maṭar”.]] until they were afflicted with severe hardship. That was because Hud prayed against them, so God sent upon them the barren wind, which is the wind that does not fertilise trees. When they looked at it they said: ﴿This is a cloud bringing us rain﴾ [Surah al-Ahqaf: 24]. When it drew near them, they saw the camels and men being carried by the wind between heaven and earth. When they saw it, they hastened to the houses [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: “tanādawā al-buyūt”, which has no meaning; the correct form, from the *Tarikh*, is “tabādarū”, they hurried.]], and when they entered the houses, it entered upon them and destroyed them within them, then it brought them out of the houses and struck them with “a day of misfortune” — and *naḥs* is ill omen — and “continuing” [*mustamirr*], which continued upon them with punishment “for seven nights and eight days in succession” [*ḥusūman*] — it uprooted everything it passed over. [[This is the explanation of the verses, from Surah al-Qamar: 19, and Surah al-Haqqah: 7.]] When it removed them from the houses, God said: ﴿Plucking people up﴾ from the houses, ﴿as if they were trunks of uprooted palm trees﴾ [Surah al-Qamar: 20] — “uprooted” from its roots — “hollow”, which fell hollow. [[This is the explanation of the verse in Surah al-Haqqah: 7: “as if they were hollow trunks of palm trees.”]] When God destroyed them, He sent upon them black birds, which carried them to the sea and cast them into it. That is His saying: ﴿So they became such that nothing could be seen except their dwellings﴾ [Surah al-Ahqaf: 25]. No wind ever went out except by measure, except on that day, for it rebelled against the keepers and overpowered them, so they did not know how great its measure was. That is His saying: ﴿So they were destroyed by a roaring, violent wind﴾ [Surah al-Haqqah: 6] — and *ṣarṣar* is that which has a strong sound.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verses 68–69 (part 1 of 3):

The explanation of His saying: ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I am a sincere and trustworthy adviser to you. (68) Are you surprised that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, so that he may warn you? And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah, and increased you in stature and bodily strength. So remember the favours of God, that you may prosper.﴾ (69)

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, "I convey to you the messages of my Lord," he means: I deliver them to you, O people [[See the explanation of "al-balagh" (conveying) above, 10:575 / 11:9.]]. "And I am a sincere adviser to you" means: and in my command to you to worship God alone, rather than the rivals and deities besides Him, and in my calling you to believe what I have brought you from God, I am a sincere adviser to you. So accept my counsel, for I am trustworthy regarding the revelation of God and regarding what God has entrusted me with of the message. I do not lie in it, add to it, or alter it; rather, I convey what I have been commanded, as I have been commanded. "Are you surprised that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, so that he may warn you?" means: Are you astonished that God has sent down His revelation, to remind and admonish you, through a man from among you, concerning your state of error in which you remain, so that he may warn you of God's punishment and frighten you with His retribution? [[See the explanation of a similar verse above, p. 501.]] "And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah" means: Fear God regarding yourselves, and remember what befell the people of Noah of punishment when they disobeyed their messenger and disbelieved in their Lord. Indeed, your Lord made you successors in the earth after them; when He destroyed them, He replaced them with you in it [[See the explanation of "khalifah" (successor) above, 1:449 / 12:288.]]. So fear God lest there befall you the like of the punishment that befell them, and He destroy you and replace you with others, in keeping with His practice regarding the people of Noah before you, for your disobedience to Him and your disbelief in Him. "And increased you in stature" means: He increased your bodies in height and largeness over the bodies of the people of Noah [[See the explanation of "bastah" (expansion) above, 5:313.]], "and in strength over their strength" [[In the printed edition: "qawāmakum 'alā qawāmihim," which is an error; the correct reading is what is in the manuscript.]], as a favour from Him upon you. So remember His favours and His bounty by which He preferred you over them in your bodies and your strength [[In the printed edition also: "wa-qawāmakum"; the correct reading is from the manuscript.]], and thank God for that by sincerely worshipping Him, abandoning associating others with Him, and forsaking idols and rivals. "That you may prosper" means: so that you may prosper, attaining eternal life and abiding in blessings in the Hereafter, and succeed in your requests from Him. [[See the explanation of "al-falah" (prosperity) above, p. 312, note 1, and the references there.]]

* *

In the same sense as what we have said regarding the interpretation of His saying, "And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah," the people of interpretation (ta'wil) said:

Those who said that:

14795 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah": he means: He destroyed the people of Noah and made you successors after them.

14796 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq: "And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah": i.e., inhabitants of the earth after the people of Noah.

* *

In the same sense as what we have said, they also said regarding His saying, "bastah" (expansion):

Those who said that:

14797 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And increased you in stature": he said: [in strength] like the strength of the people of 'Ad. [[In the printed edition: "li-qawām qawm 'Ād," and the correct reading is what is in the manuscript.]]

* *

As for "al-ala'" (favours), it is a plural whose singular is "ilan" (with a kasrah on the alif), in the pattern of "mi'an," and it is said "alan" (with a fathah on the alif) in the pattern of "qafan." And it has been transmitted from the Arabs as "ilj" like "hisy." "Al-ala'" means blessings.

* *

Likewise the people of interpretation said:

Those who said that:

14798 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: "So remember the favours of God": i.e., the blessings of God.

14799 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: As for "the favours of God," they are the blessings of God.

14800 – Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: "So remember the favours of God," he said: His favours are His blessings.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: As for "'Ad," these are the people whose description God mentioned, and to whom He sent Hud, calling them to the oneness of God and to following what he brought them from Him. Regarding them, it is reported:

14801 – Ibn Humayd narrated this to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq: The descendants of 'Ad ibn Iram ibn 'Awṣ ibn Sam ibn Noah.

* *

Their dwellings were al-Shihr, in the land of Yemen, and the regions adjoining Hadramawt up to 'Uman, as reported:

14802 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: That 'Ad was a people who lived in Yemen, in al-Ahqaf.
