14803 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sa'id al-Khuza'i, from Abu al-Tufayl 'Amir ibn Wathilah, who said: I heard 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) say to a man from Hadramawt: "Have you seen a reddish sand dune mixed with red clay [["al-madarah" is clay that is sticky and has no sand in it.]], with arak and much sidr (lote) trees in such-and-such a region of the land of Hadramawt? [["al-Arak" and "al-Sidr" are plants.]] Have you seen it?" He said: "Yes, O Commander of the Faithful! By God, you describe it as one who has seen it!" He said: "No, but I have been told about it." The Hadrami said: "What about it, O Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "In it is the grave of Hud, may God's blessings be upon him." [[Report 14803: "Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sa'id al-Khuza'i" was biographed by al-Bukhari in al-Kabir 1/1/135, who related the report, in a similar but longer form, and mentioned no criticism of him. Also Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/297.
"Abu al-Tufayl," "'Amir ibn Wathilah al-Kinani," saw the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was a youth; his seeing the Messenger of God is established, but his hearing from him is not established. They said he was the last of the Companions to die, in the year 100 or after.]]

14804 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: The dwellings of 'Ad and their community, when God sent Hud among them, were al-Ahqaf. He said: "Al-Ahqaf" means the sand, the area between 'Uman and Hadramawt, and all of Yemen. [[In the printed edition: "bi-l-Yaman," omitting "kullahu"; I have restored what is in the manuscript.]] They, moreover, had spread throughout the whole earth, and subdued its inhabitants through the excess of the strength that God had given them. They were worshippers of idols besides God: an idol called "Sada'," an idol called "Samud," and an idol called "al-Haba'." So God sent to them Hud, who was of the most central of them in lineage and the most excellent in position. He commanded them to worship God alone and not to set up any other god alongside Him, and to refrain from wronging people. He did not command them, as is reported, and God knows best, in anything other than that. But they refused him and denied him, and said: "Who is stronger than us in power!" Some of them followed him, but they were few, concealing their faith. Among those who believed in him and affirmed him was a man of 'Ad called "Murthid ibn Sa'd ibn 'Ufayr," who concealed his faith. [[In the printed edition: "yaktumūn īmānahum"; I have restored what is in the manuscript.]] When they transgressed against God, may He be blessed and exalted, and denied their Prophet, and multiplied corruption in the earth, and became tyrannical, and built on every high place a landmark in vain, without benefit, Hud addressed them, saying: ﴿Do you build on every high place a monument, playing? And you take fortresses, perhaps you will abide forever? And when you strike, you strike as tyrants. So fear God and obey me.﴾ [Surah al-Shu'ara: 128–131]. They said: ﴿O Hud, you have brought us no clear proof, and we will not abandon our gods on your word, nor will we believe in you. We say only that some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾ — meaning: what you have brought us is nothing but madness that some of these gods of ours, whom you revile, have afflicted you with. ﴿He said: "I call God to witness, and bear witness yourselves that I am free of what you associate besides Him. So plot against me all together, then give me no respite. Indeed, I have put my trust in God, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path"﴾ [Surah Hud: 53–56], up to His saying: ﴿on a straight path﴾. When they did that, God withheld the rain from the sky from them for three years, so it is claimed, until that hardship afflicted them. In that time, when affliction or hardship befell people and they sought relief from God, they would make their petition to God at His Sacred House in Mecca, Muslim and polytheist alike; so many people of various and differing religions would gather in Mecca, and all of them would revere Mecca, knowing its sanctity and its place with God.

= Ibn Ishaq said: The House in that time was known in its location, and the sanctuary (haram) was standing, as they report. The people of Mecca at that time were the 'Amaliq [[They were named "'Amaliq" because their forefather was "'Amlik ibn Lawdh ibn Sam ibn Noah."]]. The chief of the 'Amaliq at that time in Mecca, it is claimed, was a man called Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr. His father was still alive at that time, but he had grown old, and his son led his people. Leadership and nobility among the 'Amaliq, it is claimed, belonged to the people of that House. The mother of Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr was Kalhadah, daughter of al-Khaybari, a man of 'Ad. When the rain was withheld from 'Ad and they were afflicted, they said: "Send from among you a delegation to Mecca, so that they may seek rain for you, for you are surely destroyed!" So they dispatched Qayl ibn 'Anz [[In the printed edition: "ibn 'Anz"; in the manuscript: "'Atar"; in the History: "'Athar," and later in the History: "'Anz."]] and Luqaym ibn Hazzal ibn Hazil [[In the printed edition: "min Hudhayl"; I have restored what is in the manuscript, which agrees with the History of al-Tabari.]] and 'Utayl ibn Sadd ibn 'Ad al-Akbar [[In the printed edition: "wa-'Aqil ibn Sadd"; I have restored what is in the manuscript, agreeing with the History, though what is in the History reads: "wa-Luqaym ibn Hazzal ibn Hazil ibn 'Utayl ibn Dadd ..." with "Dadd" spelled with a dad, and I think the sad is more correct.]] and Murthid ibn Sa'd ibn 'Ufayr, who was a Muslim concealing his Islam, and Juhaymah ibn al-Khaybari, the maternal uncle of Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr, his mother's brother. Then they sent Luqman ibn 'Ad ibn so-and-so ibn so-and-so ibn Sadd ibn 'Ad al-Akbar. So each man of these people set out with a company of his folk, until the number of their delegation reached seventy men. When they came to Mecca, they stayed with Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr, who was outside Mecca, outside the sanctuary, and he hosted them and honoured them, for they were his maternal relatives and in-laws. [[In the printed edition: "wa-asbāruh"; I have restored what is in the manuscript, which agrees with the History.]]

= When the delegation of 'Ad stayed with Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr, they remained with him for a month, drinking wine, while two singing-girls, al-Jaradatan (the two locusts), who were Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr's slave-girls, sang to them. Their journey had lasted a month, and their stay was a month. When Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr saw how long they stayed, and that their people had sent them to seek refuge with them from the affliction that had befallen them [[In the printed edition and History: "yatghawwathūn" (seeking relief); in the manuscript: "yata'awwadhūn" (seeking refuge), unpointed, which is correct, so I have adopted it.]], it grieved him, and he said: "My maternal relatives and in-laws are destroyed! And these are staying with me, my guests, lodging with me! By God, I do not know what to do with them! I am ashamed to order them to leave for what they were sent for [[In the printed edition: "in amartuhum bi-l-khurūj"; in the manuscript: "in āmuruhum bi-l-khurūj," so it is clear that a phrase has dropped from the text, which I have supplied from the History.]], lest they think I am weary of their staying with me, while those behind them of their people have perished of hardship and thirst!" Or as he said. So he complained of their affair to his two singing-girls, the two locusts, and they said: "Compose a poem for us to sing to them, which they will not know who said it; perhaps it will stir them!" So Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr, when they advised him to do so, said:

Ah, O Qayl! Woe to you! Rise and make a sound, perhaps God will bring us a cloud [[The verses are in the History and in al-Bidayah wa-l-Nihayah 1:126. In the History: "yasqīnā al-ghamāmā" (give us to drink the clouds), as it was in the printed edition; I have adopted what is in the manuscript; in al-Bidayah: "yamnahunā" (grant us).]]
that will water the land of 'Ad, for 'Ad
have become such that they cannot speak clearly
from the severe thirst; we hope from it
neither the old shaykh nor the youth.
Their women were once in goodness,
but now their women have become widows [[In the manuscript: "nisā'uhum 'irāman," and the correct reading is what is in the History and the printed edition: "'ayāmā" (barren/without milk), since "a'āma al-qawm" means their camels died and they found no milk. "Al-'ayma" is the intense craving for milk, and "'āma al-qawm" means their milk became scarce from drought. "A man 'umān and a woman 'ayma" ... the plural being "'iyām" and "'iyāmā." In al-Bidayah: "nisā'uhum ayāmā," the plural of "ayyim," the woman whose husband has died.]].
And the wild beasts come to them openly
and do not fear the arrows of the 'Adites.
And you are here, in what you desire,
your day and your night in full.
So shameful is your delegation, from a people's delegation,
and may they never be greeted with greeting or peace.

When Mu'awiyah recited that poem, the two locusts sang it to them. When the people heard what the two girls sang, some of them said to others: "O people, your people only sent you to seek refuge with you from this affliction which has fallen on them, and you have been slow with them! Enter this sanctuary and seek rain for your people!" Murthid ibn Sa'd ibn 'Ufayr said to them: "By God, you will not be watered by your supplications, but if you obey your Prophet and turn in repentance to Him, you will be watered!" Thereupon he made his Islam manifest. Juhaymah ibn al-Khaybari, the maternal uncle of Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr, said to them, when he heard his words and knew that he had followed the religion of Hud and believed in him:

Abu Sa'd, you are of a tribe
of nobility, and your mother is from Thamud.
[[The verses are in the History of al-Tabari 1:112.]]
We will not obey you as long as we live,
and we will not do what you desire.
Do you command us to abandon the religion of Rifd
and Ramal and the family of Sadd and al-'Ubud? [[In the printed edition: "lā nuṭī'uka" (we do not obey you); I have restored what is in the manuscript, which agrees with the History. In the manuscript: "a-ta'murunā bi-l-sark" (unpointed, with a "ṭ" written above it indicating doubt and error); the correct reading is what is in the printed edition, agreeing with the History. In the printed edition: "dīn wafd, wa-ramal wa-l-ṣadā' ma'a al-ṣamūd," differing completely from the manuscript. What I have adopted from the manuscript agrees with the History.
Abu Ja'far said concerning this report, after these verses, in his History: "Rifd, Ramal, Dadd, are tribes of 'Ad, and al-'Ubud among them."]]
And that we abandon the religion of noble fathers
who have judgment, and follow the religion of Hud.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verses 68–69 (part 2 of 3):

Then they said to Mu'awiya ibn Abi Bakr and his father Bakr: "Detain Murthid ibn Sa'd for us, so that he does not come with us to Makkah, for he has followed the religion of Hud and abandoned our religion!" Then they set out for Makkah to seek rain through it for 'Ad. When they had turned toward Makkah, Murthid ibn Sa'd left the abode of Mu'awiya ibn Bakr and caught up with them there, before they had asked Allah for anything of what they had come out for. [[In the printed edition: "He said: I will not ask Allah for anything of what they came out for," adding what is not permissible for him to add. In the manuscript: "He said: that he would ask Allah for anything of what they came out for," and the correct reading is from Tarikh al-Tabari.]] When he reached them, he stood and prayed to Allah in Makkah, and there was the delegation of 'Ad gathered, calling upon Allah. He said: "O Allah, give me my request alone, and do not include me in anything for which the delegation of 'Ad calls upon You!" Qayl ibn 'Anz was the leader of the delegation of 'Ad. The delegation of 'Ad said: "O Allah, give Qayl what he asks of You, and make our request along with his request!" Luqman ibn 'Ad, who was the chief of 'Ad, had remained behind from the delegation of 'Ad when they prayed. When they had finished their supplication, he stood and said: "O Allah, I have come to You alone with my need, so give me my request!" And Qayl ibn 'Anz, when he prayed, said: "O our God, if Hud is truthful, then give us water, for we have perished!" So Allah brought forth for them three clouds: a white one, a red one, and a black one. Then a caller called out to him from the cloud: "O Qayl, choose for yourself and your people from these clouds." He said: "I have chosen the black cloud, for it is the most abundant in water!" The caller called out: "You have chosen ramadan ramdad [[Ramad ramdad: intensified in burning and fineness. It is said: "ramad aramad" and "ramdad," with the ra' vowelled with kasra, the mim sukun, and the dal kasra, and "ramdad" (with the ra' kasra, the mim sukun, and the dal fatha).]], which will leave none of the family of 'Ad alive, neither a parent who remains nor a child, but will make them all hamidan [[Hamid, hamad, and hamid: dead, perished. "Hamad, hamudan": died and perished.]], except the Banu al-Ludhiyya al-Muhadda," meaning: the Banu al-Ludhiyya are the descendants of Luqaym ibn Hazzal ibn Hazila ibn Bakr. [[In Tarikh: "... Hazal ibn Hazil ibn Hazila ibn Bakr," which is probably the correct reading.]] They were residents of Makkah with their maternal uncles, and they were not with 'Ad in their land. They are the later 'Ad, and whoever was of their lineage who remained of 'Ad.

And Allah drove the black cloud, as they relate, with the punishment it contained toward 'Ad, until it came upon them from a valley called "al-Mughith." When they saw it, they rejoiced at it and said: ﴿This is a cloud bringing us rain﴾. Allah says: ﴿Rather, it is that for which you were impatient: a wind in which is a painful punishment, destroying everything by the command of its Lord﴾ [Surat al-Ahqaf: 24–25], meaning: everything it was commanded to destroy. The first to perceive what was in it and to recognize that it was a wind, as they relate, was a woman of 'Ad called "Mahdad." When she became certain of what was in it, she cried out, [[In Tarikh: "When she clearly saw," and this is likely more correct.]] then she fell unconscious. When she regained consciousness, they said: "What did you see, O Mahdad?" She said: "I saw a wind in which were sparks of fire, and before it were men leading it!" So Allah subjected it upon them for seven nights and eight days, continuously [as Allah said], [[Surat al-Haqqa: 7.]] and "husum" means continuous. So it left none of 'Ad alive except that they perished.

Hud, as was mentioned to me, and those who were with him of the believers, withdrew into an enclosure. What afflicted him and those with him of the wind was nothing more than what was soft upon the skin and pleasant to the souls. [[In the printed edition: "and pleasant to it," adding what is not in the manuscript or in Tarikh.]] Indeed, the wind passed over 'Ad, striking between the sky and the earth, and pelting them with stones. The delegation of 'Ad left Makkah until they passed by Mu'awiya ibn Bakr and his father, [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "and his son," and the correct reading is from Tarikh and from the beginning of the report.]] and they stayed with him. While they were with him, a man came riding a she-camel on a moonlit night, in the third evening after the calamity of 'Ad. [["Al-Misy" (with a damma and then sukun): evening, like "al-subh" and "al-sabah." In the printed edition and Tarikh: "the evening of the third," and what is in the manuscript is preferred.]] He informed them of the news, and they said to him: "Where did you leave Hud and his companions?" He said: "I left them on the seashore." They seemed to doubt what he told them, so Hudhayla bint Bakr said: "He speaks the truth, by the Lord of the Ka'ba!" [[In the printed edition: "Hudhayla," and the correct reading is from the manuscript and Tarikh.]] [[The report: 14804. This report was related by al-Tabari in his History, abridged at its beginning and expanded later at its end, 1: 111–113.]]

14805 – Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash narrated to us, he said: 'Asim narrated to us, from al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri, who said: I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I passed by a woman at al-Rabadha. [[In the printed edition: "upon a woman," and what is in the manuscript is preferred.]] She said: "Will you carry me to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?" I said: "Yes!" So I carried her until we reached Madina, and I entered the mosque, and there was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the minbar, and Bilal was wearing a sword, and there were black banners. I said: "What is this?" They said: "'Amr ibn al-'As has returned from his expedition." When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) descended from his minbar, I went to him and asked permission, and he permitted me. I said: "O Messenger of Allah, at the door is a woman from the Banu Tamim, and she asked me to carry her to you." He said: "O Bilal, let her in." She entered, and when she sat down, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "Is there something between you and Tamim?" I said: "Yes! And the defeat was against them," [[In the printed edition: "and the victory was for us against them," an addition beyond the manuscript which distorts the text; the correct reading is from the manuscript. "Al-Dabara" (with fatha of the dal and sukun or fatha of the ba'): defeat for them, and dominance and victory for the others.]] so if you see fit to place Dahna' between us and them as a barrier, you may do so!" He said: The woman said: "Then where will your Mudar go, O Messenger of Allah?" [[In the printed edition: "Then where will the one who is compelled be compelled, O Messenger of Allah," which is a faulty and reprehensible alteration and an extreme distortion. The correct reading is that of the manuscript. "Mudar" is the root of the Arabs, namely "Mudar ibn Nizar ibn Ma'add ibn 'Adnan," from whom Quraysh and Banu Tamim branched. This is why the woman from Tamim said "your Mudar" to the Messenger of Allah, because he was her grandfather and his.]] I said: "My likeness is that of a goat that carried its death!" [[In the printed edition: "My likeness is like what the first one said: a goat that carried its death," adding from another narration, which is a severe distortion, and changing "hatfan" to "hatfuha." I have preferred what matches the narration in Tarikh. And his saying: "a goat that carried its death," means it carried its fate; it is a proverb for one who carries what will destroy him. It is not found in the books of proverbs.]] I said: "And I have carried you, you will be an adversary to me! I seek refuge in Allah that I become like the delegation of 'Ad!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "And what is the delegation of 'Ad?" I said: "You have fallen upon one who knows! 'Ad suffered drought, so they sent someone to seek rain for them. They sent men who passed by Bakr ibn Mu'awiya, and he gave them wine to drink, and two singing girls entertained them for a month. Then he sent a man from among them until he reached the mountains of Mahra, [["Mahra" (with fatha then sukun): a great tribe, and the ancestor of a tribe: "Mahra ibn Haydan ibn 'Amr ibn al-Haf ibn Qudha'a." The lands of Mahra are in the region of Shihr in Yemen, in the lands of al-'Anbar on the seashore. In the printed edition and the manuscript it reads: "Then they departed from his presence until they came to the mountains of Mahra," and this sentence badly disrupts the flow of the report, the pronouns shift, and the report has no coherent thread. It seems to be a scribal error, for Abu Ja'far related this report in Tarikh with its chain and wording, so I have adopted from it the text of the report, as it is what makes the speech coherent.]] and they prayed, and clouds came. He said: Whenever a cloud came, he would say: "Go to such and such," until a cloud came, and a call came from it: "Take it, ramadan ramdad, * which leaves none of 'Ad alive." He said: He heard it, and he concealed it from them until the punishment came upon them. [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "He heard them and spoke to them," and the correct reading is from Tarikh.]]

Abu Kurayb said: Abu Bakr said after that in the report about 'Ad: He said: Then the one who had come to them came, and he came to the mountains of Mahra, [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "the ones who came to them," and the correct reading is from Tarikh.]] and he climbed up and said: "O Allah, I have not come to You to free a captive so that I may ransom him, nor for a sick person so that I may cure him. So give 'Ad drink as You used to give them to drink!" He said: Clouds were raised for him, and a call came from them: "Choose!" He said: He began to say: "Go to the Banu so-and-so, go to the Banu so-and-so." He said: Then the last of them passed, a black cloud, and he said: "Go to 'Ad!" A call came from it: "Take it, ramadan ramdad, which leaves none of 'Ad alive." He said: And he concealed it from them, [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "and he spoke to them," and the correct reading is from Tarikh.]] while the people were with Bakr ibn Mu'awiya, drinking. He said: Bakr ibn Mu'awiya disliked telling them, because they were his guests and were eating his food. He said: So he began to sing and reminded them. [[Report 14805: "Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash," a trustworthy narrator, one of the devout and precise memorizers, but when he grew old his memory deteriorated, so he would err when narrating. Error and mistake are two things that no human being is free from, and whoever does not commit them frequently does not deserve to have his narrations abandoned, once his probity is established. Thus said Ibn Hibban, and he spoke truly. It has passed under numbers 2150, 3000, 5725, 8098.

And "'Asim" is "'Asim ibn Bahdala," "'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud," a trustworthy, eminent, well-known narrator, who has passed many times.

As for "al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri," it is said of him: "al-Harith ibn Yazid al-Bakri," and it is said his name is "Hurayth." Ibn 'Abd al-Barr affirmed that his name is "al-Harith ibn Hassan," saying: "Most say al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri, and this is the sound one, God willing." But it is strange that al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in al-Tahdhib: "Ibn 'Abd al-Barr affirmed that his name is Hurayth," and he erred a great error, for what I quoted is the text of Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in al-Isti'ab!! So let what is in al-Tahdhib be corrected.

"Al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri" is biographed in Ibn Sa'd 6: 22, al-Kabir of al-Bukhari 1/2/259, al-Isti'ab: 109, Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/71, Usd al-Ghaba 1: 323, al-Isaba in his biography, and al-Tahdhib. Abu Wa'il and Sammak ibn Harb related from him.

The report of "al-Harith al-Bakri" will come with another chain: "from 'Asim, from Abu Wa'il, from al-Harith ibn Yazid al-Bakri."

As for this chain, "'Asim, from al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri," with no "Abu Wa'il" between them, Ibn al-Athir said in Usd al-Ghaba in the biography of "al-Harith": "Ahmad ibn Hanbal also related it, and Sa'id al-Umawi, Yahya al-Himmani, 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Sala, and Abu Bakr ibn Shayba, all of them from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash, from 'Asim, from al-Harith, without mentioning Abu Wa'il." Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in al-Tahdhib in the biography of "al-Harith": "'Asim ibn Bahdala related from him," and the correct version is: from him, from Abu Wa'il, from al-Harith.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said in al-Isti'ab: "There is disagreement regarding his narration: some make it from 'Asim ibn Bahdala, from al-Harith ibn Hassan, without mentioning Abu Wa'il, while the correct version is: from 'Asim, from Abu Wa'il, from al-Harith ibn Hassan." Others said likewise.

This report with this chain was related by Abu Ja'far again in his History 1: 110. Ahmad in his Musnad 3: 481 related its beginning: "from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash, who said: 'Asim ibn Abi al-Fazr (??) narrated to us, from al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri," abridged, and it is the beginning of the report. As for what came in the printed Musnad, "'Asim ibn Abi al-Fazr," I deem it likely to be a distortion of "'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud," for the narration is his, and I have not known that he is called "'Asim ibn Abi al-Fazr."

Ibn Maja also related it in abridged form through this same route in his Sunan, p. 941, no. 2816, with wording similar to Ahmad's.

The takhrij of this report of "al-Harith" will come in the following report.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 7, verses 68–69 (part 3 of 3):**

14806. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Zayd ibn al-Habbab narrated to us, saying: Salam Abu al-Mundhir al-Nahwi (the grammarian) narrated to us, saying: 'Asim narrated to us, from Abu Wa'il, from al-Harith ibn Yazid al-Bakri, who said: "I set out to complain about al-'Ala' ibn al-Hadrami to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). I passed by al-Rabadhah and found an old woman who had been cut off there [[“Munqati‘ bihā” (with the *mīm* vowelled, and the *qāf* and *ṭā’* with fatḥa). It is said: “qutiʿa bi-l-rajul, fa-huwa maqṭūʿ bihi,” and “inqaṭaʿa bihi, fa-huwa munqaṭiʿ bihi” (all in the passive form), when a traveller’s mount has perished and his provisions and wealth are gone, or when a matter befalls him that prevents him from moving.]] from the Banu Tamim. She said: 'O servant of God, I have a need of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Will you convey me to him?' He said: 'So I carried her and we reached Medina. Then I saw banners [[At this point Abu Ja‘far said, in his narration in the *Tarikh*: “Abu Ja‘far said: I think he said: ‘Then I saw black banners.’”]] and said: "What is the matter with the people?" They said: "He wishes to dispatch ‘Amr ibn al-‘As on an expedition." [[In the printed edition: “‘Amr ibn al-‘As”, with the *bāʾ* omitted; it is established in the manuscript and in the narration of this report in the *Tarikh*.]] He said: 'So I sat until he had finished. Then he entered his dwelling, or he said: his camel-saddle, and I asked permission to see him, and he permitted me. I entered and sat, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to me: "Was there any dispute between you and Tamim?" I said: "Yes! And we had the upper hand over them, [[In the printed edition: “wa-kānat lanā al-dārah ʿalayhim”; in the manuscript: “wa-kānat al-dāʾirah ʿalayhim”, undotted. The narration of Abu Ja‘far in the *Tarikh* and the narration of Ahmad in his *Musnad* are preferred. See the note above, p. 514, n. 1.]] and I passed by al-Rabadhah, where there was an old woman from them, cut off there, who asked me to carry her to you, and here she is at the door." So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) permitted her, and she entered. I said: "O Messenger of God, make between us and Tamim a barrier of al-Dahna." The old woman grew angry and became agitated [[“Ḥamiyat”: she became angry, seized by zeal, pride and rage. “Istawfaza al-rajul fi qaʿdatihi”: when a man sits upright without settling down, not standing fully, like one readying to leap up; this occurs at times of evil, quarrel, dispute and contention.]] and said: "Then where will you take your Mudar, O Messenger of God?" [[In the printed edition: “fa-ila ayna yuḍṭarru muḍṭarraka”, which is a change from what is in the manuscript and an addition to it, as was done in the earlier report, p. 514, n. 2.]] He said: I said: "I am as the first one said: 'A goat that carried its own death!' [[In the printed edition: “ḥatfahā”, which agrees with Ahmad’s narration in his *Musnad*; but what I have established is what is in the manuscript and the *Tarikh*, except that in the *Tarikh* it reads “ḥayfan”, which is an error; the correct reading is what I have given. See above, p. 514, n. 3.]] I carried this one and did not realise that she would be an adversary to me! I seek refuge in God and His Messenger from being like the envoy of ‘Ad!" He said: "And what is the envoy of ‘Ad?" I said [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: “He said: ‘You have fallen upon one who knows’”; I have established what is in the *Tarikh*.]] "You have fallen upon one who knows!" He said: and he was asking me for the story [[“Istaṭʿamahu al-ḥadith”: he tempted him to narrate to him, as if he wanted to let him taste the flavour of his narration. This is said when he lures him into it while knowing the narration better than him. Its explanation is found in Ahmad’s *Musnad*: “and he knew the narration better than him, but he was asking him to tell it.” The explanation of this expression in the lexicographical books is not sufficient, so I have qualified it there.]]. I said: "Indeed ‘Ad suffered drought, so they sent Qayl as an envoy. He stayed with Bakr and they gave him wine for a month, and two slave-girls who were called ‘al-Jaradatan’ sang to him, [[In the printed edition: “wa-ghannathu jāriyatān”, different from the manuscript, and it agrees with the *Tafsir* and the *Musnad* of Ahmad.]] Then he went out to the mountains of Mahrah and called out: 'I have not come to a sick man that I might treat him, nor to a captive that I might ransom him. O God, give drink to ‘Ad as much as they used to give drink to you!' [[In the printed edition and the *Tarikh* of al-Tabari: “Allahumma asqi”; I have established what is in the manuscript. The rest of the sentence is displaced from its place in the manuscript, namely his saying: “mā kunta tusqīhi”, which is established in the *Tarikh*. But in the printed edition and the manuscript it reads “musqīhi”, as in the earlier report; yet “tusqīhi” is the narration of Abu Ja‘far in the *Tarikh* and also of Ahmad.]] Then dark clouds passed over him, and a voice called out from them: [[After his saying “a voice called out from them”, the words “mā kunta musqīhi” are placed, as I mentioned in the previous note.]] "Take it as ashes, scattering, leaving none of ‘Ad alive." He said: So the woman used to say: "Do not be like the envoy of ‘Ad!" And it did not reach me, O Messenger of God, that God sent upon them any wind except as much as flows through my ring." [[In the printed edition: “fa-fīmā balaghanī”; I have established what is in the manuscript, which agrees with Abu Ja‘far’s narration in the *Tarikh* and Ahmad’s narration in the *Musnad*.]] He said: Abu Wa'il said: "So it reached me too."] [[The report: No. 14806. This is another chain for the earlier report, the chain in which I pointed out that “Abu Wa’il” appears between “‘Asim ibn Bahdalah” and “al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri”, and that this is the correct one.

“Al-Harith ibn Yazid al-Bakri” is “al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri”, which is disputed, as I stated in the note on no. 14805.

“Salam Abu al-Mundhir al-Nahwi” is “Salam ibn Sulayman al-Muzani”. Yahya ibn Ma‘in said: “He is nothing.” Abu Hatim said: “Truthful, good in narration.” Al-Saji said: “Truthful, makes mistakes, not precise in narration.” Ibn Ma‘in said again: “His truthfulness is tolerated.” He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/2/135, Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/259, and Mizan al-I‘tidal 1:400.

As for “Abu Wa’il”, he is “Shaqiq ibn Salamah al-Asadi”, a trustworthy imam, who has been mentioned many times before.

As for the woman mentioned in this report and the earlier report, she is: “Qaylah bint Makhramah al-Tamimiyyah”, from the Banu al-‘Anbar ibn ‘Amr ibn Tamim. In some books she is mentioned as “al-Ghanawiyyah”, which is a misreading of “al-‘Anbariyyah”. The narration of Qaylah is a long narration, containing much that is strange; Ibn Hajar mentioned it in her biography in al-Isabah.

Investigating her report and the report of “al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri” or “Huraith ibn Hassan al-Shaybani”, the envoy of Bakr ibn Wa’il (as in her biography in Ibn Sa‘d 8:228), requires discussion beyond the scope of this place.

This report was narrated by Abu Ja‘far in his *Tarikh* with this same chain. Ahmad narrated it in his *Musnad* 3:481, 482, by two routes: from the route of ‘Affan, from Salam Abu al-Mundhir, from ‘Asim; then from the route of Zayd ibn al-Habbab, from Abu al-Mundhir Salam ibn Sulayman al-Nahwi, from ‘Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, in similar wording.

Ibn Sa‘d narrated it in *al-Tabaqat* 6:22, from the route of ‘Affan, from Salam Abu al-Mundhir, in abridged form.

Al-Bukhari narrated its beginning in *al-Kabir* 1/2/259.

Ibn al-Athir narrated it in the biography of “al-Harith” in *Usd al-Ghabah*, Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr in *al-Isti‘ab* in abridged form, and Ibn Hajar in *al-Isabah*. Ibn Kathir narrated it in his *Tafsir* 3:502 / 7:470, from the route of Ahmad’s *Musnad*. He also narrated it in *al-Bidayah wa-l-Nihayah* 1:127, 128, and said: “Ibn Jarir narrated it from Abu Kurayb, from Zayd ibn al-Habbab, with it. In his version it reads: ‘from al-Harith ibn Yazid al-Bakri’, and he narrated it. He also narrated it from Abu Kurayb, from Abu Bakr ibn ‘Ayyash, from ‘Asim, from al-Harith ibn Hassan al-Bakri, and he narrated it. I did not find in the copy ‘Abu Wa’il’, and God knows best.” I say: He means the earlier report; see the note there.

Ibn Kathir also said in *al-Bidayah wa-l-Nihayah*: “al-Tirmidhi narrated it from ‘Abd ibn Humayd, from Zayd ibn al-Habbab, with it. Al-Nasa’i narrated it from the hadith of Salam Abu al-Mundhir, from ‘Asim ibn Bahdalah, and Ibn Majah narrated it through him. Likewise, this hadith and this story have been cited by more than one exegete when interpreting this story, such as Ibn Jarir and others. This context may be for the destruction of the later ‘Ad, for what Ibn Ishaq and others mentioned contains no mention of Mecca, which was not built until after Abraham the Friend, when he settled Hagar and his son Ishmael there, and the Jurhum people settled with them, as will come. The first ‘Ad was before the Friend. It contains mention of ‘Mu‘awiyah ibn Bakr’ and his poetry, and this is poetry later than the time of the first ‘Ad, not resembling the speech of earlier people. It also states that in that cloud there were sparks of fire, whereas the first ‘Ad were only destroyed by a violent, roaring wind.”

This is a very good critique of all these earlier reports and the report that follows.]]

14807. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding God’s words: “And to ‘Ad their brother Hud, he said: O my people, worship God; you have no god other than Him”: that Hud came to ‘Ad, admonished them, and reminded them of what God recounted in the Qur’an, but they denied him and disbelieved, and they asked him to bring them the punishment. So he said to them: ﴿The knowledge is only with God, and I convey to you that with which I have been sent﴾ [Surah al-Ahqaf: 23]. When ‘Ad disbelieved, they were struck by a drought of rain [[In the *Tarikh*: “qaḥṭ min al-maṭar”.]] until they were afflicted with severe hardship. That was because Hud prayed against them, so God sent upon them the barren wind, which is the wind that does not fertilise trees. When they looked at it they said: ﴿This is a cloud bringing us rain﴾ [Surah al-Ahqaf: 24]. When it drew near them, they saw the camels and men being carried by the wind between heaven and earth. When they saw it, they hastened to the houses [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: “tanādawā al-buyūt”, which has no meaning; the correct form, from the *Tarikh*, is “tabādarū”, they hurried.]], and when they entered the houses, it entered upon them and destroyed them within them, then it brought them out of the houses and struck them with “a day of misfortune” — and *naḥs* is ill omen — and “continuing” [*mustamirr*], which continued upon them with punishment “for seven nights and eight days in succession” [*ḥusūman*] — it uprooted everything it passed over. [[This is the explanation of the verses, from Surah al-Qamar: 19, and Surah al-Haqqah: 7.]] When it removed them from the houses, God said: ﴿Plucking people up﴾ from the houses, ﴿as if they were trunks of uprooted palm trees﴾ [Surah al-Qamar: 20] — “uprooted” from its roots — “hollow”, which fell hollow. [[This is the explanation of the verse in Surah al-Haqqah: 7: “as if they were hollow trunks of palm trees.”]] When God destroyed them, He sent upon them black birds, which carried them to the sea and cast them into it. That is His saying: ﴿So they became such that nothing could be seen except their dwellings﴾ [Surah al-Ahqaf: 25]. No wind ever went out except by measure, except on that day, for it rebelled against the keepers and overpowered them, so they did not know how great its measure was. That is His saying: ﴿So they were destroyed by a roaring, violent wind﴾ [Surah al-Haqqah: 6] — and *ṣarṣar* is that which has a strong sound.

**Commentary on His words (ta'wil, interpretation):** ﴿They said, "Have you come to us so that we worship Allah alone and abandon what our fathers used to worship? Then bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful."﴾

Abu Ja'far said: God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: The people of 'Ad said to him [[In the manuscript: "qalat Hud lahu" ("Hud said to him"), which is clearly an error. The printed edition corrected it to "qalat 'Ad li-Hud" ("'Ad said to Hud"), and I have kept what the copyist's error suggests.]]: "Have you come to us threatening us with punishment from God for the religion we are upon, so that we worship Allah alone, submit to Him in pure obedience, abandon the worship of the gods and idols that our fathers used to worship, and disavow them? We will not do that, and we will not follow you in what you call us to [[In the printed edition: "wa la mutabi'ayka" ("nor followers of you"). In the manuscript: "wa la mutabi'uka" ("nor do we follow you"). The copyist dropped the word "nahnu" ("we"), and I have restored it.]]. So bring us what you threaten us with, of punishment and torment for our refusal to hold to pure monotheism toward Allah and for our worship of what we worship besides Him, the idols, if you are indeed among those who speak the truth in what you say and promise."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verse 71:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿He said: Indeed there has befallen you from your Lord abomination (rijs) and wrath. Do you dispute with me about names you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority? So wait; indeed I am with you among those who wait.﴾ (7:71)

Abu Ja'far said: He, exalted is His mention, says: Hud said to his people: Punishment and wrath from Allah has descended upon you.

* *

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' — as has been reported to us from him — used to claim that "al-rijz" (رجز) and "al-rijs" (رجس) have one meaning, and that they are transposed forms, the sin having been changed into a zayn, just as "sitt" (ستّ) is derived from "sadas" (سداس) with a sin. Likewise they say "qarbus" (قربوس) and "qarbut" (قربوت), and as the rajaz (poet) said:

Surely Allah curses the Banu al-Si'lat,
'Amr ibn Yarbu', the base of lineage,
They are not chaste, nor are they wise.

The word for "people" (الناس) and "wise" (أكياس) — the sin was changed into a ta', as Ru'bah said:

How often have we seen a numerous enemy...
until we trampled his plot with rijz.

Reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he would say: "al-rijs" means wrath.

Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to us, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Abomination has befallen you from your Lord﴾ — he said: wrath.

As for His saying: ﴿Do you dispute with me about names you have named, you and your fathers﴾ — He says: Do you contend with me about names you have named as idols that neither harm nor benefit? ﴿For which Allah has sent down no authority﴾ — He says: Allah has not granted you, in your worship of them, any proof by which you may argue, nor any excuse by which you may plead, because worship is only due to the One who harms and benefits, rewards obedience and punishes disobedience, provides and withholds. As for inanimate matter of stone, iron and copper, there is no benefit or harm in it, unless it is made into an instrument. There is no proof for one who worships what is other than Allah in his worship of it, because Allah has not permitted that; so the one who worships it cannot excuse himself by saying he worships it following a command of Allah regarding its worship. Nor is it — since Allah has not permitted its worship — something whose benefit is hoped for or whose harm is feared, now or later, so that it be worshipped in hope of its benefit or in averting its harm. ﴿So wait; indeed I am with you among those who wait﴾ — He says: So await the judgment of Allah concerning us and you; ﴿indeed I am with you among those who wait﴾ — awaiting His judgment and the decision of His ruling concerning us and you.

**The interpretation (ta'wil) of His words:** ﴿So We saved him and those with him by a mercy from Us, and We cut off the last remnant of those who denied Our signs, and they were not believers﴾ (7:72)

Abu Ja'far said: He, may He be exalted and remembered, says: We saved Nuh (Noah) and those who were with him of his followers, who believed in him, affirmed him, and affirmed what he called to, namely the oneness of God and the abandonment of idols and images, ﴿by a mercy from Us. And We cut off the last remnant of those who denied Our signs﴾, meaning: We destroyed those of the people of Hud who denied Our proofs, all of them, to the last of them, so that We left none of them, as:

14809: Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His words, ﴿And We cut off the last remnant of those who denied Our signs﴾: "He said: We uprooted them."

* *

We have already explained earlier the meaning of His words, ﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off﴾ (6:45), with its evidences, in a way that suffices without repeating it. [[See the tafsir (exegesis) of "cutting off their last remnant" in what preceded, vol. 11, pp. 363–364.]]

* *

﴿And they were not believers﴾, meaning: they had not been affirmers of God, nor of His messenger Hud.

**The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord. This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you, so leave her to eat in Allah's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you."﴾ (7:73)**

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is He, the One who is mentioned, says: "And We certainly sent to Thamud their brother Salih."

* * *

"Thamud" is Thamud ibn Ghathir ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh. He was the brother of Jadis ibn Ghathir. [[In the printed edition, in both places, it reads "Thamud ibn 'Abir" and "Jadis ibn 'Abir." I have adopted what is in the manuscript. In Tarikh al-Tabari 1:103 it is "Ghathir" with the letters ghayn and thaʼ, except that in Tarikh 1:115 it appears as "Jathir" with jim and thaʼ. It seems that the first is the original and the latter is a metathesis of the ghayn, unless it is an error.]] Their dwellings were al-Hijr, between the Hijaz and al-Sham, extending to Wadi al-Qura and its surroundings.

* * *

The meaning of the statement is: "And to the people of Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih."

* * *

The word "Thamud" is not declined (as a diptote) because "Thamud" is a tribe, just as "Bakr" is a tribe, and likewise "Tamim."

* * *

﴿He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him."﴾ He means: Salih said to Thamud: "O my people, worship Allah alone, with no partner. You have no deity whom it is permissible for you to worship besides Him. There has certainly come to you a proof and a demonstration confirming the truth of what I say, [[See the explanation of "al-bayyinah" in the earlier language indexes under (b-y-n).]] and the reality of what I call to: sincerely devoting monotheism to Allah and singling Him out for worship to the exclusion of everything else, and my attestation that I am His messenger. My clear evidence for what I say, and the reality of what I brought you from my Lord, and my argument against you, is this she-camel which Allah brought forth from this rocky hill, as proof of my prophethood and the truth of my speech. You know that this is one of the miracles which no one is able to produce like except Allah."

* * *

As for Salih's citing the she-camel as proof of the validity of his prophethood to his people Thamud, it is because, as it has reached me, they asked him for it as a sign and an indication of the truth of his words.

The mention of who said this, and the mention of the cause of the people of Salih's killing of the she-camel:

14810 – Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Israil informed us, from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Rafi', from Abu al-Tufayl, who said: Thamud said to Salih: "Bring us a sign if you are among the truthful!" He said: Salih said to them: "Go out to a rocky hill in the land!" So they went out, and behold, it was heaving as a pregnant woman heaves, then it split open and the she-camel emerged from its midst. Salih said: ﴿This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you; so leave her to eat in Allah's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you.﴾ (= ﴿For her is a drink, and for you is a drink on a known day.﴾ [Surah al-Shu'ara: 155]). When they became weary of her, they hamstrung her. He said to them: ﴿Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days; that is a promise not to be denied.﴾ [Surah Hud: 65]. 'Abd al-'Aziz said: A man other than him narrated to me that Salih said to them: "The sign of the punishment is that you will wake up tomorrow red, and the second day yellow, and the third day black." He said: So the punishment came upon them at dawn. When they saw that, they applied embalming spices and prepared themselves. [[The report 14810: 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Rafi' al-Asadi was a trustworthy Successor (tabi'i), whom the collectors of hadith all narrated from. He narrated from Anas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar and Abu al-Tufayl. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib. Abu al-Tufayl is 'Amir ibn Wathila al-Laythi, who passed earlier under number 9196. His saying "tahannatu" means they took the "hanut," as is done for the dead. "Hanut" is a powdered mixture of musk, ambergris, camphor or sandalwood, or aloe, prepared for the deceased so that the body does not decay or stink, or so that its smell is not noticed by the living. Number "14811" was omitted from the numbering by mistake on my part.]]

14812 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih﴾, who said: God sent Salih to Thamud, and he called them, but they denied him. He said to them what God mentioned in the Qur'an. They asked him to bring them a sign, so he brought them the she-camel, having a share of water, and they had a share on a known day. He said: ﴿Leave her to eat in Allah's earth, and do not touch her with harm.﴾ They all acknowledged her, and that is His saying: ﴿And as for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Surah Fussilat: 17]. They had acknowledged it out of hypocrisy and dissimulation. The she-camel had her share of water: on the day she drank, she would pass between two mountains, and they would have mercy on her, and her footprint remained in them until the Hour. Then she would come and stand before them until they milked the milk, and it would suffice them; she poured it out in a flow. On the day they drank water, she would not come to them. She had a young camel with her, and Salih said to them: "A boy will be born in this month of yours, and your destruction will be at his hands!" Nine of them had children born in that month, so they slaughtered their sons. Then a child was born to the tenth man, but he refused to slaughter his son, and he had not had any child before that. The son of the tenth man was blue-eyed and reddish, and he grew quickly. When he passed by the nine and they saw him, they said: "If our sons were alive, they would have been like this!" So the nine became angry at Salih, because he had commanded them to slaughter their sons. ﴿They said: "Swear by Allah that we will surely attack him and his family by night, then we will say to his heir: We did not witness the destruction of his family, and we are truthful."﴾ [Surah al-Naml: 49]. They said: "We will go out, so people will see that we have gone out on a journey; then we will come to the cave and stay in it. When it is night and Salih goes out to the mosque, we will come to him and kill him, then return to the cave and remain in it. Then we will return and say: ﴿We did not witness the destruction of his family, and we are truthful.﴾" They will believe us, knowing that we went out on a journey! So they set off, and when they entered the cave they wanted to come out at night, but the cave collapsed upon them and killed them. That is His saying: ﴿And there were in the city nine men who spread corruption in the land and did not reform.﴾ [Surah al-Naml: 48] until His saying here: ﴿So look at the outcome of their plotting, that We destroyed them and their people entirely.﴾ [Surah al-Naml: 51]. The boy, the son of the tenth man, grew up and developed astonishingly fast. He sat with a group of people who were drinking wine, and they wanted water to mix with their wine. That day was the day of the she-camel's drinking. They found that the she-camel had drunk the water. This was hard for them, and they said about the she-camel: "What shall we do with milk? If only we could take this water that this she-camel drinks, and give it to our cattle and our crops, it would be better for us!" The boy, the son of the tenth man, said: "Shall I hamstring her for you?" They said: "Yes!" They then revealed their religion. The boy came to her, and when she saw him she charged at him, and he fled from her. When he saw that, he went behind a rock on her path and hid behind it. He said: "Drive her toward me!" So they drove her toward him, and when she passed by, they called out to him: "Take her!" He seized her and hamstrung her, and she fell. That is His saying: ﴿So they called to their companion, and he took [it] and hamstrung [it].﴾ [Surah al-Qamar: 29]. At that point they revealed their matter, hamstrung the she-camel, and rebelled against the command of their Lord, and they said: "O Salih, bring us what you threaten us with!" Some of them fled to Salih and informed him that the she-camel had been hamstrung. He said: "Bring me the young camel!" They sought the young camel and found it on a hill of the land, so they went after it, but it rose up with it until it soared with it into the sky, and they could not reach it. Then the young camel cried out to God [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "then he called," and the correct reading is what I have adopted, from "rughā' al-nāqa," which is the sound of a she-camel when she cries out.]], so God revealed to Salih: "Command them to enjoy themselves in their homes for three days!" So Salih said to them: "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days, and the sign of that is that your faces will turn yellow on the first day, reddish on the second, and black on the third, and on the fourth day the punishment will come." When they saw the signs, they shrouded themselves, applied embalming spices, smeared themselves with bitter myrrh, wore leather mats, dug trenches and entered them, awaiting the cry, until the punishment came upon them and they perished. That is His saying: ﴿We destroyed them and their people entirely.﴾

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: When God destroyed 'Ad and its affair came to an end, Thamud lived long after them [["'amara ya'muru" (like faraha yafrahu) and "'amara ya'muru" (like nasara yansuru): he lived and remained for a long time.]] and they were made successors in the land. They settled in it and spread out, then they transgressed against God. When their corruption became apparent and they worshipped other than God, He sent Salih to them. They were an Arab people, and he was among the most noble of them in lineage and the best of them in position [[In the printed edition: "They were a people 'azab" and in the manuscript: "They were an Arab people, and they were among the middle of them," and what I have adopted is the correct reading.]], as a messenger [[The context: "He sent Salih to them as a messenger."]]. Their dwellings were al-Hijr up to Qurh, [["Qurh" (with a dammah then a sukun), which is the market of Wadi al-Qura.]] which is Wadi al-Qura, and between them was a distance of eighteen miles, lying between the Hijaz and al-Sham. God sent to them a young boy, and he called them to God until his hair turned white and he grew old, and only a few weak people followed him. When Salih persisted with them in calling them, and repeatedly warned them, and frightened them with God's punishment and vengeance, they asked him to show them a sign that would confirm what he said in calling them. He said to them: "What sign do you want?" They said: "Come out with us to this festival of ours." They had a festival to which they went out with their idols and what they worshipped besides God, on a known day of the year. "Then you call on your God and we will call on our gods. If yours is answered, we will follow you! And if ours is answered, you will follow us!" Salih said to them: "Yes!" So they went out with their idols to that festival, and Salih went out with them to God. They called upon their idols and asked them that Salih not be answered in anything he called upon. Then Jundu' ibn 'Amr ibn Jawwas ibn 'Amr ibn al-Duml [[In the printed edition: "Hurash," and perhaps what is in the manuscript should be read as I have given it, as will come in another lineage shortly.]], who was at that time the chief and the great one of Thamud, said to him: "O Salih, bring us out of this rock" — a single rock in an area of al-Hijr, called al-Kathiba — "a she-camel, pregnant, large-bellied and woolly." [["Al-mukhtarijah" is what resembles the Bukht camel. The explanation of "al-mukhtarijah" I have not found in any other report than this one, and it is similar in Qisas al-Anbiya' by al-Tha'labi. "Bukht" camels are long-necked camels, the Khurasani camels, produced from a cross between an Arab and a Falij camel.]] Thamud said to Salih what Jundu' ibn 'Amr had said: "If you do it, we will believe in you and affirm you, and testify that what you brought is the truth!" Salih took their solemn covenants: "If I do it, and God does it, you will surely affirm me and believe in me!" They said: "Yes!" And they gave him their covenants on that. Salih then asked his Lord to bring her out for them from that rocky hill, as they had described.

= Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Ya'qub ibn 'Utba ibn al-Mughira ibn al-Akhnas, that he related: They looked at the rocky hill when Salih called upon God with what he called upon Him, and it was heaving with the she-camel as a pregnant camel heaves with its young [["Al-nataj" (with a fatha on the nun): the pregnant one.]]. The hill shook, then the she-camel was thrown out with it [[In the printed edition: "then the she-camel fell," which differs from the manuscript, which has: "then the she-camel was ..." all unpointed, so I saw the correct reading as I have adopted.]], and it split open to reveal a she-camel, as they had described: large-bellied, woolly, pregnant, whose two sides, between them, its size is known only to God. Jundu' ibn 'Amr and those with him of his kin believed in him, and the nobles of Thamud wanted to believe and affirm him. But Dhu'ab ibn 'Amr ibn Labid, al-Habab the keeper of their idols, and Rabab ibn Sam'ar ibn Jalhas, who were among the nobles of Thamud, forbade them, and they turned the nobles away from Islam and from entering what Salih called them to of mercy and salvation. [[In the printed edition: "and they turned away its nobles," with a waw, while what is in the manuscript is more appropriate.]] Jundu' had a cousin called "Shihab ibn Khalifa ibn Makhla ibn Labid ibn Jawwas," and he wanted to become a Muslim, but those men forbade him from that, and he obeyed them. He was among the nobles of Thamud and its distinguished men. A man of Thamud called "Mahwas ibn 'Anama ibn al-Duml," who was a Muslim, said:

A band of the family of 'Amr had called Shihab
to the religion of the Prophet,
the mighty one of all Thamud together.
He was resolved to answer, and had he answered,
Salih would have been mighty among us,
and they would not have deviated from their companion Dhu'ab.
But the deviants of the family of Hujr
turned away after their rectitude, like a fly. [[In the printed edition: "dhi'ab" (wolves), and in al-Bidaya wa al-Nihaya "dha'ab," and it seems the correct reading is what is in Qisas al-Anbiya', which is what I have given. The manuscript is unpointed.]]

The she-camel that God brought forth for them remained in the land of Thamud with her young, grazing on the trees and drinking water. Salih, peace be upon him, said to them: ﴿This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you; so leave her to eat in Allah's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you.﴾ God said to Salih: "The water is a division among them; each share is attended" — that is, the water is in two halves: for them a day, and for her a day, when she attends, so on her day she does not let them drink. [[This is the explanation of the verse of Surah al-Qamar: 28.]] He said: ﴿For her is a drink, and for you is a drink on a known day.﴾ [Surah al-Shu'ara: 155]. It was, as it has reached me, and God knows best, that when she came, and she used to come every other day [["Ghibban" (with a kasra on the ghayn), that is, she came one day and left one day, then came again.]], she would place her head in a well in al-Hijr called "the Well of the She-Camel," and they claim that she drank from it when she came, placing her head in it, and would not raise it until she had drunk every drop of water in the valley. Then she would raise her head and spread her legs apart [[In the printed edition: "tafassaḥa" (she made space), while the correct reading is what I have given. "Tafashshajat al-nāqa" (with a jim) means she spread apart, which is that she distanced her legs; similarly "tafashshahat" with an unmarked ḥāʼ.]] = meaning she spread her legs apart for them = so they could milk as much milk as they wanted, and they would drink and store, until they filled all their vessels. Then she would leave by a different passage from the one by which she had come, and she could not leave by the place she came in, because it was too narrow for her, so she would not return by it. When the next day came, it was their day, and they drank as much water as they wanted and stored what they wanted for the day of the she-camel, and they had abundance from that. It is said that the she-camel, in summer, when the heat was intense, would stay on the high ground of the valley, and their livestock, sheep, cattle and camels, would flee from her, and would descend to the lowland of the valley in its heat and dryness [[Because the livestock flee from her when they see her.]], and in winter they would stay in the lowland of the valley, and their livestock would flee to the high ground of the valley in the cold and the dryness, so this harmed their livestock as a trial and a test. Their pastures, it is claimed, were al-Habab and Hisma; all of that was grazed alongside Wadi al-Hijr. This became burdensome to them, so they rebelled against the command of their Lord, and unanimously resolved to hamstring the she-camel.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verse 73 (part 2 of 3):

= There was a woman from Thamud called ʿUnayzah bint Ghanam ibn Mijlaz, who was known by the kunya Umm Ghanam. She was from the Banu ʿUbayd ibn al-Mahl, the brother of Rumayl ibn al-Mahl. [[In the printed edition: "Dumayl". In the manuscript the letter is clearly "Rāʾ". The name "al-Dumayl" was mentioned earlier in the genealogies of this report, so I do not know whether they are one person or two different names.]] She was the wife of Dhu'ab ibn ʿAmr. She was an elderly woman, and she had beautiful daughters and wealth in camels, cattle and sheep.= And another woman, called Sadūf bint al-Muhayya ibn Dahr ibn al-Muhayya, [[In the printed edition: "bint al-Muhayya ibn Zuhayr". I have kept what is in the manuscript. In Qisas al-Anbiya: "Mahr".]] was the chief of the Banu ʿUbayd and the keeper of their idols in the earlier time. The valley was called "Wadi al-Muhayya", and it was the Greater al-Muhayya, the grandfather of the Lesser al-Muhayya, who was the father of Sadūf.= Sadūf was one of the most beautiful people, and she was wealthy, with camels, sheep and cattle.= The two women were among the most hostile of the women of Thamud towards Salih, and the greatest in their disbelief in him. [[In the printed edition: "wa-aʿẓamuhum bihi kufran" (and the greatest of them in disbelief in him). It seems the editor disliked what is in the manuscript, but the manuscript reading is the correct Arabic: after the comparative form (afʿal), the pronoun is repeated in the singular masculine, as in the hadith about the women of Quraysh: "The best women who rode camels are the good women of Quraysh, the most tender to a child in its infancy and the most careful with a husband in what is in her possession." Also as Dhu al-Rummah said: "Mayya is the most beautiful of the two weights in neck, and the nape of her neck, and the best of it is the forelock." This matter was mentioned in earlier volumes: 5:448, note 2; and p. 557, note 1; 6:395, note 1; 7:87, note 4.]] They were both plotting to have the she-camel hamstrung, though they disbelieved in him, because she had harmed their livestock.

Sadūf was married to a maternal cousin of hers called Sintam ibn Harawah ibn Saʿd ibn al-Ghutrayf, from the Banu Hulayl. He became Muslim and his Islam was good. Sadūf had entrusted her wealth to him, and he spent it on those who had become Muslim with him, among the companions of Salih, until the wealth diminished. Sadūf became aware of his Islam because of this, and she rebuked him for it. He then revealed his religion to her and called her to God and to Islam, but she refused him and plotted against him at night. [[In the printed edition: "wa-sabat waladahu" (and she abducted his children). This is pure nonsense. In the manuscript it is "wa-sabba lahu", unpointed, and I believe the correct reading is what I have given. "Bayyatat lahu": she schemed about the matter, planned it and arranged it at night.]] She took his sons and daughters from him and hid them among the Banu ʿUbayd, her own clan. Sintam, her husband, was from the Banu Hulayl and was her maternal cousin. He said to her: "Return my children to me!" She said: "Not until I bring you to a contest before the Banu Sanʿan ibn ʿUbayd, or before the Banu Jundaʿ ibn ʿUbayd!" Sintam said to her: "Rather, I will bring you to a contest before the Banu Mirdas ibn ʿUbayd!" [[In the printed edition: "bal an aqūla ilā Banī Mirdās" (rather, that I say to the Banu Mirdas). The editor misread the manuscript because of its poor script, and so produced weak speech.]] This was because the Banu Mirdas ibn ʿUbayd had hastened to embrace Islam, while the others had been slow to do so. She said: "I will not bring you to a contest except before the one to whom you have called me!" The Banu Mirdas said: "By God, you will give him his children, willingly or unwillingly!" When she saw that, she gave them to him.

=Then Sadūf and ʿUnayzah conspired together to hamstring the she-camel, because of the misfortune that had come upon them. [[In the printed edition: "tahayyalā fī ʿaqr al-nāqah" (they both devised a plan to hamstring the she-camel), which is meaningless. The correct reading is what is in the manuscript, but the editor did not know its meaning. "Mahala bihi": he plotted against him and schemed to deceive him until he brought him to ruin.]] Sadūf then summoned a man of Thamud called al-Habbab to hamstring the she-camel, and offered him herself in return if he did it, but he refused her. So she summoned a cousin of hers called Musdaʿ ibn Mihraj ibn al-Muhayya and made herself his reward on condition that he hamstring the she-camel. She was one of the most beautiful people and was wealthy, with much property, so he agreed to this.= ʿUnayzah bint Ghanam summoned Qudar ibn Salif ibn Jundaʿ, a man from the people of Qurh. Qudar was a red-faced, blue-eyed, short man. They claimed that he was born of an illegitimate union with a man called Sahyad, and that he was not the son of his supposed father Salif, to whom he was ascribed, but that he had been born on the bed of Salif, and so he was called after him and attributed to him. ʿUnayzah said: "I will give you whichever of my daughters you want, on condition that you hamstring the she-camel!" ʿUnayzah was a noblewoman among the women of Thamud, and her husband Dhu'ab ibn ʿAmr was among the nobles of the men of Thamud. Qudar was mighty and protected among his people.

Qudar ibn Salif and Musdaʿ ibn Mihraj set out and incited some misguided people of Thamud, and seven men followed them, so that they were nine men. One of the nine who followed them was a man called Huwayl ibn Milgh, the maternal uncle of Qudar ibn Salif, a brother of his mother by the same father and mother. He was a powerful man from the people of al-Hijr. Also Duʿayr ibn Ghanam ibn Dāʿir, who was from the Banu Khalāwah ibn al-Mahl. And Daʾb ibn Mihraj, the brother of Musdaʿ ibn Mihraj. And five men whose names have not been preserved for us. [[The printed manuscript has a blank space to the end of the line, and in the margin is the letter "ṭ", indicating doubt and error.]] They lay in wait for the she-camel when she came back from the water, and Qudar hid for her at the foot of a rock beside her path, and Musdaʿ hid at the foot of another rock. She passed by Musdaʿ and he shot her with an arrow, which struck the sinew of her leg. ʿUnayzah's mother, Umm Ghanam, came out and ordered her daughter, who was one of the most beautiful people, to show herself to Qudar. She uncovered herself and showed him her face, and then urged him on. He attacked the she-camel with his sword, and cut the tendon of her hind leg. [[In the printed edition: "fa-kashafa ʿurqūbahā" (he uncovered her hock). I have kept what is in the manuscript: "khashafa raʾsahu bi-l-ḥajar" (he crushed his head with a stone). Anything that is crushed is "khashafa". It is also said: "sayf khāshif, khashīf, khashūf" (a sword that cuts). "Fa-ḥasaf", unpointed in the manuscript.]] She fell and bellowed a single bellow, warning her young one. Then he stabbed her in the throat and slaughtered her, and the young one ran off until it reached a high mountain, and then it came to a rock at the top of the mountain, terrified, and sheltered beside it. [[In the printed edition: "fa-rughā wa-lādha bihā" (it bellowed and sheltered beside it). In the manuscript, unpointed, and I believe the correct reading is what I have given here.]] = The name of the mountain, according to what they claim, was Sanaw. [[In the printed edition: "Ṣūr". I have kept what is in the manuscript, although I have doubts about it.]] = Then Salih came to them, and when he saw that the she-camel had been hamstrung, [[In the printed edition, "thumma" is omitted. It is present in the manuscript.]] he said: "You have violated the sanctity of God! So rejoice in the punishment of God, blessed and exalted, and His wrath!" Four men out of the nine who had hamstrung the she-camel followed the young one, and among them was Musdaʿ ibn Mihraj. Musdaʿ shot it with an arrow, which pierced its heart, and then he dragged it by its leg and brought it down. Then they threw its flesh together with the flesh of its mother.

=When Salih said to them, "Rejoice in the punishment of God and His wrath," they said to him, while mocking him: "When will that be, O Salih? And what is the sign of it?" = They used to name the days among themselves: Sunday was "Awwal", Monday "Ahwan", Tuesday "Dubār", Wednesday "Jubār", Thursday "Muʾnis", Friday "al-ʿArūbah", and Saturday "Shiyār". They had hamstrung the she-camel on Wednesday.= Salih said to them when they said that: "You will be awakened on the morning of Muʾnis, that is Thursday, with your faces yellow. Then you will be awakened on the day of al-ʿArūbah, that is Friday, with your faces red. Then you will be awakened on the day of Shiyār, that is Saturday, with your faces black. Then the punishment will overtake you on the day of Awwal, that is Sunday." When Salih said this to them, the nine who had hamstrung the she-camel said: "Come on, let us kill Salih! If he is truthful, we will hasten him to the others, and if he is lying, we will have joined him to his she-camel!" They came to him at night to attack him in his household, but the angels struck them down with stones. [[In the printed edition: "hallumū" (come on, all of you). I have kept what is in the manuscript, which is also correct.]] When they were slow to return to their companions, the people went to the house of Salih and found them crushed, struck down with stones. They said to Salih: "You killed them!" Then they intended to attack him, but his clan stood between him and them, and they put on weapons and said to them: "By God, you will never kill him! He has promised you that the punishment will descend upon you in three days. If he is truthful, you will only increase the wrath of your Lord against you, and if he is lying, you will be behind what you wish to do!" They turned away from them that night. The men whom the angels struck down with stones were the nine whom God mentioned in the Qur'an by His saying: ﴿And there were in the city nine men who spread corruption in the land and did not reform﴾, to His saying: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who know﴾. [Surah al-Naml: 48–52.]

=They awoke on the morning after the night in which they had turned away from Salih, with their faces yellow. They became certain of the punishment and knew that Salih had spoken truly, so they sought him in order to kill him. Salih went out fleeing from them until he took refuge with a clan of Thamud called the Banu Ghanam. He stayed with their chief, a man called Nufayl, who was known as Abu Hudb, and who was a polytheist. He hid him, so they could not reach him. They went to the companions of Salih and tortured them so that they would show them where he was. A man among the companions of Salih called Mida ibn Harim said: "O Prophet of God, they are torturing us so that we will point them to you. Should we point them to you?" He said: "Yes!" So Mida ibn Harim pointed them to him. When they learned where Salih was, they went to Abu Hudb and spoke to him. He said to them: "Salih is with me, and you have no means of reaching him!" They left him and let him be, and the punishment that God had sent upon them occupied them away from him. Some of them told the others what they saw in their faces on the morning of Thursday, because their faces had become yellow. Then on Friday they awoke with red faces, and then on Saturday with black faces. When the night of Sunday came, Salih went out from among them with those who had become Muslim with him, towards Syria, and he settled in the sands of Palestine. One of his companions called Mida ibn Harim stayed behind and settled in Qurh, which is the Wadi al-Qura, and the distance between Qurh and al-Hijr is eighteen miles. He stayed with their chief, a man called ʿAmr ibn Ghanam, who had eaten from the meat of the she-camel but had not taken part in killing her. Mida ibn Harim said to him: "O ʿAmr ibn Ghanam, leave this land, for Salih said: 'Whoever remains in it will perish, and whoever leaves it will be saved.'" ʿAmr said: "I did not take part in hamstringing her, and I did not approve of what was done to her!" When the morning of Sunday came, the Cry seized them, and not a child nor an adult among them survived, except for a paralysed girl called al-Zurayʿah, who was the daughter of al-Sulq, the wolf. [[In the printed edition: "al-Duraybah, wa-hiya Kulaybah ibn al-Sulq". In the manuscript: "al-Duraybah wa-hiya al-Kalbah ibn al-Sulq", which I have read as given here. "Al-Sulq" is the wolf, and they claim that the wolf impregnates a bitch and that its offspring by her is called "al-Duaysam", and dogs are called "the children of the sower". I think the correct reading is "al-Zurayʿah" with the diminutive, and that what follows it is an explanation of it, as is evident.
"Al-Sulq" (with a kasra on the sīn and a sukūn on the lām).]] She was an unbeliever and extremely hostile to Salih. God freed her legs after she had witnessed the entire punishment, and she went out faster than anything ever seen, until she came to the people of Qurh and told them what she had witnessed of the punishment and what had befallen Thamud. Then she asked for water and was given some, and when she drank it, she died. [[In the printed edition: "until she came to a tribe of the tribes, and told them", which differs from the manuscript, though the manuscript is correct. "Qurh" is the market of the Wadi al-Qura, as mentioned above.]]

14812 – al-Hasan ibn Yahya told us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq told us, saying: Maʿmar said: Someone who heard al-Hasan say informed me: When Thamud hamstrung the she-camel, her young one went off until it climbed a hill, and said: "O Lord, where is my mother?" Then it bellowed a bellow, and the Cry descended and extinguished them.

14813 – Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla told me, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr told us, from Maʿmar, from al-Hasan, something similar, except that he said: "It climbed a hill."

Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr told us, from Maʿmar, from Qatadah: that Salih said to them when they had hamstrung the she-camel: "Enjoy yourselves for three days!" And he said to them: "The sign of your destruction is that your faces will become yellow in the morning, then on the second day they will become red in the morning, then on the third day they will become black in the morning." And so it happened. When the third day came and they were certain of their destruction, they shrouded themselves and applied spices to their bodies, and then the Cry seized them and destroyed them. Qatadah said: The one who hamstrung the she-camel said to them: "I will not kill her until you all are content!" So they went to the woman in her seclusion and said: "Are you content?" She said: "Yes!" And to the child, until they were all content, and then he hamstrung her. [[In the printed edition: "fī khidrihā" (in her curtained room). I have kept the manuscript: "fī ḥijrihā" (in her protection/seclusion), meaning where she hides. If it were read "fī ḥujratihā", the plural of "ḥujrah" (a room), it would be very good.]]

Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Ishaq told us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq told us, from Maʿmar, from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUthman ibn Khuthaym, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, who said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by al-Hijr, he said: "Do not ask for signs, for the people of Salih asked for them. The she-camel used to come from this path and go out from this path. They disobeyed the command of their Lord, and hamstrung her. She used to drink their water one day, and they would drink her milk on another day. When they hamstrung her, the Cry seized them, and God destroyed everyone beneath the sky's surface among them, except for one man who was in the sanctuary of God." It was asked: "Who is he?" He said: "Abu Righal." When he left the sanctuary, what had befallen his people befell him. [[Report 14817: ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUthman ibn Khuthaym, the reciter, a reliable Successor. Mentioned earlier under numbers 4341, 5388, 7831, 9642.
This report was narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad 3:296 by this same route, with the same wording.
Ibn Kathir mentioned it in his Tafsir 3:505, and in al-Bidayah wa-al-Nihayah 1:137, and said: "This hadith meets the conditions of Muslim, but it is not in any of the six books."
The hafiz Ibn Hajar also mentioned it in al-Fath (6:270), and said: "Ahmad and al-Hakim narrated it with a good chain, from Jabir," and he mentioned the report.
It will come with another chain, number 14820.]] ... ʿAbd al-Razzaq said, Maʿmar said: Isma'il ibn Umayyah informed me that the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by the grave of Abu Righal, and said: "Do you know what this is?" They said: "God and His Messenger know best!" He said: "This is the grave of Abu Righal." They said: "Who was Abu Righal?" He said: "A man from Thamud who was in the sanctuary of God. The sanctuary of God protected him from the punishment of God, but when he left it, what had befallen his people befell him. He was buried here, and buried with him was a branch of gold!" The people dismounted and rushed to it with their swords, and dug around it, and brought out the branch. [[Report 14818: This report is mursal (its chain lacks a companion).
Isma'il ibn Umayyah al-Umawi is reliable, mentioned earlier under numbers 2615 and 8458.
This report was narrated by Abu Dawud in his Sunan 3:245, number 3088, as a connected report from the hadith of Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Isma'il ibn Umayyah, from Bujayr ibn Abi Bujayr, who said: I heard ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr say: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say, when we went out to al-Ta'if, and we passed by a grave.
Ibn Kathir mentioned Abu Dawud's hadith in his Tafsir 3:508 and in al-Bidayah 1:137, then said: "Thus Abu Dawud narrated it, from Yahya ibn Ma'in, from Wahb ibn Jarir ibn Hazim, from his father, from Ibn Ishaq, with it." Our shaykh Abu al-Hajjaj al-Mizzi said: "It is a good, rare hadith." I say: Bujayr ibn Abi Bujayr alone narrated it as a connected report, and he is a shaykh known only through this hadith. Yahya ibn Ma'in said: "I did not hear anyone narrate from him except Isma'il ibn Umayyah." I say [the speaker is Ibn Kathir]: In light of this, it is feared that he erred in raising this hadith, and that it may be a statement of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr taken from the two books of the Jews. Our shaykh Abu al-Hajjaj said, after I had presented this to him: "This is possible, and God knows best."
It will come with another chain, number 14823.]]

14814 – ... ʿAbd al-Razzaq said: Maʿmar said: al-Zuhri said: Abu Righal is Abu Thaqif.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verse 73 (part 3 of 3):

Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Abd Allah ibn Uthman ibn Khuthaym, from Jabir, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by al-Hijr = then he mentioned something similar, except that in his narration he said: They said: "Who is he, Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Abu Righal." [[The report: 14820. This is another chain for the earlier report no. 14817.]]

14815. Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Mu'adh ibn Hisham narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Qatadah, who said: It was said that the red one of Thamud, the one who hamstrung the she-camel, was the son of an adulterous union (zinyah).
