[[(1) The mention of "the calf" (al-ʿijl) has passed earlier at 2:63, 72, 354, 357 and 9:356, but he did not explain it except in this place.]] Then Exalted is His remembrance explained what that calf was, saying: "a body that had no lowing," and "al-khuwar" is the sound of cattle. He, great is His majesty, informs about them that they went astray by means of something by which people of intellect would not go astray. That is because the Lord, majestic is His majesty, to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and who manages them, may not be a body that has a lowing sound, that speaks to no one and does not guide to good. And those whose stories God has related said, for this: "This is our god and the god of Moses," so they clung to it, worshipping it, out of ignorance, and turning away from God and straying.

* *

We have already explained the cause of their worship of it, and how the taking of the calf occurred by those who took it among them, earlier, in a way that makes repeating it unnecessary. [[(2) See what has passed at 2:63–68, and then p. 74–78.]]

* *

In "al-ḥilī" (ornaments) there are two readings: the vowelling of the "ḥāʾ" with a ḍamma, which is the original form, and its vowelling with a kasra; likewise in every similar form such as "ṣallā," "juthiyy," and "ʿattiyy." Whichever of the two a reader recites, he is correct, because both readings are widely transmitted in recitation, and their meanings agree. [[(3) In the printed edition: "lā tufāriq bayna maʿnayayhimā" ("does not separate between their two meanings"), differing from the manuscript, which corrupts and distorts the sense. The correct reading is that of the manuscript, but I added the waw, because it is required by the sense of the sentence.]]

* *

As for His saying: "Did they not see that it does not speak to them and does not guide them to a way?" — it means: Did not those who clung to the calf which they had made from their ornaments, worshipping it, see that the calf does not speak to them and does not guide them to a way? That is, does it not guide them to a path? [[(1) See the explanation of "sabīl" (way) earlier in the language indexes under (s-b-l).]] And that is not a description of their Lord, to whom worship is truly due; rather His description is that He speaks to His prophets and messengers, guides His creation to the way of good, and forbids them the way of destruction and perdition. God, mentioned in praise, says: "They took it," that is, they took the calf as a god, and in taking it as a lord to be worshipped they were wrongdoers to themselves, by worshipping other than the One who deserves worship, and by ascribing divinity to other than the One who is truly divine.

* *

We have already explained the meaning of "ẓulm" (wrongdoing) earlier, in a way that makes repeating it unnecessary. [[(2) See the explanation of "ẓulm" earlier in the language indexes under (ẓ-l-m).]]

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And when they regretted and saw that they had gone astray, they said, "If our Lord has not mercy upon us and forgive us, we will surely be among the losers."﴾ (7:149)

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is He, by His saying "And when they regretted" He means: when those who worshipped the calf, whose description He, may His praise be extolled, has given, regretted upon the return of Musa to them, and submitted to Musa and his judgment concerning them.

* *

Thus the Arabs say of everyone who regrets a matter that has passed or elapsed from him, or who is incapable of something: "qad suqita fi yadayhi" (he was made to fall into his hands) and "uqsita" (he was made to fall), both being eloquent dialects. Its origin is from "al-istisar" (being taken captive), which is when a man strikes another man or throws him down, casting him from his hands to the ground in order to take him captive, and then binds him. So the one thrown down is "maswut fi yadayi" (fallen into the hands of) the one who threw him. It is then said of everyone who is unable to do something, and who is overcome by his incapacity, and regrets what he has done: "saqata fi yadayhi" and "usqita." [Footnote: See Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1:393, and Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubaydah 1:228. What Abu Ja'far said is a good elaboration and an explanation of the origin of the expression, which rarely is matched in the books of lexicography.]

* *

And by His saying "and saw that they had gone astray," He means: and saw that they had deviated from the right path, departed from the religion of God, and disbelieved in their Lord. They said, repenting to God and turning back to Him from their disbelief in Him: "If our Lord has not mercy upon us and forgive us, we will surely be among the losers."

* *

Then the readers differed in the recitation of this.

Some of the readers of Madinah, Makkah, Kufa and Basra recited: ﴿لَئِنْ لَمْ يَرْحَمْنَا رَبُّنَا﴾ with a nominative (ḍamm), as a statement (of fact).

* *

The majority of the readers of Kufa recited it: ﴿لَئِنْ لَمْ تَرْحَمْنَا رَبَّنَا﴾ with an accusative (naṣb), interpreting it as: "If You do not have mercy upon us, O our Lord" — as an address from them to their Lord. The readers of this reading argued that in one of the two recitations (of Ibn Mas'ud): ﴿قَالُوا رَبَّنَا لَئِنْ لَمْ تَرْحَمْنَا رَبَّنَا وتَغْفِرْ لَنَا﴾, and this is evidence of address. [Footnote: In the printed edition and the manuscript: "They said: If You have mercy upon us, our Lord, and forgive us," as in the verse in our copy of the Qur'an, and this contains no evidence of address. But what I have established is the one containing the evidence of address, by the placing of "our Lord" first; it is the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and it is likewise in the codex of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, as al-Farra' mentioned in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:393. His saying "The readers of this argued that in one of the two recitations" most likely refers to one of the two recitations of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. Also, the verse will come a few lines later correctly in the manuscript, but the editor of the printed edition altered it, as in the following note.]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The recitation most correct regarding this is the reading in the form of a statement, with the yā' in ﴿يَرْحَمْنَا﴾ and the nominative in His saying ﴿رَبُّنَا﴾, because nothing preceding it requires that it be directed as an address.

* *

The recitation whose transmission we have mentioned, ﴿قَالُوا رَبَّنَا لَئِنْ لَمْ تَرْحَمْنَا﴾, [Footnote: In the printed edition: "They said: If You do not have mercy upon us, our Lord," with "our Lord" delayed; the correct form is with it placed first as in the manuscript. This is a poor alteration by the editor. See the previous note.] we do not know its soundness from the aspect which must be submitted to.

* *

The meaning of His saying ﴿If our Lord has not mercy upon us and forgive us﴾: If our Lord does not turn kindly toward us with repentance through His mercy, and cover over our sins with it, then we will surely be among the destroyed whose deeds have failed. [Footnote: See the explanation of "mercy" (al-rahmah), "forgiveness" (al-maghfirah) and "loss" (al-khusran) in what has preceded: (r-ḥ-m), (gh-f-r), (kh-s-r).]

The interpretation of His words: ﴿When Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved, he said: "Evil is what you did after me. Did you hasten the command of your Lord?"﴾

Abu Ja'far said: May He be exalted in remembrance, says: When Moses returned to his people from the Children of Israel, he returned angry and grieved, because God had informed him that his people had been tested and that the Samiri had led them astray. This is why his return was angry and grieved.

* *

"Al-asaf" (grief mingled with anger) is intense anger and rage at one who has provoked it, as related:

1512[4]: Imran ibn Bakkar al-Kalla'i told me, saying: Abd al-Salam ibn Muhammad al-Hadrami told us, saying: Shurayh ibn Yazid told me, saying: I heard Nasr ibn Alqama say: Abu al-Darda' said: The words of God, "angry and grieved" (asafan): "Al-asaf" is a station beyond anger, more intense than it. Its explanation in the Book of God is: "He went to his people angry, and he went grieved."

[[Report 15124: Abd al-Salam ibn Muhammad al-Hadrami, known as "Sulaym," is biographied in al-Tahdhib, and al-Bukhari said of him: "He has been mentioned, and no criticism of him is recorded." Ibn Abi Hatim (3/1/48) also mentions him, and Ibn Hibban included him among the reliable narrators. Shurayh ibn Yazid al-Hadrami, Abu Hayya: al-Bukhari recorded no criticism of him, and Ibn Hibban judged him reliable. He is biographied in al-Tahdhib and al-Kabir (2/2/231). Nasr ibn Alqama al-Hadrami, Abu Alqama: Duhaym and Ibn Hibban judged him reliable, and al-Bukhari recorded no criticism of him. He is biographied in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir (4/2/102), and Ibn Abi Hatim (4/1/469). His narration from Abu al-Darda' is mursal (broken in its chain).]]

* *

Others said regarding this:

1512[5]: Musa ibn Harun told me, saying: Amr told us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: "asafan" means "grieved."

1512[6]: Muhammad ibn Sa'd told me, saying: My father told me, saying: My uncle told me, saying: My father told me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: "And when Moses returned to his people angry and grieved," he says: "asafan" means "grieved." And regarding the word in Al-Zukhruf, ﴿When they angered Us﴾ [43:55], he says: it means "they angered us." And "al-asaf" has two meanings: anger and grief.

1512[7]: Nasr ibn Ali told us, saying: Sulayman ibn Sulayman told us, saying: Malik ibn Dinar told us, saying: I heard al-Hasan say regarding His words, "And when Moses returned to his people angry and grieved," he said: angry and grieved.

* *

As for His words, "He said: Evil is what you did after me," meaning: How evil is the deed you committed after my departure from you, and how evil is what you did with the people I left behind and the religion your Lord commanded you. It is said of one who is left in charge of a family or people after someone departs from them: "Khalafahu bi-khayr" and "Khalafahu bi-sharr," meaning he was left in charge of them for good or for evil. [[(1) See the explanation of "khalafa" in what has preceded, p. 88, note 1, and the references there.]]

* *

As for His words, "Did you hasten the command of your Lord?" meaning: Did you get ahead of your Lord's command in your own selves, and turn away from it?

* *

It is said of this: "A certain person hastened this matter" when he preceded it. "A certain person hastened another" when he got ahead of him. "Do not hasten me, O so-and-so" means: do not leave me and abandon me. "Aajaltuhu" means: I urged him.

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿And he threw down the tablets and seized his brother by the head, dragging him towards him. He said: "Son of my mother! The people deemed me weak and nearly killed me, so do not let the enemies gloat over me, and do not place me with the wrongdoing people."﴾

Abu Ja'far said: May He be exalted in remembrance, says: And Moses threw down the tablets.

* *

Then the scholars differed about the reason he threw them down.

Some said: He threw them in anger at his people who worshipped the calf.

Those who said this:

1512[8]: Tamim ibn al-Muntasir told us, saying: Yazid informed us, saying: Al-Asbagh ibn Zayd informed us, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Ayyub, who said: Sa'id ibn Jubayr told me, saying: Ibn Abbas said: When Moses returned to his people angry and grieved, he seized his brother by the head, dragging him towards him, and threw down the tablets out of anger.

1512[9]: And Abd al-Karim told me, saying: Ibrahim ibn Bashshar told us, saying: Ibn Uyayna told us, saying: Abu Sa'd said, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: When Moses returned to his people, and he was near them, he heard their voices and said: "I hear the voices of a people at play." When he saw them, and they were devoted to the calf, he threw down the tablets and broke them, and he seized his brother by the head, dragging him towards him.

1512[10]: Musa told us, saying: Amr told us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, who said: Moses took the tablets, then returned to his people angry and grieved, and said: ﴿O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise?﴾ up to His words: ﴿So the Samiri cast [them]﴾ [20:86-87]. Then Moses threw down the tablets and seized his brother by the head, dragging him towards him. ﴿He said: "Son of my mother, do not seize my beard or my head"﴾ [20:94].

1512[11]: Ibn Humayd told us, saying: Salama related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: When Moses reached his people and saw what they were doing in worshipping the calf, he threw the tablets from his hand, then seized his brother by the head and beard, saying: ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me? Did you then disobey my command?﴾ [20:92-93].

* *

Others said: Moses only threw down the tablets because of virtues he had found in them that belonged to other than his people, and that weighed heavily on him.

Those who said this:

1512[12]: Bishr ibn Mu'adh told us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, regarding His words, "He took the tablets." Qatada said: He said: "My Lord, I find in the tablets a nation, the best nation brought forth for mankind, who enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. So make them my nation!" He said: "That is the nation of Ahmad!" He said: "My Lord, I find in the tablets a nation who are the last [in the order of creation] and the first to enter Paradise. My Lord, make them my nation!" He said: "That is the nation of Ahmad!" He said: "My Lord, I find in the tablets a nation whose Gospels are in their breasts; they recite them. Those before them read their Book by looking at it, and when they lifted it they retained nothing and understood nothing." Qatada said: God has given you, O nation, a memory that He has given to no other nation. He said: "My Lord, make them my nation!" He said: "That is the nation of Ahmad!" He said: "My Lord, I find in the tablets a nation who believe in the first Book and the last Book, and fight the remnants of error until they fight the one-eyed liar (al-Dajjal). So make them my nation!" He said: "That is the nation of Ahmad!" He said: "My Lord, I find in the tablets a nation whose charities they eat within their own bellies, and for which they are rewarded. The nations before them, when someone gave charity and it was accepted, God sent a fire that consumed it; and if it was rejected, it was left for birds and beasts to eat." Qatada said: God has taken your charities from your rich for your poor. He said: "My Lord, make them my nation!" He said: "That is the nation of Ahmad!" He said: "My Lord, I find in the tablets a nation, if one of them intends a good deed but does not perform it, a good deed is recorded for him; and if he performs it, ten times its like up to seven hundred is recorded for him. My Lord, make them my nation!" He said: "That is the nation of Ahmad!" He said: "My Lord, I find in the tablets a nation, if one of them intends an evil deed, it is not recorded against him until he does it; and if he does it, one evil deed is recorded against him. So make them my nation!" He said: "That is the nation of Ahmad!" He said: "My Lord, I find in the tablets a nation who are the responders and those to whom response is made. So make them my nation!" He said: "That is the nation of Ahmad!" He said: "My Lord, I find in the tablets a nation who are the intercessors and those for whom intercession is made. So make them my nation!" He said: "That is the nation of Ahmad!" Qatada said: It was mentioned to us that the Prophet of God, Moses, peace be upon him, cast down the tablets and said: "O God, make me one of the nation of Ahmad!" Then the Prophet of God, Moses, peace be upon him, was given two things that no prophet had been given. God said: ﴿O Moses, I have chosen you above mankind by My messages and My speech﴾ [7:144]. He said: The Prophet of God was content. Then he was given the second: ﴿And among the people of Moses is a nation who guide by the truth and by it act justly﴾ [7:159]. He said: The Prophet of God, peace be upon him, was fully content.

1512[13]: Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la told me, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr told us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, who said: When Moses took the tablets, he said: "My Lord, I find in the tablets a nation who are the best of nations, who enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. So make them my nation!" He said: "That is the nation of Ahmad!" He said: "My Lord, I find in the tablets a nation who are the last and the first on the Day of Resurrection. So make them my nation!" He said: "That is the nation of Ahmad." Then he mentioned something similar to the report of Bishr ibn Mu'adh, except that in his report it says: Then Moses, peace be upon him, threw down the tablets and said: "O God, make me one of the nation of Muhammad, may God bless them both."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The view closest to the truth regarding this matter is that the reason Moses threw down the tablets was his anger at his people for worshipping the calf, because God, may His praise be exalted, informed of this in His Book when He said: ﴿And when Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved, he said: "Evil is what you did after me. Did you hasten the command of your Lord?" And he threw down the tablets and seized his brother by the head, dragging him towards him.﴾

* *

It is mentioned that when God wrote the Torah for Moses, peace be upon him, on the tablets, He brought him near until he heard the scratching of the pen.

Those who said this:

1512[14]: Al-Harith told me, saying: Abd al-Aziz told us, saying: Isra'il related to us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Umara, from Ali, peace be upon him, who said: God wrote the tablets for Moses, peace be upon him, while he was hearing the scratching of the pens upon the tablets.

1512[15]: ... He said: Isra'il related to us, from Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: He brought him near until he heard the scratching of the pens. [[(1) Report 15135: Dots were placed in this report to indicate that this chain is appended to the preceding chain, whose opening reads: "Al-Harith told me, saying: Abd al-Aziz told us, saying: Isra'il told us..."]]

* *

It is said: The Torah was in seven parts. When Moses threw down the tablets, they broke, and six of its parts were lifted up. What was lifted included "the detailed explanation of everything," concerning which God said: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of every matter an admonition and a detailed explanation of all things﴾ [7:145]. The guidance and mercy remained in the seventh part, which is what God referred to in His words: ﴿He took the tablets, and in their inscription was guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord﴾ [7:154].

* *

The Torah, it is related, was seventy camel-loads, of which one section was read in a year, as related:

1512[16]: Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Muhammad ibn Khalid al-Makfuf told us, saying: Abd al-Rahman related to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: The Torah was revealed as seventy camel-loads, of which one section was read in a year. None read it except four men: Moses son of Imran, Jesus, Ezra, and Joshua son of Nun, peace be upon them.

* *

They differed regarding the "tablets."

Some said: They were of green emerald.

* *

Some said: They were of ruby.

* *

Some said: They were of hail (or crystal).

* *

Mention of the reports for what we have related on this:

1512[17]: Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Dawraqi told me, saying: Hajjaj ibn Muhammad related to us, from Ibn Juraij, who said: Ya'la ibn Muslim informed me, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Moses threw down the tablets and they broke, and only a sixth of them was lifted up. Ibn Juraij said: He informed me that the tablets were of chrysolite (zabarjad) and emerald from Paradise.

1512[18]: Musa ibn Sahl al-Ramli, Ali ibn Dawud, Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Shabawayh, and Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Tirmidhi told me, saying: Adam al-Asqalani informed us, saying: Abu Ja'far related to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliya, who said: The tablets of Moses, peace be upon him, were of hail. [[(1) Report 15138: See report no. 914 and the commentary on it.]]

1512[19]: Ibn Humayd told us, saying: Hakkam related to us, from Abu al-Junayd, from Ja'far ibn Abi al-Mughira, who said: I asked Sa'id ibn Jubayr about the tablets, of what material were they? He said: They were of a ruby, with writing in gold. The All-Merciful wrote them with His hand, and the people of the heavens heard the scratching of the pen as He wrote them.

1512[20]: Al-Harith told me, saying: Al-Qasim told us, saying: Abd al-Rahman related to us, from Muhammad ibn Abi al-Wadah, from Khusayf, from Mujahid or Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: The tablets were emerald. When Moses threw down the tablets, the guidance and mercy remained, and the detailed explanation was gone.

1512[21]: He said: Al-Qasim told us, saying: Al-Ashja'i related to us, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Khusayf, from Mujahid, who said: The tablets were of green emerald.

* *

Some claimed that the tablets were two tablets. If the one who said this is correct, then it is said: "And We wrote for him on the tablets," and they were two, just as it is said: ﴿If he has brothers﴾ [4:11], and they were two brothers. [[(2) See what was said about the plural and its meaning of two in what has preceded, 8:41-44, and the Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1:394.]]

* *

As for His words, "and he seized his brother by the head, dragging him towards him," this was an act of the Prophet of God, peace be upon him, out of his displeasure with his brother Harun for abandoning his followers and remaining among the Children of Israel in the place where he had left them. As God, may His praise be exalted, related of Moses' words to him: ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me? Did you then disobey my command?﴾ [20:92-93], when Harun informed him of his excuse and Moses accepted it. And that was Moses' saying to him: ﴿Do not seize my beard or my head. I feared that you would say, "You caused division among the Children of Israel and did not heed my word"﴾ [20:94]. And he said: "Son of my mother, the people deemed me weak and nearly killed me, so do not let the enemies gloat over me," to the end of the verse.

* *

The readers differed regarding the recitation of His words: "Son of my mother" (ya ibn umm).

The majority of the readers of Medina and some of the people of Basra recited it: ﴿Ya ibna Umma﴾, with a fatha on the "mim" of "umm."

* *

The majority of the readers of Kufa recited it: ﴿Ya ibna Ummi﴾, with a kasra on the "mim" of "umm."

* *

The grammarians of Arabic differed regarding the fatha and kasra of this word, while all of them agreed that both are dialects used among the Arabs.

Some grammarians of Basra said: It was said with a fatha because the two words were made into one name, as it is said: "Ya ibn amm" ("O son of my paternal uncle"). He said: This is an anomaly that is not to be analogized upon.

He said: As for the one who recited "Ya ibn Ummi," it is according to the dialect of those who say "hadha ghulamin qad ja'a" (this is a boy who has come), making it one name whose last letter is kasra, like the phrase "khaz-baz" (a kind of fly, whose two words are imitative sounds of a fly's buzzing, combined and built on the kasra, unchanged in the nominative, accusative, and genitive). [[(1) "Al-khazbaz" is a kind of fly; "khaz" and "baz" are two sounds from the buzzing of a fly, which were made into one word and built on the kasra, unchanged in the nominative, accusative, and genitive.]]

* *

Some grammarians of Kufa said: It was said "Ya ibn Umma" and "Ya ibn Amma" with a fatha, as the declinable noun is put in the accusative in some cases, as in "Ya hasratan" and "Ya waylatan" (O my regret! O my woe!). He said: It is as if they said "Ya ummah" and "Ya ammah" (O my mother! O my aunt!). They did not say this for "akh" (brother), but if it were said, it would be correct. He said: As for those who used the genitive with a kasra in this, it became so common in their speech that they dropped the "ya" (the first-person suffix). He said: The Arabs rarely drop the "ya" except from a vocative noun that the speaker attaches to himself, except for their saying "Ya ibn Umm" and "Ya ibn Amm," because these two are used frequently in their speech. When something not commonly used occurs, they retain the "ya," saying: "Ya ibn abi," "Ya ibn ukhti and akhi," "Ya ibn khalati," and "Ya ibn khali." [[(1) All of these are the statements of al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:394.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct position on this matter is that if you open the "mim" in "ibn umm," it is intended as a lament, meaning "Ya ibn ummah" (O son of my mother!), and likewise for "ibn amm." If you use the kasra, it is intended as an annexation (idafa), and the "ya" which is the pronoun of the speaker referring to himself has been dropped. Perhaps those who denied the comparison of this kasra when it is kasra to the kasra of the "zay" in "khaz-baz" did so because "khaz-baz" is not recognized for its second part except by its first, nor its first except by its second, so it became like imitative sounds.

Al-Yazidi (Yunus al-Jarmi) reported the feminine form of "umm" and of "amm" [in the vocative]. He said: it is not made a single word except with the masculine "ibn" (son). They said: but the good language and the sound analogy is the dialect of the one who says "O son of my mother" (yā ibna ummī) with the "ya" retained (yā ibna ummī, as the first person suffix is kept), as Abu Zubayd said:

O son of my mother, and O Shuqayq of my soul, you left me to a harsh age.

[Footnote 2 is in the original: Amali al-Yazidi 9; Jamharat ash'ar al-Arab: 139; al-Lisan (sh-q-q); Shawahid al-Ayni (margin of Khizanat al-Adab): 4: 222, and others. From a selected qasida, lamenting his nephew al-Lajlaj, and it is said he lamented his brother al-Lajlaj. The verse is also narrated: "O son of Khansa', split my soul, O Lajlaj, you left me to a harsh age." As for this narration, it is the narration of all the grammarians in their books in the chapter on the vocative. In it he says: "Every dead one I have forgiven, so I do not grieve for parent or child. Except that al-Lajlaj broke my wing on the day I parted from him at the high ground, in a tomb upon which lies a heavy burden of dust and piled stones, to the right of the road near Sadd Harran, calling by night, never answered, thirsty, seeking help, unaided; and he was the mainstay of the one who was saved." And his saying "Shuqayq" is the diminutive of "shaqiq," which means brother.]

And as the other said [footnote 1: he is Ghalfa' ibn al-Harith, who is Ma'd Yakrib ibn al-Harith ibn 'Amr ibn Hujr Akil al-Murar al-Kindi, and he is the paternal uncle of Imru' al-Qays ibn Hujr, the imam of poets. He was named "Ghalfa'" because he used to smear his head with musk. It is said he was the first to do so]:

O son of my mother! Had I witnessed you when you called upon Tamim while you were unanswered...

[Footnote 2: Naqa'id: 457, 1077; al-Wahshiyyat no. 213; al-Aghani: 12: 213. From a qasida in which he laments his brother Sharahbil ibn al-Harith, slain on the day of al-Kulab I (see the account in al-Naqa'id and al-Aghani). He says before it, and this is the opening of the poem: "My side is restless away from the bed, like the rubbing of a sick camel on the rough stones..." "...from a report that reached me, so my eye does not sleep and I cannot swallow my drink; a bitterness like poison that I conceal from people, upon hot ashes like a meteor, concerning Sharahbil, when the arrows passed over him in the time of his pleasure and youth... O son of my mother... I would have left the sword whose edges run with the blood of enemies on the day of al-Kulab; then I would have thrust from behind you until I reached the wide space, or my garments were stripped." And his saying "al-Asar" means a camel with a sore in its hindquarters which prevents it from kneeling except on level ground. "Al-Zirab" is the plural of "zarb" (with fatha then kasra), meaning stones that protrude from a mountain or a ruined land, whose protruding tip is sharp. "Al-Mallah" (with fatha on the mim) is hot ash.]

These [people] kept the "ya" in "umm" because it is not being addressed; the one addressed is only "ibn" apart from it. The Arabs drop the "ya" from the vocative only when they add it to themselves, not when they add it to other than themselves, as we have explained. [Footnote 1: see Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1: 394.]

* *

It was said: Harun only said to Musa, peace be upon him, "O son of my mother," and did not say "O son of my father," though they were of one father and one mother, seeking his tenderness through the bond of the mother. [Footnote 1: see Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1: 394.]

* *

As for His saying, "Indeed, the people oppressed me and nearly killed me": by "the people" he means those who devoted themselves to worshipping the calf and said, "This is your god and the god of Musa," and who opposed Harun. Their oppression of him was their abandoning obedience to him and following his command, [footnote 2: see the explanation of "istad'afa" above, p. 76, note 1, and the references there] "and nearly killed me," meaning: they came close but did not do it. [footnote 3: see the explanation of "kada" above, 2: 218.]

* *

The readers differed regarding the recitation of His saying, "fa-la tushmit."

The readers of the cities recited it: ﴿So let not the enemies rejoice over me﴾, with a dammah on the "ta'" of "tushmit" and a kasrah on its "mim," from the expression "ashmata fulan fulanan bi-fulan," when he makes him glad in it with what the one who is gloated over dislikes.

* *

It is related from Mujahid that he recited it: ﴿fa-la tashmit bi al-a'da'﴾ (with a fatha on the "ta'" and a fatha on the "mim").

15142 - Abd al-Karim told me, saying: Ibrahim ibn Bashshar told us, saying: Sufyan told us, saying: Humayd ibn Qays said: Mujahid recited: ﴿fa-la tashmit bi al-a'da'﴾.

15143 - al-Muthanna told me, saying: Ishaq told us, saying: Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr told us, from Ibn 'Uyaynah, from Humayd, who said: Mujahid recited: ﴿fa-la tashmit bi al-a'da'﴾.

15144 - I was told on the authority of Yahya ibn Ziyad al-Farra', who said: Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah told us, from a man, from Mujahid, that he said: ﴿la tushmit﴾. [Footnote 1: The report 15144 was narrated by al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 394, and he said regarding "from a man": "I think he is al-A'raj," meaning Humayd ibn Qays al-Makki mentioned in the two preceding chains.]

* *

Al-Farra' said: al-Kisa'i said: "I do not know; perhaps they meant: fa-la tashmit bi al-a'da'," and if it is sound, it has parallels. The Arabs say "faragha and farigha": whoever says "faragha" says "ana afrughu," and whoever says "farigha" says "ana afraghu," and likewise "rakina and rakana," and "shamilahum amr" and "shamalahum," [footnote 2: in the printed and manuscript texts: "rakabat wa rakabat," the correct form being in al-Farra's Ma'ani] [footnote 3: in Ma'ani: "wa shamalahum sharr"] in much speech. He said: "al-a'da'" is in the nominative, because the verb belongs to them, for whoever says "tashmat" or "tashmit." [Footnote 4: Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1: 394.]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The reading which I do not consider permissible to recite except with it is the reading of those who recited: ﴿fa-la tushmit﴾ with a dammah on the first "ta'" and a kasrah on the "mim," from "ashmatu bihi 'aduwwahu, ushmituhu bihi" (I made his enemy rejoice over him), with the "al-a'da'" in the accusative, because the proof of the readers of the cities agrees upon it, and what opposes it is an anomalous reading, and that suffices as evidence against whatever opposes it. This is in addition to the denial by the general body of scholars of knowledge of Arabic speech of the phrases "shamita fulan fulanan bi-fulan" and "shamita fulan bi-fulan yashmat bihi." What is known in their speech, when they report the gloating of a man over his enemy, is "shamita bihi" (with a kasrah on the mim) in the past tense, and "yashmat bihi" with a fatha in the future.

* *

As for His saying, "and do not place me with the wrongdoing people," this is the statement of Harun to his brother Musa. He means: do not place me, in your anger at me and your punishment of me, where I am placed with one who disobeyed you, opposed your command, and worshipped the calf after you, thereby wronging himself and worshipping other than the One who alone deserves worship, while I did not follow them in any of that, as:

15145 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr told me, saying: Abu 'Asim told us, saying: 'Isa told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "and do not place me with the wrongdoing people," he said: "the companions of the calf."

15146 - al-Muthanna told me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah told us, saying: Shibl told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verse 151–152:

The explanation of His words: ﴿He said, "My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, for You are the most merciful of the merciful."﴾ (151)

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: He, exalted is His remembrance, says: Musa said, when the excuse of his brother became clear to him, and he knew that he had not neglected the duty that was incumbent upon him from the command of God, in the commission of what the ignorant worshippers of the calf had done, "My Lord, forgive me," seeking forgiveness for his deed toward his brother, and for his brother from a past lapse that had occurred between him and God [[(1) In the printed edition: "min sālif lahu" (from a past lapse of his), omitting "salaf", which is from the manuscript.]] — that You veil our sins with a covering by which You conceal them [[(2) See the explanation of "al-maghfirah" in the glossary of language under (ghafara).]] — "and admit us into Your mercy," meaning: have mercy upon us with Your vast mercy, us Your believing servants, for You are more merciful to Your servants than anyone who shows mercy to anything.

* *

The explanation of His words: ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf [as a deity] will attain anger from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world. Thus do We recompense the fabricators.﴾ (152)

Abu Ja'far said: He, exalted is His remembrance, says: "Indeed, those who took the calf" as a god, "will attain anger from their Lord," by God hastening that for them [[(3) See the explanation of "nāla" in what preceded, 12:408, note 3, and the references there.]], "and humiliation," which is disgrace, as the punishment of God upon them for their disbelief in their Lord, "in the life of this world," in the hastened part of the world before the deferred part of the Hereafter.

* *

Ibn Juraij used to say concerning this:

15147 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, concerning His words: "Indeed, those who took the calf will attain anger from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world. Thus do We recompense the fabricators," he said: This applies to those among those who took the calf who died before Musa, peace be upon him, returned, and to those among them who fled when Musa commanded them that they kill one another.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: What Ibn Juraij said, although it is an opinion that has some basis, the apparent meaning of the Book of God, together with the interpretation of most of the exegetes, contradicts it. That is because God related generally, concerning those who took the calf, that anger from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world would attain them. And the reports from the exegetes among the Companions and the Successors were widely transmitted that when God turned back to the Children of Israel with Musa, peace be upon him, He accepted the repentance of the calf-worshippers for their deed, as He informed of in His Book, quoting the words of Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿And when Musa said to his people, "O my people, indeed you have wronged yourselves by your taking of the calf, so repent to your Creator and kill yourselves"﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 54]. So they did what their Prophet commanded them. Thus God's command to them, to kill some of them, each other, was out of anger from Him toward them for their worship of the calf. So the killing of some of them by others was a humiliation for them and a disgrace with which God humbled them in the life of this world, and a repentance from them to God before it. No one has the right to make a report that the Book has stated in general terms applicable to a particular matter that the apparent meaning covers, without evidence from a proof of report or reason. We know of no report that requires transferring the apparent meaning of His words, "Indeed, those who took the calf will attain anger from their Lord," to a specific hidden meaning, nor is there any rational evidence for it, so that its apparent meaning would have to be referred to its inner meaning.

* *

As for His words, "Thus do We recompense the fabricators," they mean: just as We requited those who took the calf as a deity by inflicting anger upon them and abasement in the life of this world, for their disbelief in their Lord and their apostasy from their religion after their faith in God, so likewise We recompense everyone who fabricates against God, lies about Him, acknowledges the divinity of another, and worships something else besides Him of idols, after his affirmation of the oneness of God and after his faith in Him and His prophets and messengers and what was revealed, if he does not repent of his disbelief before being killed. [[(1) See the explanation of "al-ifticha'" in what preceded, 12:562, note 1, and the references there.]]

* *

A group of the exegetes said something similar to what we have said on this matter.

Those who said that:

15148 – Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Ayyub, who said: Abu Qilabah recited: "Indeed, those who took the calf will attain anger from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world," the verse, and said: It is a recompense for every fabricator that will exist until the Day of Resurrection: that God, mighty and majestic, will humiliate him.

15149 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu al-Nu'man Arim narrated to us, saying: Hammad ibn Zayd narrated to us, from Ayyub, who said: Abu Qilabah recited one day this verse: "Indeed, those who took the calf will attain anger from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world. Thus do We recompense the fabricators," and said: By God, it is for every fabricator until the Day of Resurrection.

15150 – ... He said: Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, from Thabit and Humayd: that Qays ibn Abbad and Jariyah ibn Qudamah entered upon Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: Tell us about this matter in which you are and to which you call: is it a covenant that the Messenger of God ﷺ made with you, or an opinion you hold? He said: What do you two have to do with this? Turn away from this! They said: By God, we will not turn away from it until you inform us! He said: The Messenger of God ﷺ made no covenant with me except a book in the scabbard of this sword of mine! He drew it out and took the book from the scabbard of his sword, and in it was: "Indeed there has never been a prophet except that he had a sanctuary, and I have declared Medina sacred as Ibrahim, peace be upon him, declared Mecca sacred. Weapons shall not be carried in it for fighting. Whoever introduces an innovation or shelters an innovator, upon him is the curse of God, the angels, and all people; no repentance or ransom will be accepted from him." When the two went out, one of them said to his companion: Do you not see this book? So they returned, left it, and said: We have heard God say, "Indeed, those who took the calf will attain anger from their Lord," the verse, and that the people have fabricated a lie, and we do not know but that humiliation will befall them. [[(1) Report 15150: In the printed edition the chain read: "qāla, ḥaddathanā Ḥammād, ʿan Thābit: anna Ḥumayd ibn Qays ibn ʿAbbād, wa-Ḥārithah ibn Qudāmah", while in the manuscript it read: "qāla ḥaddathanā Ḥammād ʿan Thābit wa-Ḥumayd ibn Qays ibn ʿAbbād, wa-Ḥārithah ibn Qudāmah". The word "Ḥārithah" is unpointed. Both are errors, and the correct form is what is recorded here. "Ḥammād" is Ḥammād ibn Salamah, a reliable and well-known narrator who has passed several times. "Thābit" is Thābit ibn Aslam al-Bunani, who has passed several times.

"Ḥumayd" is Ḥumayd al-Ṭawīl, namely Ḥumayd ibn Abi Ḥumayd, the well-known imam, who has passed several times, and he was the maternal uncle of Ḥammād ibn Salamah.

As for Qays ibn Abbad al-Qaysi al-Dab'i, he is reliable but rarely narrates hadith; al-Hasan narrated from him. He came to Medina in the caliphate of Umar. He is among those whom al-Hajjaj killed among those who rebelled with Ibn al-Ash'ath. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, Ibn Sa'd 7/1/95, al-Kabir 4/1/145, Ibn Abi Hatim 3/12/101, and in al-Isabah in its third section.

See nos. 615, 872, 874, 954, 962, 1037, 1297, 1306, and none of them mentions "Jariyah ibn Qudamah." Nevertheless, the report of Abu Ja'far is sound in its chain, so it seems these are two different incidents. 15151 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr narrated to us, from Ibn Uyaynah, concerning His words: "Thus do We recompense the fabricators," he said: Every possessor of innovation is humiliated.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verse 151–152:

The explanation of His words: ﴿He said, "My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, for You are the most merciful of the merciful."﴾ (151)

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: He, exalted is His remembrance, says: Musa said, when the excuse of his brother became clear to him, and he knew that he had not neglected the duty that was incumbent upon him from the command of God, in the commission of what the ignorant worshippers of the calf had done, "My Lord, forgive me," seeking forgiveness for his deed toward his brother, and for his brother from a past lapse that had occurred between him and God [[(1) In the printed edition: "min sālif lahu" (from a past lapse of his), omitting "salaf", which is from the manuscript.]] — that You veil our sins with a covering by which You conceal them [[(2) See the explanation of "al-maghfirah" in the glossary of language under (ghafara).]] — "and admit us into Your mercy," meaning: have mercy upon us with Your vast mercy, us Your believing servants, for You are more merciful to Your servants than anyone who shows mercy to anything.

* *

The explanation of His words: ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf [as a deity] will attain anger from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world. Thus do We recompense the fabricators.﴾ (152)

Abu Ja'far said: He, exalted is His remembrance, says: "Indeed, those who took the calf" as a god, "will attain anger from their Lord," by God hastening that for them [[(3) See the explanation of "nāla" in what preceded, 12:408, note 3, and the references there.]], "and humiliation," which is disgrace, as the punishment of God upon them for their disbelief in their Lord, "in the life of this world," in the hastened part of the world before the deferred part of the Hereafter.

* *

Ibn Juraij used to say concerning this:

15147 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, concerning His words: "Indeed, those who took the calf will attain anger from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world. Thus do We recompense the fabricators," he said: This applies to those among those who took the calf who died before Musa, peace be upon him, returned, and to those among them who fled when Musa commanded them that they kill one another.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: What Ibn Juraij said, although it is an opinion that has some basis, the apparent meaning of the Book of God, together with the interpretation of most of the exegetes, contradicts it. That is because God related generally, concerning those who took the calf, that anger from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world would attain them. And the reports from the exegetes among the Companions and the Successors were widely transmitted that when God turned back to the Children of Israel with Musa, peace be upon him, He accepted the repentance of the calf-worshippers for their deed, as He informed of in His Book, quoting the words of Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿And when Musa said to his people, "O my people, indeed you have wronged yourselves by your taking of the calf, so repent to your Creator and kill yourselves"﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 54]. So they did what their Prophet commanded them. Thus God's command to them, to kill some of them, each other, was out of anger from Him toward them for their worship of the calf. So the killing of some of them by others was a humiliation for them and a disgrace with which God humbled them in the life of this world, and a repentance from them to God before it. 15151 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr narrated to us, from Ibn Uyaynah, concerning His words: "Thus do We recompense the fabricators," he said: Every possessor of innovation is humiliated.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 7, verse 153:

The interpretation of His words: ﴿And those who committed evil deeds and then repented after them and believed—indeed your Lord, after them, is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (7:153).

Abu Ja'far said: This is an informing from Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, that He accepts from every penitent who turns to Him from a sin he has committed, whether his disobedience was minor or major, whether it was disbelief or other than disbelief, just as He accepted the repentance of the worshippers of the calf after their disbelief in Him by worshipping the calf and their apostasy from their religion. He, may His praise be exalted, says: And those who committed evil deeds, then returned to seeking the pleasure of Allah by turning back to what He loves in place of what He hates, and to what He is pleased with in place of what He is angered by, after their evil deeds, and believed that Allah accepts the repentance of sinners and turns in forgiveness toward those who turn back to Him, with the sincerity of their hearts and certainty on their part of that— ﴿Forgiving﴾ to them, meaning: concealing their evil deeds from them and not exposing them by them; ﴿Merciful﴾ to them, and to everyone who was like them among the penitents. [[(1) See the explanation of the words of this verse in the lexical indexes.]]

**The interpretation of His words:** ﴿And when the anger subsided from Moses, he took up the tablets, and in their inscription was guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words "And when the anger subsided from Moses," the Exalted means: when it ceased from him and calmed down. [[(2) In the printed edition: "And when Moses restrained himself from anger," which is an interpretation by the editor of the first printed edition, and it is not correct. The manuscript omitted the explanation of the phrase, and it reads thus: "And when the anger subsided from Moses, and likewise every one who restrains (kāff)..." The explanation that the first editor adopted is one mentioned by al-Zajjaj, who said: "It means: when it calmed down. It has also been said: it means: when Moses ceased from anger, by inversion (qalb), as they say: 'I put the cap on the head,' meaning: 'I put my head into the cap.' He said: The first view, whose meaning is 'calmed down,' is the view of the grammarians (ahl al-'Arabiyya)." If Abu Ja'far had intended it, he would have explained it as al-Zajjaj did, but I preferred to set down the explanation of Abu 'Ubaydah in Majaz al-Qur'an 1: 229, because what follows it is Abu 'Ubaydah's statement in Majaz al-Qur'an.]]

* *

And likewise, everyone who restrains from something is said to be "silent about it" (sākit 'anhu). The one who is silent from speech is called "silent" (sākit) only because he restrains himself from it. [[(1) See Majaz al-Qur'an by Abu 'Ubaydah 1: 229.]]

It is related from Yunus al-Jurmi that he said: it is said, "Sorrow fell silent about him (sakata 'anhu al-huzn)," and everything, so he claimed, [is said in this way]. From it is the verse of Abu al-Najm:

*"The viper was about to glide away, and the dove fell silent from crying out."* [[(3) I have not found the two verses. In the printed edition it read "tasbaha" and "tadbaha," which is an error and corruption. Abu al-Najm has many verses of rajaz in this meter, but I did not find the rajaz in full. The correct reading of what was in the manuscript is what I have recorded.]]

* *

[The phrase] "He took up the tablets" means: he took them up after he had thrown them down, and some of them had been lost. [The phrase] "and in their inscription was guidance and mercy" means: and in what was copied (nusikha) in them, that is, what was written in them. [[(4) See the explanation of "nuskha" above, 2: 472. In the printed edition, in place of "that is, what was written in them," it read: "that is, from them," which was a failure to read the manuscript correctly, since the copyist wrote in a small hand at the end of the line, so the words ran together and his writing became unclear.]] [The word] "guidance" is an explanation of the truth. [The phrase] "and mercy for those who fear their Lord" means: for those who fear God and dread His punishment for their disobedience. [[(5) See the explanation of "guidance" above in the indexes of language (hudā).]]

* *

The grammarians (ahl al-'Arabiyya) differed over the reason for the entry of the preposition "lām" in His words "for their Lord they dread," given that the Arabs disapprove of saying in speech "rahibtu laka" in the sense of "rahibtuka" (I feared you), and "akramtu laka" in the sense of "akramtuka" (I honored you).

Some of them said: it is like His saying, may His praise be exalted: ﴿If you are able to interpret dreams﴾ [Surah Yusuf: 43], where the verb is connected by "lām."

And some of them said: [it means] "because of their Lord they dread."

And some of them said: it entered after the idāfa (the genitive construction), [meaning]: "those who are dreading their Lord" (alladhīna hum rāhibūna li-rabbihim), and "those who fear their Lord" (rāhibū rabbihim); then the "lām" was introduced on this sense, because it comes after the idāfa, not on the basis of taklīf. [[(1) In the printed edition it read "not on the basis of ta'līq" (attachment). I have kept what is in the manuscript, and it seems he means by "taklīf" the sense of "ta'līq," because "taklīf" means "imposition" (taḥmīl). I did not find the explanation of this term anywhere else, and perhaps it is from the terminology of some early grammarians.]]

* *

And some of them said: he only did that because the noun came before the verb, so the introduction of "lām" was fine.

* *

And others said: a similar case has come with the postponement of the noun in His words: ﴿Some of what you are seeking to hasten has drawn near to you﴾ [Surah al-Naml: 72]. [[(2) See what has passed, 6: 511 / 7: 164, and Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1: 233.]]

* *

It is related from 'Isa ibn 'Umar that he said: I heard al-Farazdaq say: "I counted out for him a hundred dirhams (naqadtu lahu mi'at dirham)," meaning: "I counted out to him a hundred dirhams." [[(3) Al-Farra' transmitted it in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 233 from al-Kisa'i, who said: "I heard some of the Arabs say: naqadtu lahā mi'atan dirham, meaning: naqadtuhā mi'atan, for a woman he married."]] He said: and the speech is broad.

**The Interpretation of His Words (Exalted is He):** ﴿And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time. So when the earthquake seized them, he said, "My Lord, if You had willed, You could have destroyed them before, and me too."﴾

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is He says: Moses chose from his people seventy men for the appointed time and the term that Allah promised to meet him with them,[[(1) See the explanation of "al-Miqat" (the appointed time) above, 3:553–555 / 13:87, 90.]] to repent for what their foolish ones had done regarding the calf, as related:

1515152. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: Allah commanded Moses (peace be upon him) to come to Him with some people of the Children of Israel who would apologize to Him for worshipping the calf. He promised them a meeting, so Moses chose seventy men from his people, by his own selection, and went with them so that they might apologize. When they came to that place, they said: "We will not believe you, O Moses, until we see Allah plainly, for you have spoken to Him, so show Him to us!" Then the thunderbolt seized them and they died. Moses stood weeping, calling upon Allah and saying: "My Lord, what shall I say to the Children of Israel when I come to them, having destroyed their best? If You had willed, You could have destroyed them before, and me too!"[[(2) The report 1515152 has been given in full above as no. 958, see its sources there.]]

1515153. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: Moses chose from the Children of Israel seventy men, the best of the best, and said: "Go to Allah, repent to Him for what you have done, ask Him to accept the repentance of those you left behind of your people, fast and purify yourselves, and wash your garments!" So he went out with them to Mount Sinai, at the appointed time that his Lord had set for him. He would not come to Him except by His permission and knowledge. The seventy said, as was related to me, when they had done what he commanded them and set out with him to meet their Lord, to Moses: "Ask for us that we may hear the speech of our Lord!" He said: "I will do so." When Moses drew near the mountain, a column of cloud descended upon it until it covered the whole mountain. Moses drew near and entered it, and said to the people: "Come near!" When Moses was spoken to by Allah, a bright light would fall upon his forehead, which no human could look upon. So a veil was set between him and them. The people drew near until, when they entered the cloud, they fell prostrate, and they heard Him speaking to Moses, commanding and forbidding: "Do this, and do not do that!" When Allah finished His command, the cloud cleared away from Moses, and he came to them. They said to Moses: "We will not believe you until we see Allah plainly!" So the earthquake, which is the thunderbolt, seized them, and their souls departed,[[(1) In the printed edition: "...the cloud cleared away from Moses..." differing from the manuscript; this is as in the manuscript.]] [[(2) In the printed and manuscript editions: "fa-iltaqat arwahuhum" (their souls met), which has no meaning; the correct reading is what I have given: "uftultat nafsuhu" (passive), meaning he died suddenly. See above 2:87, note 1.]] and they all died. Moses (peace be upon him) stood, pleading with his Lord, calling upon Him and beseeching Him, saying: "My Lord, if You had willed, You could have destroyed them before, and me too! They have acted foolishly! Will You destroy those behind me of the Children of Israel?"[[(3) This report has been given as no. 957 above, see its sources there.]]

1515154. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: "And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time," he said: Allah had commanded him to choose seventy men from his people, so he chose seventy men and set out with them to supplicate their Lord. Among what they supplicated to Allah, they said: "O Allah, give us what You have not given anyone after us!" Allah disliked this from their supplication, so the earthquake seized them. Moses said: "My Lord, if You had willed, You could have destroyed them before, and me too!"

1515155. Ibn Wakic narrated to us, saying: Khalid ibn Hayyan narrated to us, from Ja'far, from Maymun, regarding "And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time," he said: For their appointed time which He had promised them.

1515156. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding "seventy men for Our appointed time," he said: He chose them for the completion of the promise.

* * *

Others said: The earthquake only seized them because of their claim against Moses that he had killed Harun.

Mention of those who said this:

1515157. Ibn Bashshar and Ibn Wakic narrated to us, both saying: Yahya ibn Yaman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, saying: Abu Ishaq narrated to me, from Umarah ibn Abd al-Salluli, from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: Moses, Harun, Shabbar and Shabbir set out and went to the foot of a mountain. Harun lay down to sleep on a couch, and Allah took his soul. When Moses returned to the Children of Israel, they said to him: "Where is Harun?" He said: "Allah has taken him." They said: "You killed him, out of envy for his character and his gentleness" – or words similar to this. He said: "Choose whom you wish!" So they chose seventy men. He said: That is His saying: "And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time." When they came to him, they said: "O Harun, who killed you?" He said: "No one killed me, but Allah took me!" They said: "O Moses, you will never disobey again after today!" He said: So the earthquake seized them. He said: Moses began turning right and left, saying: "My Lord, if You had willed, You could have destroyed them before, and me too. Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did? This is only Your trial, by which You lead astray whom You will and guide whom You will." He said: So Allah brought them back to life and made them all prophets. [[The report: 1515157 – "Umarah ibn Abd al-Sallulі" is the brother of "Sulaym ibn Abd al-Sallulі" and "Zayd ibn Abd al-Sallulі." Al-Ajli said: "They are three brothers: Sulaym ibn Abd, Umarah ibn Abd, and Zayd ibn Abd, trustworthy, Sallulis, Kufans." He related from Ali and Hudhayfah. Only Abu Ishaq al-Hamdani related from him. Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: "Umarah ibn Abd is sound in narration; only Abu Ishaq relates from him." Abu Hatim said: "An unknown shaykh whose narration is not used as proof." He is biographed in Ibn Sa'd 6:158, Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/367, and Mizan al-I'tidal 2:248, and was mentioned in the note on no. 8754.
Ibn Kathir mentioned this report in his Tafsir 3:561–562, saying: "This is a very strange report, and I do not know this Umarah ibn Abd." But it has become clear from what I have mentioned that he is known, and that Ibn Kathir did not fully investigate. Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur 3:128, attributing it to Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in his book "Man 'Ashа Ba'd al-Mawt," Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh. I did not find it in the printed edition of "Man 'Ashа Ba'd al-Mawt," which indicates that the printed copy is deficient.]]

1515158. Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from a man of the Banu Sulul, that he heard Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) say regarding this verse: "And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time," he said: Harun had a good character and was beloved among the Children of Israel. He said: When he died, Moses buried him. He said: When he came to the Children of Israel, they said to him: "Where is Harun?" He said: "He died!" They said: "You killed him!" He said: So he chose seventy men from them. He said: When they came to the grave, Moses said: "Were you killed, or did you die?" [Harun] said: "I died!" So they were struck down, and Moses said: "My Lord, what shall I say to the Children of Israel? When I return they will say: 'You killed them!'" He said: So they were brought back to life and made prophets.

1515159. Abdullah ibn al-Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to us, saying: al-Rabi' ibn Habib narrated to us, saying: I heard Abu Sa'id – meaning al-Raqashi – recite this verse: "And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time," and he said: They were the sons of those who were beyond twenty and did not exceed forty, because a person of twenty has lost his ignorance and youth, and one who has not exceeded forty has lost nothing of his intellect. [[(1) The report 1515159 – I have not found a biography of "Abdullah ibn al-Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal." His father is "al-Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal al-Anmati," who has appeared many times before.
"al-Rabi' ibn Habib al-Hanafi," "Abu Sa'id." He related from al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, and Abu Ja'far al-Baqir. Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, Yahya al-Qattan, and Abd al-Samad ibn Abd al-Warith related from him. Ahmad and Yahya declared him trustworthy. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/1/253, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/457. "Abu Sa'id al-Raqashi" is, in my estimation, "Qays, mawla of Abu Sasan Hudayn ibn al-Mundhir al-Raqashi," and Abu Sa'id narrated little. He is biographed in Ibn Sa'd 7/1/154, al-Kabir 4/1/151, and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/106. There is also another "Abu Sa'id al-Raqashi," of Basra, who was "Bayan ibn Jundub al-Raqashi," who related from Anas. He is biographed in al-Kabir 1/2/133, Ibn Abi Hatim 1/1/424, and Lisan al-Mizan 2:69. Ibn Hibban said in al-Thiqat: "He makes mistakes."]]

* * *

Others said: The people were only seized by the earthquake because of their failure to separate themselves from the worshippers of the calf, and not because they themselves were among its worshippers.

Mention of those who said this:

1515160. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: "And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time," and he recited until he reached: "for the foolish ones among us." It was mentioned to us that Ibn Abbas used to say: The earthquake only overtook them because they did not separate from the people when they set up the calf, and they disliked joining them in it.

1515161. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding His words: "And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time," (they were) among those who had not said that statement, but they had not joined them in it, so the earthquake seized them because they had not separated themselves from their people when they took the calf. He said: When they went out and supplicated, Allah caused them to die, then brought them back to life. When the earthquake seized them, he said: "My Lord, if You had willed, You could have destroyed them before, and me too. Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?"

1515162. Al-Harith narrated to me, saying: Abd al-'Aziz narrated to us, saying: Abu Sa'd narrated to us, saying: Mujahid said: "And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time" – and "al-miqat" means the promise. When the earthquake seized them, after Moses had gone out with the seventy of his people, supplicating Allah and asking Him to remove the affliction from them, and He did not respond to them, Moses knew that they had committed the same sin that their people had committed. – Abu Sa'd said: [in the manuscript and printed edition: "Ibn Sa'd said"; the correct reading is what I have given, as in the chain above] – Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi narrated to me, saying: He did not respond to them because they had not forbidden the wrong and commanded the right. He said: So the earthquake seized them, and they died, then Allah brought them back to life.

1515163. Ibn Wakic narrated to us, saying: Abu Usamah narrated to us, from Awn, from Sa'id ibn Hayyan, from Ibn Abbas: that the seventy whom Moses chose from his people were only seized by the earthquake because they did not approve of the calf and did not forbid it.

1515164. Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Awn narrated to us, saying: Sa'id ibn Hayyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abbas, similarly.

* * *

The scholars of Arabic grammar differed on the grammatical construction of His words: "qawmahu sab'īna rajulan li-miqatina" (his people, seventy men, for Our appointed time). Some of the grammarians of Basra said: The meaning is: "And Moses chose from his people seventy men." When the preposition "min" (from) was dropped, the verb took effect directly, as the poet al-Farazdaq said:

"And among us is the one chosen for men's nobility and generosity, when the blustering winds blow."[[(1) His Diwan: 516; al-Naqa'id: 696; Sibawayh 1:18; al-Kamil 1:21; Amali al-Shajari 1:186; al-Khizanah 3:669, 672; al-Lisan (kh-y-r) and many others. This is the first qasidah in which he countered Jarir, mentioning the virtues and glories of his people, the Banu Tamim. By this verse he meant his father Ghalib, one of the generous men of Banu Tamim. Then he said after it:
"And among us is the one who gave the Messenger a gift: captives of Tamim, while eyes were still weeping." He means al-Aqra' ibn Habis, who spoke to the Messenger of Allah concerning the people of the chambers, who were the Banu Amr ibn Jundub ibn al-Anbar ibn Amr ibn Tamim, and the Messenger returned their captives. Then he elaborated on their glories.]]

And as another said:
"I commanded you the good, so do what you were commanded, for I have left you possessing wealth and property."[[(2) It is by al-A'sha Tarud: Iyas ibn Amir ibn Sulaym ibn Amir. This verse is also reported in poetry attributed to Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib, to al-Abbas ibn Mirdas, to Zur'ah ibn al-Sa'ib, and to Khifaf ibn Ghudbah (al-Khizanah 1:166).]]

Diwan al-A'sha: 284; Sibawayh 1:17; al-Mu'talif wa'l-Mukhtalif: 17; al-Kamil 1:21; Amali al-Shajari 1:265 / 2:240; al-Khizanah 1:164–167; and many others. Whoever attributes it to al-A'sha Tarud says after several verses describing his father's advice to him:
"I have gathered upon the people noble deeds of old, and my father warned me of what they guard against.
He said to me the words of one with knowledge and experience, of the past affairs of time and its eras.
I commanded you the right course, so do what you were commanded, for I have left you possessing wealth and property.
Do not be stingy with wealth in what is due for it, in other than the fault of extravagance, and do not waste it.
For its heirs will never praise you for it when they bury you between the clay and the wood."
(Al-Tagharrub: destruction, meaning the destruction of wealth where it is not due. It is also narrated as "dhu mal wa dhu nasab" with the letter sin, which is better, since "nashab" is the wealth itself. His saying "bayn al-nashab wa'l-khashab" means what is spread over him in his grave of clay and wood.)

As for the poetry attributed to Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib or others, it is:
"I have gathered upon the people noble deeds of old, and my father warned me of what they guard against.
He said to me the words of one of judgment and capability, experienced, wise, free of doubt.
You have attained glory, so beware lest you soil it: a noble father, and a grandfather not disreputable.
I commanded you the good ............................
And leave the characters of a people who have no portion, and aim for the characters of people of virtue and refinement.
And if you are called to treachery or commanded to it, then flee from it with yourself, in a headlong flight."

And al-Ra'i said:
"I chose you above the people when their characters had become base, and when the one from whom help was hoped had become ill-disposed."[[(1) I did not find this verse anywhere. In the printed and manuscript editions it reads "idh 'anat" with ayn and nun, which has no meaning. I think the correct reading is "ghathhat" with ghayn and thaa: one says "ghathutha fi khuluqika wa halika ghathathatan wa ghathuthan" when one's character and state become bad. "Al-ghath" is the bad of everything. "I'tall" means to seek pretexts to withhold a gift.]]

* * *

Some of the grammarians of Kufa said: It is only permitted for the verb to take effect upon them when "min" is omitted, because it is derived from your saying: "These are the best of the people" and "the best from among the people." When the annexation (idafah) was permitted in place of "min" and the meaning did not change,[[(2) In the printed and manuscript editions: "fa-idha jazat al-idafah" (if annexation is permitted); I have adopted the correct wording from al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an, which is his exact words.]] they permitted saying: "I chose you a man," and "I chose from you a man." And the poet said:[[(3) He is al-Ra'i al-Numayri.]]

"I said to him: choose her, a fat she-camel,"[[(4) Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shu'ara' by Ibn Sallam: 450, and what precedes it; Sharh al-Hamasah 4:37, and what precedes it; Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1:395 (this is his narration), and others. It is from a poem the al-Ra'i composed when a guest from the Banu Kilab came to him in a year of drought and barrenness, and he had no hospitality to offer. The Kilabi was on a she-camel which was old. Al-Ra'i ordered his nephew Habtar, who slaughtered it without the Kilabi knowing, and fed him its meat. Then al-Ra'i said in his qasidah, mentioning that he had looked at the Kilabi's she-camel:
"I saw her as a plump, sturdy one, a white camel among those who had grown fat on the trees.
So I winked a secret wink to Habtar, and by Allah, Habtar's two eyes! What a youth!
I said to him: Stick to the whiteness of her leg, for if the hamstring is set, the sinew will not stop."
Then Habtar rose to her with his weapon, going without being humiliated, and drew his sword.]]

كَأَنِّي وَقَدْ أشْبَعْتُهُ مِنْ سِنَامِهَا ... كَشَفْتُ غِطَاءً عَنْ فُؤَادِي فَانْجَلَى
(As if I, having fed him his fill from her hump, had lifted a veil from my heart, and it cleared.)

وهذا تصوير جميل جيد، لهذه الحادثة الطريفة. ثم قال: فَقُلْتُ لِرَبِّ النَّابِ: خُذْهَا فَتِيَّةً ... وَنَابٌ عَلَيْهَا مِثْلُ نَابِكَ فِي الحَيَا
(This is a fine and beautiful image for this amusing incident. Then he said: I said to the owner of the camel: take her, a young she-camel, and a mature camel like your mature camel in the year of rain.)

أي: خذ مكانها ناقة فتية، وناقة أخرى مسنة مثل نابك المسنة، يوم يأتي الخصب، وتحيي أموالنا.]] وقال الراجز: [[(١) هو العجاج.
(That is: take in her place a young she-camel, and another mature camel like your mature one, on the day the fertility comes and revives our property.]] And the rajaz poet said: [[(1) He is al-Ajjaj.

تَحْتَ الَّتِي اخْتَارَ لَهُ اللهُ الشَّجَرْ * [[(٢) ديوانه: ١٥، معاني القرآن للفراء ١: ٣٩٥، ومجاز القرآن لأبي عبيدة ١: ٢٢٩، اللسان (خير) ، ورواية الديوان، ومعاني القرآن: ((تحت الذي)) . وهو من قصيدته في مدح عمر بن عبيد الله بن معمر التيمي، مضت منها أبيات كثيرة، انظر ما سلف ١٠: ١٧٢، تعليق: ٢، وهذا البيت في ذكر نبى الله صلى اله ﷺ أصحابه، وبيعتهم تحت الشجرة. وهي بيعة الرضوان في عمرة الحديبية، فذكر عهد رسول الله، وعهد الصديق، وعهد عمر، وعهد المهاجرين، وعهد الأنصار، ثم ذكر بيعة الرضوان فقال: وَعُصْبَةِ النَّبِيِّ إِذْ خَافُوا الحَصَرْ ... شَدُّوا لَهُ سُلْطَانَهُ حَتَّى اقْتَسَرْ
بِالْقَتْلِ أَقْوَامًا وَأَقْوَامًا أَسَرْ ... تَحْتَ الَّذِي اخْتَارَ لَهُ اللهُ الشَّجَرْ
وفي المخطوطة: ((تحت التي اختارها له الله)) ، وهو خطأ ظاهر، صوابه ما في المطبوعة.]]
(Under the one whom God chose for him from among the trees.)
(2) Diwanuhu (his Diwan): 15; Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1: 395; Majaz al-Qur'an by Abu 'Ubayda 1: 229; Lisan (kh-y-r). This is the version of the Diwan and of Ma'ani al-Qur'an: "taht al-ladhi" (under the one who). It is from his qasida praising Umar ibn Ubayd Allah ibn Ma'mar al-Taymi, many verses of which have passed; see above 10: 172, note 2. This verse mentions the Prophet ﷺ and his companions and their pledge under the tree, which was the Pledge of Ridwan during the lesser pilgrimage of al-Hudaybiyya. He mentions the covenant of the Messenger of God, the covenant of al-Siddiq, the covenant of Umar, the covenant of the Muhajirun, the covenant of the Ansar, and then mentions the Pledge of Ridwan, saying: "And the band of the Prophet when they feared confinement; they strengthened his authority until it was seized, / by killing some peoples and taking others captive, / under the one whom God chose for him from among the trees." In the manuscript it reads "taht al-lati ikhtarahā lahu Allah" (under the one that God chose for him), which is an obvious error; the correct reading is that of the printed edition.]]
بمعنى: اختارَها له الله من الشجر. [[(٣) انظر مجاز القرآن ١: ٢٢٩، ونصه: ((تحت الشجرة التي اختار له الله من الشجر)) .]]
(Meaning: God chose it for him from among the trees. [[(3) See Majaz al-Qur'an 1: 229, whose text reads: "under the tree that God chose for him from among the trees."]]

* *

قال أبو جعفر: وهذا القول الثاني أولى عندي في ذلك بالصواب، لدلالة "الاختيار" على طلب "من" التي بمعنى التبعيض، ومن شأن العرب أن تحذف الشيء من حَشْو الكلام إذا عُرِف موضعه، وكان فيما أظهرت دلالةٌ على ما حذفت. فهذا من ذلك إن شاء الله.

(Abu Ja'far said: In my view, this second opinion is closer to the correct meaning here, because "choosing" indicates the need for "min" (from) in the partitive sense, and it is the habit of the Arabs to omit a word from the middle of speech when its place is known and what remains shows what was omitted. This is one of those cases, God willing.)

* *

وقد بينا معنى "الرجفة" فيما مضى بشواهدها، وأنّها: ما رجف بالقوم وزعزعهم وحرّكهم، [[(١) في المطبوعة: ((ما رجف بالقوم وأرعبهم)) ، لم يحسن قراءة المخطوطة لأنها غير منقوطة، ولأنها سيئة الكتابة، فاجتهد واخطأ. وقد مضى اللفظ على الصواب فيما سلف، انظر التعليق التالي رقم: ٣، في المراجع.]] أهلكهم بعدُ فأماتهم، [[(٢) في المطبوعة، زاد ((واو)) فكتب: ((وأهلكهم)) عطفاً على ما قبله، فأفسد معنى أبي جعفر. وإنما أراد أبو جعفر أن الرجفة: إما أن تعقب الهلاك، وتصعق من تنزل به فتسلبه فهمه من شدة الروع.]] أو أصعقهم، فسلب أفهامهم. [[(٣) انظر تفسير ((الرجفة)) فيما سلف: ١٢: ٥٤٤، ٥٤٥، ٥٦٦.]]

(We have already explained the meaning of "ar-rajfa" (the quake) earlier, with its evidence, and that it is: that which shook the people, unsettled them and stirred them, [[(1) In the printed edition: "that which shook the people and terrified them." The editor did not read the manuscript well, because it is unpointed and poorly written, so he guessed and erred. The wording was given correctly earlier; see the next note, no. 3, in the references.]] then destroyed them, causing them to die, [[(2) In the printed edition, a waw has been added, writing "wa-ahlakahum" (and destroyed them) as a conjunction with what precedes it, which spoils Abu Ja'far's meaning. Abu Ja'far meant that the quake either follows the destruction, and strikes down the one upon whom it descends, depriving him of his understanding from the severity of the terror.]] or struck them unconscious, depriving them of their faculties. [[(3) See the explanation of "ar-rajfa" earlier: 12: 544, 545, 566.]]

* *

وقد ذكرنا الرواية في غير هذا الموضع وقول من قال: إنها كانت صاعقة أماتتهم. [[(٤) انظر ما سلف قديماً ٢: ٨٤ - ٩٠، ثم ما سلف حديثاً ص: ١٤٠.]]

(We have mentioned the report in another place, and the view of those who said that it was a thunderbolt that caused their death. [[(4) See what passed long ago, 2: 84-90, then what passed recently, p. 140.]]

١٥١٦٥- حدثني محمد بن عمرو قال، حدثنا أبو عاصم قال، حدثنا عيسى، عن ابن أبي نجيح، عن مجاهد: "فلما أخذتهم الرجفة"، ماتوا ثم أحياهم.
(15165: Muhammad ibn 'Amr told me, he said: Abu 'Asim told us, he said: 'Isa told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "When the quake seized them" — they died, then God revived them.)

١٥١٦٦- حدثني المثنى قال، حدثنا أبو حذيفة قال، حدثنا شبل، عن ابن أبي نجيح، عن مجاهد: "سبعين رجلا لميقاتنا"، اختارهم موسى لتمام الموعد= "فلما أخذتهم الرجفة"، ماتوا ثم أحياهم الله.
(15166: al-Muthanna told me, he said: Abu Hudhayfa told us, he said: Shibl told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "seventy men for Our appointment" — Musa chose them to complete the appointed time — "when the quake seized them" — they died, then God revived them.)

١٥١٦٧- حدثني عبد الكريم قال، حدثنا إبراهيم قال، حدثنا سفيان قال، قال أبو سعد، عن عكرمة، عن ابن عباس: "فلما أخذتهم الرجفة"، قال: رُجف بهم.
(15167: 'Abd al-Karim told me, he said: Ibrahim told us, he said: Sufyan told us, he said: Abu Sa'd said, from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas: "When the quake seized them," he said: they were shaken.)
